Comparative
French laicite, US establishment clause, Turkey’s changing model — one contrast, precisely drawn.
Minority rights
T.M.A. Pai (2002) and Aligarh Muslim University (2024) on minority-institution status.
Value addition
Article 51A(e) — promoting harmony is a fundamental duty; a strong line to close on.

topics.q: Regionalism in India has been both a threat to and a resource for national integration. Critically examine.
body: Regionalism is the assertion of a territorially defined identity — linguistic, cultural, ethnic or economic — against a perceived centre.
India’s experience is that it is dangerous when denied and manageable when accommodated.
Its forms and drivers
• Identity-based:  linguistic reorganisation, the Dravidian movement, Assamese and Naga sub-nationalism — language and ethnicity seeking recognition.
• Development-based: Telangana (2014), Vidarbha and Bundelkhand rest on claims of internal neglect, not cultural difference.
• Sons-of-the-soil: job competition where in-migration meets a slow labour market — Shiv Sena’s Bombay, Assam 1979–85.
• Fiscal federalism: the newest form — southern States’ objection to devolution formulas and to post-2026 delimitation, which would penalise demographic performance.
Threat and resource
• As threat: insurgency where accommodation failed — Naga and Mizo before their accords; nativism; North–South polarisation.

• As resource: regional parties in national coalitions deepen democracy; diversity a unitary state would erode is preserved; and States compete on policy. The Mizo Accord (1986) turned the worst insurgency into the most peaceful State.

WAY FORWARD The toolkit is asymmetry — Article 371, the Sixth Schedule, autonomous councils and accords; plus fiscal fairness in Finance Commission design and inter-State forums. Regionalism becomes secession only when the constitutional route to recognition is closed — India’s federal success lies in having kept that route open, and its present test is whether fiscal and representational grievance can be met by the same method.
topics.draw: Nothing, or a two-column ‘threat / resource’ table with one named case in each cell. Named accords and Articles are what score here.
bank: Accords
Mizo 1986, Assam 1985, Punjab (Rajiv-Longowal) 1985, Bodo 2020, Naga Framework Agreement 2015.
Constitutional
Article 3 (state formation), Article 371A–J, Fifth and Sixth Schedules — asymmetric federalism.
Theory
Paul Brass on ethnicity and elite competition; Kohli on ‘crisis of governability’ and its resolution.
Regional parties
From 1989 onward they made coalition politics the norm — regionalism as a national stabiliser.
Delimitation
The post-2026 seat readjustment is the coming regionalism flashpoint — link to demographic transition.
Distinguish
Regionalism, sub-regionalism, sons-of-the-soil and secessionism are different things — separate them.

topics.q: Globalisation has produced both cultural homogenisation and a revival of regional identity. Examine.
body: Globalisation moves goods, images and people, so it acts on culture in two directions — standardising the market while making the local newly valuable. Both effects are real.
Homogenising pressures
• Consumption and media:       global brands and platforms; Ritzer’s ‘McDonaldisation’; English as the language of mobility, devaluing the vernacular.
• Language loss: UNESCO lists nearly 200 endangered Indian languages, transmitted less each generation.
• Craft and food: industrial substitutes displace handloom, and standardised diets displace millet and regional cuisine.
Revival and assertion
• Glocalisation: Robertson’s term — the global adapts to the local (regional menus, dubbed and regional-language streaming, festival marketing).

• Market for distinctiveness: GI tags — over 600 now — convert regional identity into income: Kanchipuram silk, Pochampally ikat, Darjeeling tea, Mithila painting. Tourism does the same for a monument or a festival.
• Digital vernacular: cheap data made Indian-language internet the fastest-growing segment, and regional cinema now reaches national audiences as regional cinema.

• Reactive identity: Castells’s ‘resistance identity’ — assertion intensifies precisely where homogenisation is felt, which is why language politics and cultural revivalism grow together with globalisation.

WAY FORWARD The question is not whether to resist but what to protect — mother-tongue early schooling (NEP), GI and handicraft market access, digitisation of oral traditions, and regional-language publishing. Globalisation does not erase local culture — it forces it to become explicit, marketed and politically self-conscious; what disappears is not distinctiveness but the unselfconscious practice of it.
topics.draw: Nothing, or a two-column ‘homogenising / reviving’ table. One theorist and one GI tag in each column are worth more than a diagram.
bank: Theorists
Ritzer (McDonaldisation), Robertson (glocalisation), Appadurai’s ‘scapes’, Castells on resistance identity.
GI
Over 600 registered GIs; the Act of 1999; Darjeeling tea as India’s first — one concrete instrument.
Language
NEP 2020’s mother-tongue medium; the Eighth Schedule; Bhasha Sangam and classical-language status.
Food
Millets’ revival and the International Year of Millets (2023) — local recovered through a global platform.
Diaspora
Diaspora demand sustains regional craft, cuisine and festivals abroad — globalisation as a preserver.
Caution
Distinguish cultural revival from cultural politics; the same energy can serve inclusion or exclusion.

topics.q: Migration in India is increasingly circular and increasingly climate-driven, yet policy still assumes permanent settlement. Examine.
body: Census 2011 counted about 450 million internal migrants; the Economic Survey’s Cohort-based Migration Metric put annual work-related movement near 9 million. Most is circular — seasonal, repeated, never registered at destination.
Why circular, and why climate

• The push is now partly climatic: drought in Bundelkhand and Marathwada, salinity in the Sundarbans, erratic rainfall shortening the season — climate rarely creates a new migrant; it accelerates an existing one.
• Circularity is rational: land, entitlements and social security do not travel — so the household splits itself rather than moving.
• Destination pull: construction, brick kilns and hospitality — contractor-mediated informal work offering no reason to settle.
Why policy misses them
• The address problem: PDS, health, schooling and housing are tied to residence, so the circular migrant is a nonperson at both ends — Covid-19’s return migration made this visible at national scale.
• Data: the Census undercounts short-duration movement, so the group is invisible in planning — the Working Group on Migration (2017) said so.
• Law: the Inter-State Migrant Workmen Act 1979 was barely enforced, now folded into the labour codes; e-Shram is a start.

WAY FORWARD Portability first — ONORC, portable health, school admission without domicile; rental housing (ARHC); migrant resource centres at both ends; and climate adaptation at source so migration is a choice, with loss-and-damage finance targeted at these districts. The migrant is not moving from one place to another but living in two — and every entitlement designed around a single address will keep missing him.
topics.draw: Two boxes, two curved arrows, one line beneath. Circularity must be drawn as a loop, never as a one-way arrow.
topics.figure: ◆ Circular migration — the household split in two lean season → SOURCE                                  DESTINATION land, ration card,                       wage work, no address, MGNREGA, family                              no entitlement ← harvest, festival, illness climate stress accelerates                   ONORC, ARHC, portable an existing move                          health and schooling he does not move from one place to another — he lives in two Two boxes and two arrows in opposite directions. The two-way arrow is the point most answers miss — draw it and cut the destination-pull bullet.
bank: Data
Census 2011, Economic Survey 2016–17 CMM, PLFS migration module, e-Shram registrations — name the source.
Theory
Lee’s push–pull, Todaro’s expected-income model, and the new economics of labour migration (risk diversification).
Corridors
Bihar/UP/Odisha → Delhi, Punjab, Gujarat, Kerala; Kerala’s Guest Worker/Awaz insurance scheme.
Climate
IPCC and the World Bank Groundswell projections; ‘climate refugee’ has no legal status — say so precisely.
Women
Left-behind women take on farm work (feminisation of agriculture) — and female migration is under-counted.
Urban
Migrants sustain city economies while being excluded from city planning — the peri-urban and housing link.

topics.q: The peri-urban interface is where India’s urbanisation is actually happening, and where governance is weakest. Examine.
body: The peri-urban is where a city’s land, labour and waste extend past its municipal boundary — neither village nor city in law. Census 2011 counted 3,894 census towns: urban by density and occupation, governed as panchayats.
What happens there
• Land converts faster than records: farmland is sold for plotted development ahead of any master plan — the result is built-up area with no trunk infrastructure.
• The city externalises costs: landfills, sewage, quarrying and polluting industry move outward; benefits stay in the core.
• Livelihood transition: farmers become plot-sellers, then service workers — compensation is one-time, the livelihood loss permanent.
• Ecology: wetlands and floodplains in this belt are built over — which is why urban flooding worsens.
Why governance fails

• Jurisdictional void: panchayats lack urban functions and revenue instruments, development authorities plan without accountability, and municipal boundaries lag reality by a decade. The 74th Amendment never reached this zone.
• Fiscal: census towns get rural budget norms for urban needs, so per-capita infrastructure spending falls exactly where growth is fastest.

WAY FORWARD Recognise census towns as statutory urban bodies with matching finance; plan at the metropolitan region scale by constituting the Article 243ZE Metropolitan Planning Committees; use land pooling instead of acquisition; notify blue-green assets before conversion; and add skilling and rental housing. India is not urbanising into its cities but around them — and until the planning unit becomes the region rather than the municipality, the fastest-growing part of urban India will keep being governed as a village.
topics.draw: Two concentric circles, the outer dashed, and three labels to the right. The dashed ring is the ungoverned zone.
topics.figure: ◆ The peri-urban gap peri-urban — urban in fact, rural in law census towns: 3,894 — panchayat-governed city                      landfill, sewage, quarry, municipal                       water extraction wetlands built over → urban flooding plan the region — Art. 243ZE Metropolitan Planning Committees A core circle and a dashed ring — the ring is the answer. Draw it and cut the ecology bullet, which the figure already carries.
bank: Definitions
Statutory town, census town, urban agglomeration, outgrowth — Census definitions; use them precisely.
Data
India’s urban share (31% in 2011) is understated because census towns are counted as rural in governance.
Cases
Gurugram’s private-developer urbanism, Bengaluru’s eastern belt, Kolkata’s east — one named case suﬀices.
Land
LARR 2013’s consent and SIA provisions; land pooling in Amaravati and Delhi as the alternative model.
Constitutional
Article 243Q, 243ZD/ZE — District and Metropolitan Planning Committees, largely unconstituted.
Reports
HPEC on urban infrastructure (2011), 2nd ARC on local governance, NITI’s urban planning capacity report (2021).

topics.q: Development-induced displacement has fallen disproportionately on tribal communities. Critically examine, with reference to the PVTGs.
body: Scheduled Tribes are 8.6% of the population but a far larger share of those displaced by dams, mines and protected areas — the resource frontier and the tribal habitat are the same geography. The 75 PVTGs are the most exposed.
Why the burden falls there
• Geography: the mineral and forest belt of central-eastern India coincides with Fifth Schedule areas.
• Weak tenure: customary and shifting cultivation was never recorded, so occupation without title reads as encroachment — the Xaxa Committee (2014) documented the under-compensation.
• Compensation mismatch: cash for land cannot replace a commons-based livelihood of forest produce, grazing and fishing.
• Conservation displacement: parks and tiger reserves displace too — the same eviction under a different justification.
The PVTG dimension, and the safeguards
• PVTGs — pre-agricultural technology, low literacy, stagnant population (Birhor, Baiga, Sahariya) — lose most, their livelihood least substitutable and their bargaining weakest.

• The safeguards exist: Fifth Schedule, PESA 1996 consent, FRA 2006 individual, community and PVTG habitat rights (s. 3(1)(e)), and LARR 2013’s consent and SIA. Niyamgiri (2013) made gram sabha consent decisive.
• The gap is implementation: CFR covers a fraction of eligible area, PVTG habitat rights are rare, and consent is procedurally diluted.

WAY FORWARD Complete CFR and habitat-rights recognition; make consent prior and substantive; move from cash to land-for-land and benefit-sharing (DMF, spent transparently); and run PM-JANMAN as habitat-based delivery. Displacement is not the price of development but a transfer from those least able to bear it — and Niyamgiri showed the law already contains the answer, if consent is treated as a right rather than a formality.
topics.draw: Nothing, or a three-column table — safeguard, what it guarantees, why it fails. The named Acts and Niyamgiri are what score.
bank: Committees
Xaxa (2014), Bhuria on PESA, and the Virginius Xaxa finding on displacement share — cite one.
Cases
Samatha (1997) on tribal land transfer in Scheduled Areas; Niyamgiri/Orissa Mining (2013).
Numbers
75 PVTGs across 18 States and the A&N Islands; ST share 8.6%; DMF collections under MMDR.
Conservation
Tiger reserve relocation and the FRA’s critical wildlife habitat provisions — the unresolved tension.
Schemes
PM-JANMAN (2023), Dharti Aaba Janjatiya Gram Utkarsh Abhiyan, Eklavya schools, TRIFED value chains.
Concepts
Displacement, dispossession and ‘development-induced displacement and resettlement’ (DIDR) — use the term.

topics.q: Constitutional and legal measures have delivered representation to Scheduled Castes more successfully than they have delivered equality. Examine.
body: The Constitution attacked caste on four fronts — Article 17, non-discrimination (15, 16, 29), reservation in legislatures, services and education, and Article 338 machinery. The record is uneven across them.
Where it has worked
• Political representation: reserved constituencies and panchayat seats give a continuous SC presence in every legislature — Ambedkar’s priority of political power is vindicated here.
• Employment and education: reservation created a first-generation salaried class; scholarships and hostels raised enrolment sharply.
• Assertion: autonomous Dalit mobilisation and literature is itself an outcome — what can be demanded has changed as much as what is delivered.
Where it has not
• The private sector: reservation does not reach private employment, and public-sector shrinkage narrows it — Thorat and Attewell demonstrated hiring discrimination directly.
• Assets: land ownership remains far below population share and business ownership lower still — representation was distributed; capital was not.
• Atrocity: exclusion persists in housing, water and marriage; PoA conviction rates stay low, and violence follows assertion.
• Within-group inequality: benefits concentrate in some sub-castes — which is what Davinder Singh (2024) permits States to address through sub-classification.

WAY FORWARD Enforce the PoA Act on conviction, not registration; extend anti-discrimination law to private employment and rental housing; spend SC sub-plan funds on assets and enterprise (venture funds, procurement preference) rather than stipends alone; and fill backlog vacancies. Reservation redistributed oﬀices faster than it redistributed assets or dignity — and the next phase of SC empowerment has to be fought where the state does not employ.
topics.draw: Nothing, or a two-column ‘worked / not worked’ table with one Article or case per row. Articles, the PoA Act and Davinder Singh are the value addition.
bank: Articles
17, 15(4), 16(4) and 16(4A), 46, 330, 332, 335, 338, 341 — name them precisely, not ‘several Articles’.
Cases
Indra Sawhney (1992), Nagaraj (2006), Jarnail Singh (2018), Davinder Singh (2024).
Ambedkar
‘Political democracy without social democracy is a life of contradictions’ — the closing quotation to carry.
Data
NCRB atrocity data, NFHS on untouchability practice, and land-ownership share from the Agriculture Census.
Manual scavenging
Prohibition Act 2013, NAMASTE scheme, and continuing sewer deaths — the sharpest illustration.
Comparative
US aﬀirmative action’s retreat and Brazil’s quotas — one comparison, used carefully.

topics.q: India will age before it becomes rich. Examine the implications and the policy response required.
body: The 60-plus share is projected to rise from about 10% in 2021 to over 20% by 2050 (India Ageing Report) — and Kerala and Tamil Nadu reach that level well before the Hindi belt. India ages unevenly, and at lower income than the countries that aged before it.
What makes Indian ageing distinctive
• Feminisation: women outlive men, so the elderly are majority female — widowhood, no income and low property ownership compound.
• Ruralisation: the young migrate and the old remain — left-behind elderly households where health infrastructure is weakest.
• No income security: most work is informal, so under a fifth of the elderly have a pension, and NSAP amounts are nominal.
• Morbidity shift: to NCDs, dementia and multi-morbidity — needing continuing care, while the system is built for episodic treatment.
The care gap
• The joint family is contracting while institutional care stays scarce, unregulated and stigmatised; care work falls on women, unpaid.
• Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act 2007 makes maintenance a legal duty enforceable through tribunals — a legal answer to a social change, and weakly used.

WAY FORWARD Universalise a meaningful pension floor and extend contributory coverage; build geriatric capacity into primary care under NPHCE and Ayushman Bharat’s over-70 cover; license home care with a trained workforce — care as employment, not only cost; and make housing and transport age-friendly. The demographic dividend and the ageing burden are the same population thirty years apart — which is why what India invests in its workers now determines whether ageing arrives as a crisis or as a transition.
topics.draw: Nothing, or a two-column table — the ageing South against the young North, with one number in each. This is the same figure as demographic transition; do not draw it twice.
bank: Data
India Ageing Report 2023 (UNFPA-IIPS), LASI (Longitudinal Ageing Study in India) — name one dataset.
Concepts
Old-age dependency ratio, feminisation and ruralisation of ageing, ‘ageing before affluence’, active ageing.
Law and schemes
MWPSC Act 2007, NPHCE, Atal Vayo Abhyuday Yojana, SACRED and Elderline (14567).
Comparative
Japan’s long-term care insurance and China’s post-one-child ageing — one comparison scores.
Care economy
ILO estimates on care-sector job creation — link ageing to employment policy, not only welfare.
Dignity

Elder abuse data (HelpAge), loneliness and digital exclusion — the qualitative dimension worth one line. PART III ◆ SYLLABUS FILLERS — the lines the sixty-six topics do not cover Compressed notes, not model answers. Each entry is the minimum you must be able to write if the paper turns to a syllabus line outside Parts I and II: the named specifics, the one analytical point that earns the mark, and the debate where one exists. GS-1’s currency is the name — monument, dynasty, movement, text, theorist, place — so these entries are deliberately dense with names and dates rather than with argument. A ◆ ART AND CULTURE Indus urbanism c. 2600–1900 BCE, over 1,000 sites, mostly in India post-1947. Grid plan on cardinal axes, citadel and lower town (Harappa, Mohenjo- daro, Kalibangan), standardised baked brick in a 1:2:4 ratio, covered drains with soak pits, the Great Bath, Mohenjo-daro’s granary, Lothal’s dockyard, Dholavira’s water reservoirs and signboard, Rakhigarhi the largest site. Craft: carnelian beads, steatite seals, the bronze dancing girl, standardised weights in binary ratios, cotton (sindon). Point: the civilisation is distinguished by municipal uniformity without monumental kingship — no palace, no temple, no royal tomb; its authority is inferred from standardisation, not from display. Decline: Ghaggar-Hakra desiccation, monsoon weakening, trade collapse, de-urbanisation into Cemetery H, Jhukar, Rangpur. Gupta classicism as political aesthetic c. 320–550 CE. Sculpture — Sarnath and Mathura schools, the Sarnath Preaching Buddha with transparent drap- ery and the halo; Deogarh Dashavatara temple with its Sheshashayi Vishnu panel; Ajanta’s Padmapani and Vajrapani murals. Architecture — the first structural stone temples, flat-roofed with a garbhagriha: Sanchi Temple 17, Tigawa, Bhitargaon in brick. Literature — Kalidasa, Vishakhadatta’s Mu- drarakshasa, Amarasimha; science — Aryabhata, Varahamihira; the Mehrauli iron pillar. Point: classicism is a political choice — restraint, symmetry and idealised form advertise an ordered polity, and the term ‘Golden Age’ is contested precisely because that order rested on land grants, growing caste rigidity and the decline of urban and guild economies (R. S. Sharma’s feudalism thesis). Painting traditions Prehistoric Bhimbetka; murals at Ajanta (fresco-secco, tempera), Bagh, Sittanavasal, Lepakshi (Vijayanagara), Kerala’s temple murals. Miniatures — Pala manuscript illumination, western Indian Jain Kalpasutra; Mughal (Persian technique + Indian naturalism; Basawan, Daswanth, Mansur’s birds); Rajasthani schools — Mewar, Bundi, Kishangarh’s Bani Thani, Kota hunting scenes; Pahari — Basohli’s bold colour, Guler and Kangra’s lyricism, Nainsukh; Deccan — Bijapur, Golconda, Ahmadnagar. Folk — Madhubani, Warli, Pattachitra, Kalamkari, Phad, Gond, Cheriyal. Modern — Company School, Raja Ravi Varma, Bengal School (Abanindranath, Nandalal Bose), Progressive Artists’ Group (Husain, Souza, Raza), Amrita Sher-Gil. Point: school = patron + pigment + subject; name all three when asked to distinguish. Literature, language, performing arts Sangam (Tolkappiyam, Ettuthogai, Pattupattu; akam and puram poetry; Silappadikaram and Manimekalai as the twin epics); classical Sanskrit (Kalidasa, Bhasa, Bhavabhuti, Banabhatta); Prakrit Gathasaptashati; Pali canon; Bhakti vernaculars. Classical lan- guages recognised: Tamil, Sanskrit, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam, Odia, and the 2024 additions (Marathi, Pali, Prakrit, Assamese, Bengali). Dance — Bharatanatyam, Kathak, Kathakali, Kuchipudi, Odissi, Manipuri, Mohiniyattam, Sattriya (8, per Sangeet Natak Akademi). Music — Hindustani and Carnatic; raga-tala; Sharngadeva’s Sangita Ratnakara; gharanas. Theatre — Koodiyattam (first UNESCO ICH from India), Yakshagana, Bhavai, Nau- tanki, Jatra, Ramlila. Point: for any ‘preservation’ question, the instruments are the Sangeet Natak and Sahitya Akademis, Guru-Shishya scholarships, UNESCO ICH listing (15 elements) and GI tags. Religion and philosophy Six darshanas — Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Samkhya, Yoga, Mimamsa, Vedanta; heterodox — Buddhism, Jainism, Ajivika, Char- vaka. Buddhist councils and schools (Theravada, Mahayana, Vajrayana); Jain sects (Digambara, Shvetambara), the five mahavratas, anekantavada and syadvada. Vedanta’s three schools (Shankara, Ramanuja, Madhva). Point: the heterodox challenge is best explained sociologically — it arose in the sixth century BCE with the second urbanisation, appealing to the vaishya trading class that ritual hierarchy subordinated. B ◆ MODERN INDIAN HISTORY
1857 as a social turning point

Causes — doctrine of lapse and annexation (Awadh, 1856), Enfield cartridge, revenue settlements dispossessing talukdars, disbanded soldiers of annexed states, missionary anxiety, and the disruption of artisanal livelihoods. Centres — Meerut, Delhi (Bahadur Shah Zafar), Kanpur (Nana Saheb, Tantia Tope), Jhansi (Lakshmibai), Lucknow (Begum Hazrat Mahal), Bihar (Kunwar Singh). Consequences — Government of India Act 1858 transferring power to the Crown, the end of the Company and of the Mughal title; the army reorganised on the ‘martial races’ and divide-and-balance principle; a policy of non-interference in religion and social custom that slowed reform for a generation; and the beginning of formal racial separation. The debate: ‘sepoy mutiny’ (Seeley) against ‘first war of independence’ (Savarkar) — the defensible position is that it was a popular revolt with feudal leadership and no national programme, whose importance is what it produced, not what it intended. Colonial education and the nationalist critique Charter Act 1813 (Rs 1 lakh for education); the Orientalist–Anglicist dispute settled by Macaulay’s Minute (1835) and Bentinck’s resolution; Wood’s Despatch (1854) — the ‘Magna Carta of English education’, creating departments, universi- ties (Calcutta, Bombay, Madras, 1857) and grants-in-aid; Hunter Commission 1882; Indian Universities Act 1904; Sadler and Sargent. The critique: downward filtration left mass literacy at about 16% in 1951; the curriculum produced clerks, not scientists; vernaculars and indigenous learning were defunded. The counter-current: the National Council of Education (1906), Kashi Vidyapith, Jamia Millia (1920), Gandhi’s Nai Talim (Wardha, 1937), Tagore’s Santiniketan. Point: colonial education created both the instrument of rule and the class that ended it — the standard ‘unintended consequence’ argument.
Indentured emigration — the girmitiyas

After the abolition of slavery (1833), the indenture system moved over a million Indians (1834–1917) to Mauritius, British Guiana, Trinidad, Fiji, Natal, Suriname and Malaya — ‘girmit’ from the agreement they signed. Conditions: five-year contracts, sex-ratio imbalance, penal sanctions for breach — ‘a new system of slavery’ (Hugh Tinker). Gokhale’s resolution and Gandhi’s South African campaign led to abolition in 1917. Point: indenture is the origin of today’s Indian diaspora in the Caribbean, Fiji and Mauritius, and the first issue on which Indian nationalism made an international argument — the direct ancestor of India’s later anti-apartheid position. Moderates, Extremists, revolutionaries Moderates (1885–1905) — Naoroji, Gokhale, Ranade, Mehta: constitutional agitation, the ‘prayer, petition, protest’ method, and economic critique as its weapon. Extremists — Tilak, Lala Lajpat Rai, Bipin Chandra Pal, Aurobindo: swaraj as birthright, boycott and self-reliance; Surat split 1907, reunion at Lucknow 1916. Revolutionaries — Anushilan and Jugantar; Savarkar’s Abhinav Bharat; the Ghadar Party (1913, San Francisco); HSRA, Bhagat Singh, Azad, the Assembly bomb (1929) and Why I am an Atheist; Surya Sen’s Chittagong armoury raid (1930). Point: the three streams are best read as a division of labour rather than a succession — each supplied what the others could not. Partition Causes — separate electorates (1909), the two-nation formulation, the League’s 1940 Lahore Resolution, the 1946 elections, Direct Action Day, the Cabinet Mission’s collapse, and the advancement of the date to 15 August 1947. The Radcliffe Line was published after independence. Consequences — 10–15 million displaced, up to a million dead, the largest migration in modern history; princely state accession problems (Kashmir, Hyderabad, Junagadh); Punjab and Bengal divided; the canal-water dispute leading to the Indus Waters Treaty (1960); refugee rehabilitation as independent India’s first administrative task. Point: Partition is remembered as an event and was experienced as a process — which is why oral- history work (Urvashi Butalia, Ritu Menon) changed the historiography. C ◆ WORLD HISTORY French Revolution Causes — fiscal crisis after American intervention, an estate system taxing the Third Estate, Enlightenment ideas (Rousseau, Voltaire, Montesquieu), bread prices. Sequence — Estates General and the Tennis Court Oath (1789), the Bastille, the Declaration of the Rights of Man, abolition of feudal privilege, the Constitution of 1791, the Republic, the Jacobin Terror, Thermidor, Directory, and Napoleon’s coup (1799). Exports — the Napoleonic Code, metric system, conscription and mass nationalism. Point: where the American Revolution was political and federal, the French was social and centralising — and it introduced the modern vocabulary of left and right, citizenship and nationalism. Legacy in India: ‘liberty, equality, fraternity’ enters the Preamble through Ambedkar, who attributed it to the Buddha rather than to France.

topics.t: Article 142 — Complete Justice and Its Limits
topics.q: Article 142 enables the Supreme Court to do complete justice; it does not authorise the Court to supply what the Constitution has deliberately left unsaid.
body: Examine.
Article 142 empowers the Court to pass any decree for complete justice in a cause before it. It fills a remedial gap in the case at hand — it is not a legislative competence.
Where it has been used well
• Divorce on irretrievable breakdown, which no statute permits — Shilpa Sailesh (2023).
• The Bhopal settlement; the Ayodhya decree; environmental directions where regulators failed; release of prisoners held beyond sentence.
• In each, a real party before the Court had a right without a remedy.
The limits the Court itself has drawn
• Prem Chand Garg (1963) and A. R. Antulay (1988) — Article 142 cannot override express statutory provisions or fundamental rights.
• SCBA (1998) — it cannot build a new edifice ignoring substantive law.
• In re Assent (20 Nov 2025) — Art 142 cannot create a time limit under Art 200 or invent deemed assent: a considered omission is policy space, not a gap.
topics.position: Confine the power to the parties and the cause; require reasons distinguishing a remedial from a legislative gap. The distinction is between a silence that is an oversight and a silence that is a decision — Article 142 reaches only the first.
topics.draw: The same fork, hand-drawn in four boxes. Write Prem Chand Garg and Antulay beside the left branch as the internal limits, and In re Assent 2025 beside the dashed branch.
topics.figure: ◆ Article 142 — the two silences constitutional / statutory silence oversight                                                     deliberate omission a right without a remedy                                                  policy space Art 142 reaches it                                              Art 142 cannot reach it Shilpa Sailesh, Bhopal, Ayodhya                                           In re Assent 2025 One node, two branches, one dashed. The dashed branch is the whole answer — and the 2025 reference is the case that put it there.
bank: Judicial overreach
Article 142 directions of general application are legislation without a legislature — the critique is institutional, not doctrinal.
Article 32 / PIL link
Continuing mandamus in PIL raises the same complaint — remedy without a party and supervision without a cause.
Curative jurisdiction
Rupa Ashok Hurra (2002) created the curative petition under Art 142 — the Court’s own remedy for its own error.
Environmental cases
Article 142 has repeatedly substituted for regulatory failure — the fix is a functioning regulator, not a wider power.
Federal dimension
Directions to States under Art 142 bypass the Union’s own constitutional route — In re Assent was decided on exactly this ground.
Comparative
No comparable general power exists in the US or UK — the closest analogue is equitable jurisdiction, which is confined to the parties.

topics.t: Article 143 — Presidential Reference and Constitutional Dialogue
topics.q: Article 143 enables constitutional dialogue between the President and the Supreme Court, but it must not become a substitute for ordinary adjudication. Explain.
body: Article 143 permits the President to refer a question of law or fact of public importance; the Court may report its opinion, obligatorily under 143(2) for pre-Constitution treaties. The opinion is advisory — no res judicata — yet carries the Court’s full authority.
How the jurisdiction has been used

• Delhi Laws Act (1951) on delegation; Berubari (1960), cession of territory needs an amendment; Kerala Education Bill (1958); Special Courts Bill (1978); Cauvery; the 2012 2G reference; and the 2025 reference on Articles 200–201.
Why the Court may decline, and should be cautious
• In the Ayodhya reference (1993) the Court returned the question as vague and unnecessary.

• The dangers are structural: no contest between real adversaries, so the Court decides on argument not facts; it may overtake pending adjudication; and it invites political questions dressed as legal ones. The 2025 reference revisited a decision already rendered inter partes.
topics.position: Appoint amici and hear affected States; answer only what is necessary; decline references that relitigate a decided matter.
topics.conc: Article 143 is a channel of dialogue between the branches — valuable while it clarifies the law, corrosive the moment it substitutes for deciding a case.
topics.draw: A two-way arrow between ‘President / Union executive’ and ‘Supreme Court’, with three boxes hanging below the arrow — ‘advisory, not res judicata’, ‘no contesting parties’, ‘must not relitigate a decided case’.
bank: 2025 assent reference
It followed the two-judge State of Tamil Nadu ruling — a five-judge opinion effectively overruling a judgment delivered inter partes.
Binding effect
Not res judicata, but Art 141 precedent value in practice — courts have followed advisory opinions without exception.
Comparative
Canada’s reference procedure is routine; the US Supreme Court refuses advisory opinions entirely as non-justiciable.
Federalism
References touching State powers must hear the States — otherwise the Union frames the question and the States get the answer.
Political questions
The Court’s discretion to decline is the safeguard; using it is what keeps Art 143 from becoming a political instrument.
Reform
Publish a settled practice on when references will be declined — predictability is the discipline the text does not supply.

topics.t: The Data Protection Board of India
topics.q: The credibility of a data-protection regime depends as much on the independence and capacity of its enforcement body as on the rights the law declares. Assess with reference to the Data Protection Board of India.
body: The DPDP Act 2023 creates the Data Protection Board as a digital by design adjudicator, empowered to inquire into breaches and penalise up to ₹250 crore. A rights statute is worth what its enforcer is worth.
The design weaknesses

• Appointment and tenure:      Central Government appointment, two-year renewable term — renewability being the standing threat to independence named in Madras Bar Association (2014) and Rojer Mathew (2019).
• Truncated mandate: an adjudicating body only — no regulation-making, no suo motu inquiry, no codes of practice, so it lacks the preventive arm regulators rely on.
• Scope: wide State exemptions under Section 17(2)(a) place a large class of processing outside its reach; appeal lies to TDSAT, a telecom tribunal.
• Capacity: digital-only functioning is an access barrier; no field presence, investigative cadre or independent budget.
topics.position: A plural selection committee with a judicial member; a fixed non-renewable tenure; suo motu and audit powers; a charged budget; offline filing; and a proportionality limit on the State exemption. A data-protection regime is credible only when the citizen believes a complaint will be decided by someone the government cannot remove.
topics.draw: Four-cell grid — rows ‘independence’ and ‘capacity’, columns ‘what the Act gives’ and ‘what it withholds’. Fill the withheld column: renewable tenure, no regulation-making, no suo motu, no budget.
bank: Section 44(3) / RTI
The same Act amended RTI s.8(1)(j) to exempt all personal information — enforcement weakness and transparency loss arrive together.
Comparative
The EU GDPR’s supervisory authorities have investigative, advisory and corrective powers; the Board has only the third.
Puttaswamy compliance
Blanket State exemptions fail the necessity and proportionality limbs of the four-part test.
Consent architecture
Consent managers are registered with the Board — an entire market regulated by a body with no rule-making power.
Children’s data
Verifiable parental consent and a ban on tracking need technical standards no one is empowered to issue.
Federalism
States are large data fiduciaries; a wholly Union-appointed Board adjudicating State processing raises a federal objection.

topics.q: When the State uses an algorithm to affect rights or entitlements, constitutional fairness requires notice, reasons, audit and human appeal. Analyse.
body: When the State uses an algorithm to decide eligibility, allocate a benefit or police a locality, it exercises public power whatever the technology. Automation changes the instrument, not the constitutional obligation.
What the Constitution already requires
• Article 14 forbids arbitrariness (Royappa (1974)); Maneka Gandhi (1978) makes fair procedure part of Article 21 — an adverse decision needs reasons an unexplainable model cannot supply.
• Puttaswamy (2017) requires legality, legitimate aim, proportionality and procedural safeguards — automated profiling on citizen databases engages every limb.
• Anita Kushwaha (2016) recognises access to justice as a facet of Article 21, which an unappealable automated denial defeats.
Where automation fails in practice

• Training data encodes past exclusion, so the model repeats old errors with new authority; vendor proprietary claims block audit; Aadhaar and eKYC mismatches turn a technical error into a denial of entitlement; and responsibility diffuses between oﬀicial and vendor.
topics.position: Four design obligations, not later additions — notice of automation; reasons in the person’s language; audit through impact assessments and retained logs; a human appeal on a statutory clock. The State may automate the process; it cannot automate the answerability.
topics.draw: The same one-to-four fan, and write the constitutional source under each duty — notice/reasons (Art 21, Maneka), audit (Art 14, Royappa), appeal (Anita Kushwaha).
topics.figure: ◆ Algorithmic decision — the four duties State uses an algorithm to affect a right notice it is        reasons in          audit: logs,        human appeal, automated          the person’s         bias, impact        statutory clock language Art 14 arbitrariness ◆ Art 21 fair procedure ◆ Puttaswamy proportionality design obligations, not later additions Four duties from one node with the constitutional source underneath. It works for AI in welfare, in policing and in the Data Protection Board question alike.
bank: India AI Governance Guidelines
They adopt exactly this framing — accountability, transparency and human oversight as procurement conditions.
Welfare exclusion
Aadhaar seeding mismatch is the commonest automated denial; Puttaswamy (Aadhaar) barred denial for authentication failure.
Predictive policing
Automated risk scoring imports historical policing bias into Art 21 liberty decisions — the highest-stakes use case.
Procurement as regulation
Banning unauditable black boxes at the tender stage regulates faster than any statute can.
DPDP interface
Automated decision-making has no dedicated right in the DPDP Act, unlike GDPR Article 22 — a drafting gap worth naming.
Accountability
Name a responsible oﬀicer for every deployed system — diffusion of responsibility is the actual failure mode.

topics.q: Recent judicial developments have moved reservation jurisprudence from formal group identity towards measured relative deprivation. Examine.
body: Indra Sawhney (1992) settled the framework under Article 16(4) — caste may identify a class, the creamy layer is excluded from OBC benefit, the ceiling is fifty per cent, no reservation in promotions.
The two structural changes since
• Janhit Abhiyan (2022) upheld EWS reservation (103rd Amendment), holding economic criteria permissible and the fifty per cent ceiling not inviolable.
• Davinder Singh (2024) overruled Chinnaiah: States may sub-classify Scheduled Castes, since the SC list is not homogeneous; several opinions urged extending the creamy layer to SC/ST.
The unresolved tensions
• Sub-classification needs quantifiable data on relative backwardness and representation, which most States lack — the gap driving the caste-enumeration debate.
• Promotion quotas rest on Nagaraj (2006) as modified by Jarnail Singh (2018). EWS sits uneasily in a framework built on social backwardness, excluding the groups it was designed for.
topics.position: A statutory periodic evidence base — the Rohini Commission report is the template; a published creamy-layer methodology; and investment in schooling, since reservation distributes existing opportunity rather than creating it. The jurisprudence has moved from formal group identity to measured relative deprivation — making credible data, not doctrine, the binding constraint.
topics.draw: A ladder of four rungs — Indra Sawhney 1992 (framework) → Nagaraj/Jarnail (promotion data) → Janhit Abhiyan 2022 (EWS, ceiling unsettled) → Davinder Singh 2024 (sub-classification). Write ‘data’ beside the top two rungs.
bank: Caste census link
Sub-classification is unimplementable without enumeration — the judgment created the demand for the data.
Fifty per cent ceiling
Janhit Abhiyan treated it as a rule of prudence, not a basic-structure limit — the doctrinal shift most answers miss.
Creamy layer for SC/ST
Judicially urged, politically resisted; the objection is that SC disadvantage is untouchability-based, not income-based.
Private sector
Art 15(5) permits reservation in private unaided institutions; employment reservation would need fresh legislation.
Women’s reservation
The 106th Amendment is conditional on delimitation following the census — representation and enumeration are again linked.
Eﬀiciency argument
Art 335 requires consistency with administrative eﬀiciency; B. K. Pavitra II (2019) treated diversity as itself enhancing eﬀiciency.

topics.t: The Speaker in India and the United Kingdom
topics.q: Compare the position of the Speaker in India and in the United Kingdom with special reference to party aﬀiliation and impartiality.
body: Both are elected by the House and expected to be impartial. They diverge on what produces impartiality: the British Speaker resigns from the party and is returned unopposed; the Indian Speaker retains party membership and contests as a party candidate.
The consequences of that difference
• The British Speaker has no career interest in the party’s fortunes; the Indian Speaker’s future depends on it.
• It matters most under the Tenth Schedule, where the Speaker decides defection — and the government’s survival.
Kihoto Hollohan (1992) held the Speaker acts as a tribunal, reviewable only after decision; Keisham Meghachandra Singh (2020) urged an independent tribunal and three-month disposal.
The other divergences
• The casting vote follows the Denison convention in Britain; India has none. Money Bill certification under Art 110(3) is ‘final’, deciding whether the second chamber is bypassed.
• Anti-defection has no British analogue: the whip is a party matter.
topics.position: Transfer defection adjudication to an independent tribunal; adopt resignation from the party, or at minimum a convention against contesting on a party ticket. Impartiality is produced by removing the interest, not by exhorting the oﬀiceholder to ignore it.
topics.draw: Reproduce the four-row table. The first row carries the thesis; the second row carries the marks.
topics.figure: ◆ Speaker — India and the United Kingdom India                                          United Kingdom retains party membership; contests             resigns from party; returned on a party ticket                              unopposed by convention decides defection under the Tenth              no anti-defection analogue; Schedule; no time limit                        floor-crossing lawful Money Bill certification ‘final’ (Art          certification exists, but Lords’ powers 110(3)); bypasses Rajya Sabha                  already limited by statute casting vote unregulated by                    Denison convention governs the convention                                     casting vote A comparison table is the correct form for any ‘compare with another country’ question — four attributes, both columns, no prose needed.
bank: Deputy Speaker
Art 93 requires the oﬀice; prolonged vacancy in the 17th Lok Sabha shows a constitutional requirement without a deadline.
Kihoto qualification
Review lies only after the order — so delay, not error, is the effective immunity.
Rajya Sabha Chairman
The Vice-President presides while being a political appointee — the same structural objection, differently sourced.
State Assemblies
Subhash Desai (2023) on Maharashtra showed a Speaker’s inaction deciding which faction governs.
Reform proposals
Dinesh Goswami Committee and the Law Commission’s 170th Report both recommend removing adjudication from the Speaker.
Committee chairmanship
The British Public Accounts Committee is chaired by the Opposition by convention — India follows this, and it works.

topics.q: The independence of the Election Commission rests not on any single provision but on the combined design of appointment, tenure, removal and financial autonomy. Examine.
body: Article 324 vests superintendence of elections in the Commission but leaves composition and appointment to Parliament. Independence rests on statutory design, not constitutional guarantee.
The four legs

• Appointment: Anoop Baranwal (2023) directed selection by the PM, the Leader of the Opposition and the Chief Justice; the CEC Act 2023 substituted a Cabinet Minister for the Chief Justice — restoring the executive majority the judgment had removed.

• Tenure and removal: Article 324(5) protects only the Chief Election Commissioner; the others are removable on his recommendation — a disparity Tarkunde (1975), Dinesh Goswami (1990) and the Second ARC all urged be ended.
• Finance: expenditure is voted, not charged as for the CAG and UPSC, so the budget passes through the executive it regulates.
• Plurality: multi-member since 1993; majority decision-making resists single-point capture.
topics.position: Parity of removal protection for all three Commissioners; a plural appointment body with a judicial nominee; charged expenditure; and a bar on post-retirement government appointment. Independence is a property of design, not of character — the present arrangement asks the oﬀice to be braver than its terms of service require.
topics.draw: Reproduce the four-row table and tick only the last row. A reader should see three crosses and one tick without reading the prose.
topics.figure: ◆ Election Commission — four legs of independence leg                            present design appointment                    PM + Cabinet Minister + LoP (2023 Act) — executive majority tenure / removal               only the CEC protected under Art 324(5) finance                        expenditure voted, not charged plurality                      multi-member since 1993 — the one leg that holds Four rows, one column of design. Three legs are weak and one is sound — stating that pattern is the argument.
bank: Model Code of Conduct
It has no statutory force — compliance rests entirely on the Commission’s moral authority, which is what independence buys.
Electoral bonds
ADR v. Union (2024) struck down the scheme; transparency of funding is an EC-adjacent but distinct reform.
Art 329(b)
No judicial interference once the electoral process has begun — the election petition is the sole remedy.
State Election Commissions
Weaker still — appointed by State governments, and local poll delays are routine.
Simultaneous elections
The ‘One Nation One Election’ proposal expands the Commission’s logistical burden without strengthening its design.
Comparative
The UK Electoral Commission reports to a Speaker’s Committee; the design lesson is legislative rather than executive accountability.

topics.t: Electoral Roll Revision and the SIR
topics.q: The Election Commission’s power over the revision of electoral rolls is plenary in method but limited in object. Examine in the light of recent judicial pronouncements.
body: Article 324 with Sections 21–23 of the RP Act 1950 empowers the Commission to revise electoral rolls. The Special Intensive Revision tested that power, and ADR v. ECI (2025) upheld it: Article 324 is not a dead letter.
Plenary in method
• Section 21(3) permits special revision for recorded reasons; Mohinder Singh Gill (1978) treats Article 324 as a reservoir of power where the statute is silent.
• The Court allowed it while directing that Aadhaar be accepted as a twelfth identity document.
Limited in object
• It determines eligibility under Article 326 — citizenship, age, residence — but does not determine citizenship, which only an authority under the Citizenship Act 1955 may decide.
• Deletion affects the vote, not status. The risk is procedural: the burden shifts to the elector, hardest on migrants and the undocumented poor.
topics.position: Reconcile purity with inclusiveness through procedure, not the document list — notice, a hearing, a reasoned order before deletion and a statutory appeal. The power to clean the roll is plenary; the power to decide who belongs to the country is nonexistent — and that distinction must be visible in the procedure.
topics.draw: Two boxes side by side — ‘method: plenary (Art 324, s.21(3), Mohinder Singh Gill)’ and ‘object: limited (Art 326 eligibility, not citizenship)’. A single arrow below both to ‘procedural safeguards: notice, hearing, reasoned order, appeal’.
bank: Citizenship / NRC
Conflating roll revision with citizenship determination is the constitutional error; the Act of 1955 is the only route.
Migrants
Ordinary residence is the hardest condition for circular migrants to document — remote voting pilots address the same problem.
Aadhaar
Accepted as identity, not as proof of citizenship — Puttaswamy (Aadhaar) keeps that line.
Federal friction
States allege targeted revision; publishing objection statistics State-wise is the cheapest confidence-building measure.
Art 329(b) timing
Challenges must come before the notification; after it, only an election petition lies.
Booth-level agents
Party-appointed BLAs are the built-in verification mechanism the Act already provides and parties under-use.

topics.q: The certification of a Bill as a Money Bill bears directly upon bicameralism and upon the scope of judicial review. Discuss.
body: Article 110(1) defines a Money Bill exhaustively through ‘only’, confining it to seven heads; 110(4) requires the Speaker to certify and 110(3) makes it ‘final’. Certification converts a bicameral process into a substantially unicameral one.
The effect on bicameralism
• Under Article 109 the Rajya Sabha may only recommend within fourteen days; the Lok Sabha may ignore it and the President cannot return the Bill — the chamber of federal review is bypassed.
• Tribunal restructuring and FCRA and PMLA amendments travelled through Finance Acts — substantial nonfinancial consequence without the second chamber.
The scope of review

• Raja Ram Pal (2007) held that finality does not oust review for illegality. Puttaswamy (Aadhaar) (2018) upheld Aadhaar’s certification over Chandrachud J.’s dissent; Rojer Mathew (2019) referred the scope of ‘only’ to a sevenjudge bench, still undecided.
topics.position: A reasoned certification in writing disclosing which head each clause falls under; early disposal of the reference; and a convention against omnibus Finance Bills carrying unrelated amendments. ‘Final’ has never meant unreviewable — the constitutional harm is not the Speaker’s decision but the absence of any recorded reason for it.
topics.draw: Reproduce the flow in six boxes and keep the dashed box. If short of space, draw only the top box, the Speaker box and the dashed box — that trio carries the argument.
topics.figure: ◆ Money Bill — the route and the review Art 110(1): the seven heads — ‘only’ these Speaker certifies, Art 110(4) Lok Sabha passes                            Rajya Sabha: recommend only, 14 days President: assent — cannot return 110(3) ‘final’ ̸= unreviewable — Raja Ram Pal; scope referred to 7 judges in Rojer Mathew Write the seven heads into the top box — they are the whole test. The dashed side box is the review question, and it is what converts a procedural answer into a constitutional one.
bank: Financial Bill distinction
Arts 117(1) and (3) create categories the Rajya Sabha can vote on — naming them shows the misuse is a classification choice.
Aadhaar dissent
Chandrachud J. called it a fraud on the Constitution — the sharpest available line, worth one sentence.
Comparative
The UK Parliament Act 1911 gives the Commons Speaker the same power, but the Lords’ financial role was already extinguished by statute.
Federalism
The Rajya Sabha is the States’ chamber — bypassing it on FCRA or PMLA amendments is a federal question, not just a procedural one.
Ordinances
Krishna Kumar Singh (2017) condemned re-promulgation as a fraud on the Constitution — the same bypass logic under Art 123.
Reform
A pre-legislative classification note published with the Bill would let the House contest certification before it becomes final.

topics.q: Parliamentary control over delegated legislation has not kept pace with the growth of executive rule-making. Examine.
body: Modern statutes settle principle and leave detail to rules. The limit is that essential legislative function cannot be delegated (Delhi Laws Act (1951)); the instrument of control is the Committee on Subordinate Legislation.
The mechanism
• Rules are laid under simple, negative or aﬀirmative procedure; the Committee tests them — within the parent Act, retrospective, tax-imposing — and may recommend annulment.
Why control has thinned
• Laying without consequence: default carries no statutory consequence, and rules are notified long before laying — the House confronts a fait accompli.
• Capacity: no technical secretariat; laying is observed unevenly.
• Skeletal statutes: substance is migrating to rules — the DPDP Act 2023 left core obligations to rules notified two years later, so the executive settled a right’s content.
• Weak substitutes: consultation policy is advisory; courts test vires, not wisdom.
topics.position: Mandatory pre-publication of draft rules with a comment period; a statutory consequence for non-laying; and a limit on how much substance may be left to rules. Parliament has retained the form of control and lost the timing of it — a rule that operates before it is laid has already done its work.
topics.draw: A timeline, not a flowchart: parent Act → rule notified → rule operates → rule laid → committee scrutiny. Draw a bracket under the gap between ‘operates’ and ‘laid’ and label it ‘the control gap’.
bank: Skeleton legislation
DPDP 2023 and the three criminal codes all left substance to rules — name one example, not the trend.
Judicial review
Vires review under Delhi Laws Act tests competence, not policy — so courts cannot substitute for scrutiny.
Comparative
The UK’s Statutory Instruments Act and the US Administrative Procedure Act both require notice and comment as a matter of law.
Federalism
State legislatures’ subordinate legislation committees are weaker still, and most States have no laying discipline at all.
Regulatory State link
Regulators’ regulations escape laying altogether in several statutes — the largest unscrutinised body of rules.
Emergency rule-making
Pandemic-era rules under the Disaster Management Act showed how far governance can run on unlaid instruments.

topics.t: The Finance Commission as Constitutional Arbiter
topics.q: “The Finance Commission is a constitutional arbiter and not an advisory body.” Comment in the light of the award of the Sixteenth Finance Commission.
body: Article 280 obliges a Finance Commission every fifth year; Article 281 requires the report and an action-taken memorandum laid before Parliament. Its recommendations are advisory — but the convention of acceptance makes it an arbiter in substance.
The Sixteenth Commission’s award, 2026-31

• Chaired by Arvind Panagariya, it retains devolution at 41%.   The formula is reworked — income distance 42.5%, population 17.5%, demographic performance 10%, area 10%, forest 10%, and a new contribution to GDP criterion at 10%.
• Local body grants total ₹7.91 lakh crore, disaster management ₹1.55 lakh crore; the Centre is set at a 3.5% deficit by 2030-31.
Why the divisible pool remains the fulcrum

• Cesses and surcharges are not shareable under Article 270, so their rising share shrinks the base on which 41% is computed — the effective transfer falls below the headline. And the terms of reference are set by the Union — one party to the dispute it arbitrates.
Cap cesses and surcharges or bring them into the pool; settle terms of reference through the Inter-State Council. The
topics.position: Commission arbitrates the share but not the pool — and the pool is where the federal bargain is actually being renegotiated.
topics.draw: Reproduce the two-branch split and write the footnote line under it. The dashed cess box is the mark-earning element.
topics.figure: ◆ Where the divisible pool goes Gross tax revenue cesses + surcharges                          divisible pool, Art 270 not shareable (Art 270) States 41% Centre the headline share is 41% of a shrinking base — which is why the pool, not the percentage, is the federal question Two branches from one node. This single figure answers both the Finance Commission question and the fiscal-federalism half of any devolution answer.
bank: Demographic performance
The 10% weight offsets the political penalty States face for succeeding on fertility — link it to delimitation.
Contribution to GDP
A new criterion rewarding richer States — eﬀiciency against equalisation, the core trade-off to name.
Local bodies
₹7.91 lakh crore strengthens balance sheets, not autonomy, because the grants are tied and conditional.
GST compensation
Its end transferred full revenue risk to States without added autonomy — read alongside the shrinking pool.
Disaster allocation
₹1.55 lakh crore, 90:10 for NE and Himalayan States, 75:25 for others — a usable number in DM answers too.
Article 275 / 282
Grants under Art 282 bypass the Commission entirely — the discretionary channel that grows when the pool shrinks.

topics.t: The GST Council and Fiscal Federalism
topics.q: “GST reforms have profound consequences for Indian federalism.” Discuss.
body: Article 279A creates the GST Council with weighted voting — Centre one-third, States two-thirds, three-quarters to carry. Mohit Minerals (2022) held its recommendations persuasive, not binding, Union and States having simultaneous power.
What GST did to the federal bargain
• States surrendered independent indirect-taxing power, so a collectively taken rate decision transmits directly into every State budget.
• Rationalisation from September 2025 into 5% and 18% with a 40% demerit rate improved design, but created revenue foregone that only volume growth recovers.
• The 14% guaranteed-growth compensation has ended, transferring full revenue risk to States with no addition to their autonomy.
The structural asymmetries

• As a destination-based tax GST favours consuming over producing States; the Centre’s one-third bloc is an effective veto; and Mohit Minerals cuts both ways, aﬀirming State autonomy while weakening the Council’s finality.
topics.position: Bring petroleum, electricity and real estate into the base; make the GST Appellate Tribunal functional; publish Council voting records; and institutionalise revenue-risk sharing. The Council is India’s only working instrument of continuous federal bargaining — its legitimacy now depends on how residual revenue risk is shared, not on how rates are set.
topics.draw: One decision node — ‘GST Council: 3/4 majority, Centre 1/3’ — with two arrows down to ‘Centre’ and ‘every State budget’, and a dashed box under the State arrow reading ‘compensation ended: full revenue risk, no added autonomy’.
bank: Mohit Minerals
Persuasive-not-binding restores State autonomy in form; in practice no State legislates against a Council decision.
Compensation cess
Extended only to service loan repayment — its end is the single largest fiscal shock to State budgets.
Inverted duty
Refund blockage is the operational MSME grievance; rationalisation addresses it directly.
Petroleum inclusion
States resist because fuel taxes are their last autonomous lever — any deal needs explicit compensation design.
Cooperative federalism
The Council is the template the Punchhi Commission wanted for non-tax disputes too.
Dispute resolution
Art 279A(11) allows the Council to create a dispute mechanism — it never has, so disputes go to court.

topics.q: Explain the concept of a social audit. Why has it succeeded in some programmes and remained a formality in others? A social audit verifies a programme’s records against reality by the people entitled to it, in a public forum where oﬀicials must respond — making the beneficiary a co-producer of accountability.
body: Why it succeeded in MGNREGS
• The Act made it statutory and mandatory every six months, so it did not depend on administrative goodwill.
• An independent Social Audit Unit, outside the implementing department and funded from programme costs — the crucial structural point.
• Records are individually verifiable — a muster roll read against a named person — and findings feed a public hearing with an action-taken report.
Why it is a formality elsewhere
• Where the unit sits under the implementing department, it audits its own employer.
• Where the entitlement is not individually verifiable — a road, a training — nothing can be checked.
• Records are withheld or unreadable, and findings produce no consequence, so participation collapses.
topics.position: Meghalaya’s Social Audit Act 2017 supplies the template — a statutorily funded unit reporting outside the department, pre-audit disclosure, extension to PDS and health, and an action-taken obligation. Social audit works where it is statutory, independently staffed and consequential — everywhere else it is a meeting.
topics.draw: Six boxes in a loop; mark the two break points with a cross. Naming where the chain breaks is what separates this from a list of problems.
topics.figure: ◆ Why social audit works, or does not statutory       independent          records disclosed mandate          audit unit        before the gram sabha participation          action taken: public hearing sustained          recovery, discipline break any link and it becomes a meeting — the commonest break is the second (unit under the implementing department) and the fifth (no consequence) A closed chain with the two habitual break points named. It converts ‘implementation is weak’ into a located diagnosis.
bank: Right to information link
Social audit is RTI exercised collectively and in advance — disclosure before the event rather than a query after it.
Andhra Pradesh model
The SSAAT unit reporting outside the department is the most cited domestic example of structural independence.
Gram sabha
Art 243A gives the gram sabha powers ‘as the legislature may provide’ — social audit is the one power it actually exercises.
Auditor safety
Whistle-blower protection is not incidental — local elite capture makes the auditor the most exposed person present.
Digital records
Online muster rolls make verification cheaper but exclude the non-literate unless read aloud at the hearing.
Urban gap
No urban analogue exists; ward committees under the 74th Amendment are the natural forum and are largely unconstituted.

topics.t: Citizen’s Charters and Public Service Guarantee Acts
topics.q: Citizen’s charters in India have largely failed to transform service delivery. Examine why, and what has worked instead.
body: A citizen’s charter declares the services an agency provides, the standards it will meet and the remedy if it does not. India adopted it in 1997; it failed for one reason: it created a promise without a right.
Why the voluntary model failed
• Charters were drafted by the department, not with users, so standards reflected what was convenient.
• They carried no legal force, so breach produced no consequence; they were rarely updated; and no oﬀicer was named as responsible.
What worked — the statutory turn

• Public Service Guarantee Acts, from Madhya Pradesh (2010) and now in over twenty States, convert the promise into an entitlement: a notified service, time limit, designated oﬀicer, appeal, and penalty on the defaulting oﬀicer.
• The central Time Bound Delivery Bill 2011 lapsed.            CPGRAMS improved traceability but measures disposal, not resolution.
topics.position: The Second ARC’s prescription — charters drafted with users, few measurable commitments, statutory backing with a named oﬀicer and penalty; independent call-back verification; and root-cause analysis so redress feeds into process reform. A charter changes behaviour only when breaching it costs the oﬀicer something.
topics.draw: Two columns — ‘charter (1997): promise, no right, no oﬀicer, no penalty’ against ‘PSG Act (2010–): notified service, time limit, named oﬀicer, appeal, penalty’. The second column is the answer.
bank: Sevottam model
The Second ARC’s framework of charter + grievance redress + capability, assessed by an IS standard — one line, high value.
RTI comparison
RTI worked because it carried a penalty on the Public Information Oﬀicer; the charter had no equivalent.
Digital delivery
Faceless assessment and DigiLocker meet timelines automatically — process design substitutes for enforcement.
Local bodies
Municipal service charters matter most and are weakest; the 74th Amendment gives no service-standard obligation.
Measurement
Disposal rate is the wrong indicator; independent call-back sampling is the cheapest correction.
Comparative
The UK Citizen’s Charter of 1991 also failed voluntarily and was replaced by statutory service standards.

topics.q: Digital public infrastructure has solved delivery at scale. Examine why this is a governance change rather than a technology change, and the problems that remain unresolved.
body: e-Governance has moved through three stages — digitisation, transaction services, and now digital public infrastructure: open, interoperable, population-scale rails — Aadhaar, UPI, DigiLocker, ONDC — which State and market both build on.
Why DPI is a governance change, not a technology one
• It unbundles identity, payment and data-sharing into shared layers, so a department builds a service, not a stack; and transactions become auditable.
• DBT rests entirely on it: JAM converted subsidy delivery from a physical to a payment problem.
The unresolved problems
• Exclusion at authentication: biometric failure and seeding mismatch deny at the moment of need — Puttaswamy (Aadhaar) (2018) barred such denial, imperfectly implemented.
• Divide and data: device ownership and literacy remain gendered, and the DPDP Act’s State exemptions weaken the safeguard.
• Grievance redress: the least developed layer — a failed transaction rarely has a human route to resolution.
topics.position: Mandatory offline and assisted channels with a legal bar on denial for authentication failure; open-standard mandates; published service levels; and a grievance guarantee attached to every digital entitlement. DPI has solved delivery at scale; whether it becomes governance depends on whether the person it fails can still reach a human being.
topics.draw: Three stacked layers — identity, payment, data — with a service riding on top, and two arrows leaking out of the stack labelled ‘authentication failure’ and ‘no grievance route’.
bank: India Stack export
DPI is now a development export; the credibility test abroad is exactly the exclusion record at home.
ONDC
Open protocols in commerce apply the same unbundling logic to markets rather than to the State.
Federalism
States build on national rails but own the delivery failure — accountability and control are misaligned.
Function creep
A welfare database becoming an identification and surveillance infrastructure is the standing risk.
Cost
DPI’s marginal cost per transaction is near zero, which is why it scales where physical delivery could not.
Disability access
Accessibility must be a procurement condition; retrofitting it is costlier and worse (Rajive Raturi, 2024).

topics.q: Mission Karmayogi can shift civil-service training from rule familiarity to role-based competence, but course completion is not the same as administrative capability. Examine.
body: Mission Karmayogi (2020) shifts training from rule familiarity to role-based competence, through a competency framework, the iGOT platform and a Capacity Building Commission.
Why the design is right
• Training was input-based and front-loaded into induction; a role-competence model makes learning continuous and matched to the post.
• A common platform scales at low marginal cost, and a standards body prevents each department reinventing curricula.
Why completion is not capability
• Completion measures consumption, not application — a certificate does not show a District Magistrate handles a hearing better.
• Self-paced digital learning suits knowledge transfer, not judgement or crisis handling, which need simulation and mentoring.
• There is no link between competence and posting eligibility, so the incentive is to complete rather than learn; transfers defeat role-matched training; and the frontline is reached least.
topics.position: Tie competencies to eligibility for specified posts; assess by demonstrated performance rather than completion; blend digital modules with practicum and mentoring; extend to State and frontline cadres in vernacular; and publish outcome evaluation rather than usage statistics. A platform distributes knowledge at scale; only consequences attached to competence convert it into administrative capability.
topics.draw: A funnel: enrolment → completion → competence → posting/promotion. Draw the last arrow as a broken line — the missing link is the whole answer.
bank: Tenure link
T. S. R. Subramanian (2013) required a minimum two-year tenure — training is wasted where transfers are arbitrary.
Domain specialisation
The Second ARC wanted oﬀicers to choose a domain after a period of general service; Karmayogi supplies the curriculum for it.
Lateral entry
It imports specialists but not institutional memory; capacity building is the alternative route to the same skill.
State capacity
Most citizen-facing service is delivered by State and local cadres, where iGOT penetration is thinnest.
Appraisal reform
360-degree appraisal with published criteria is the accountability half Karmayogi does not itself supply.
Comparative
Singapore’s civil service college ties learning to posting boards — the consequence India has not attached.

topics.q: India has built the instruments of accountability and withheld from each the one power that would make it work. Examine with reference to the CAG, the Lokpal and whistle-blower protection.
body: Accountability runs through three institutions with three problems. The CAG (Art 148) has independence but no enforcement power; the Lokpal (2013) has enforcement power but a weak start; and whistleblowers have a statute never brought into force.
The CAG
• Salary charged on the Consolidated Fund, removal as a Supreme Court judge, reports laid under Art 151 and examined by the PAC.
• The weaknesses are downstream: audit is ex post, PAC scrutiny lags by years, and the CAG cannot audit private parties in a PPP — where much public risk now sits.
The Lokpal and whistleblowers
• Constituted only in 2019; its appointment committee has sat without a Leader of the Opposition; Section 44’s asset declaration was diluted.
• The Whistle Blowers Protection Act 2014 was passed but never notified — the person on whom every other mechanism depends has no protection.
topics.position: Statutory timelines for action-taken replies on CAG reports; audit extended to PPP concessionaires; an independent Lokpal investigation wing; and notification of the 2014 Act. India has built the instruments of accountability and withheld from each the one power that would make it work.
topics.draw: Reproduce the three-row table. The third row does the most work, because a statute passed and never notified is the sharpest single fact in the answer.
topics.figure: ◆ Accountability institutions and what each lacks institution                            the missing power CAG, Art 148                           no enforcement; PAC scrutiny lags by years Lokpal, 2013                           capacity; no own investigation wing Whistle Blowers Act, 2014              never notified Three rows. Each institution is given a power and denied the one that would make it work — stating that pattern is the argument.
bank: CVC and CBI
Vineet Narain (1997) gave the CVC statutory status and the CBI Director a fixed tenure — the same design logic.
PoC Act 2018
Prior approval to investigate a public servant raises the threshold for initiating inquiry — a protection that cuts against disclosure.
RTI link
Information Commission vacancies mean the first-line transparency institution is itself under-resourced.
Social audit
Downward accountability to beneficiaries complements upward accountability to Parliament — pair them in the conclusion.
PPP audit
CAG access to concessionaire records is the single most consequential extension, given asset monetisation.
Lokayuktas
No uniform statute; a model law under Art 252 or a central floor would end the variance.

topics.t: The National Education Policy at Five Years
topics.q: Five years after the National Education Policy, 2020, examine the progress achieved in restructuring school education and the principal implementation bottlenecks.
body: NEP 2020 restructured school education to 5+3+3+4 for ages 3–18, brought early childhood into schooling and set foundational literacy first. Five years on, the structural change is largely on paper.
What has moved
• NIPUN Bharat operationalised the FLN mission and the NCF Foundational Stage (2022) was issued.
• PM SHRI exemplar schools were designated, Balvatika began the preparatory year, and PARAKH took up assessment and board equivalence.
The bottlenecks
• Teachers: large vacancies, persistent single-teacher schools, and four-year ITEP reform will take a decade to change the stock.
• Early childhood: anganwadis sit under another ministry, staffed for nutrition not pedagogy — so the structure’s first three years have no qualified teacher.
• Finance: the 6% of GDP target, set in 1968, remains unmet.
• Federalism: education is Concurrent and several States have not adopted the structure; ASER shows outcomes, not structure, bind.
topics.position: Fill teacher vacancies on a statutory timeline; converge anganwadi and pre-primary under one authority; and publish State-wise outcomes annually. NEP restructured the container; the outcome depends on the teacher, and that is the one input the policy did not secure.
topics.draw: The 5+3+3+4 ladder drawn as four blocks, with a cross on the first block labelled ‘no qualified teacher — anganwadi under a different ministry’. The cross is the mark.
bank: Higher education
NEP’s multidisciplinary universities, ABC credit bank and four-year UG programme are the tertiary half — one line each.
RTE amendment
Extending RTE to 3–18 years would give the 5+3+3+4 structure a legal anchor it presently lacks.
Digital / DIKSHA
Content is not the constraint; teacher time consumed by non-teaching duties is.
Equity
Dropout is concentrated at the secondary stage among girls, SC/ST and first-generation learners — name the stage, not the group.
Regulation
A single higher-education regulator is the institutional companion reform (Viksit Bharat Shiksha Adhishthan Bill 2025).
Assessment
PARAKH’s equivalence work matters because board disparity distorts national admissions.

topics.q: Foundational literacy and numeracy is the binding constraint on later learning. Assess the implementation priorities for achieving the NIPUN Bharat goal.
body: Foundational literacy and numeracy is reading with meaning and basic arithmetic by Grade 3. It is the binding constraint on later learning — a child who cannot read by Grade 3 cannot learn from a textbook. NIPUN Bharat (2021) sets the goal.
Why the deficit persists despite near-universal enrolment
• The curriculum moves at the syllabus’ pace, not the child’s, so one who falls behind never catches up — the case for teaching at the right level.
• Automatic promotion under RTE’s no-detention rule, without the assumed remedial support, moved children up without the competency.
• Instruction is often in a language the child does not speak at home; teacher time goes to surveys and mid-day meals; multi-grade classrooms are the norm; and pandemic learning loss compounded it.
topics.position: Assess each child by level rather than grade, with remedial instruction on the ‘Teaching at the Right Level’ evidence; protect instructional time by statute; supply structured pedagogy in the child’s language; and give early-grade teachers mentoring.
topics.conc: Enrolment was a supply problem and was solved; foundational learning is a classroom process problem, and nothing outside the classroom will solve it.
topics.draw: Two lines on one axis — enrolment rising to near-universal, learning outcomes flat. Label the gap ‘the classroom process problem’. One figure, whole argument.
bank: No-detention debate
Restoring detention without remedial support repeats the original error — the missing input is support, not failure.
Teacher accountability
Attendance monitoring raises presence, not pedagogy; structured lesson plans raise both.
Mother tongue
Multilingual classrooms need bilingual materials, not a single-language mandate.
Anganwadi convergence
Oral language and number sense built at ages 3–6 determine Grade 3 outcomes — the cheapest intervention point.
Measurement
ASER is sample-based and household-level, so it captures out-of-school children NAS misses — cite both.
Nutrition link
Stunting lowers cognitive attainment permanently — FLN and Poshan are the same policy at different ages.

topics.q: Caste enumeration can improve the evidentiary basis of welfare policy, but its public value will depend on data quality, comparability and privacy. Discuss.
body: Caste enumeration records jati oﬀicially. India has counted SCs and STs since 1951 but no other castes since 1931; SECC 2011 data was never released, and caste is now to be included in the Census.
Why the data is needed
• Indra Sawhney (1992) requires quantifiable data to establish backwardness and inadequacy of representation.
