• Davinder Singh (2024) makes that operational — no sub-classification of Scheduled Castes without evidence of relative deprivation. Shares presently rest on 1931 proportions.
Why data alone cannot settle it
• Backwardness is social and educational, not numerical — a headcount records how many, not how deprived.
• Comparability is a real problem: jati names vary by region, sub-castes merge and split, and self-reporting is unstable where reclassification carries benefit.
• Privacy is engaged under Puttaswamy (2017); and the colonial precedent cautions that counting hardens categories that were fluid.
topics.position: A published methodology with a standardised jati directory; collection under the Census Act 1948’s confidentiality provisions; release of aggregates only; and anti-discrimination enforcement alongside. Enumeration can make social justice evidencebased; it cannot make it just — that depends on what is redistributed after the counting stops.
topics.draw: Reproduce the four cells. The right column is where the marks are, because most answers only argue the left.
topics.figure: ◆ Caste data — what it settles and what it does not settles                                      does not settle quantifiable data (Indra Sawhney)            backwardness is social and educational sub-classification (Davinder Singh)          comparability, privacy, hardening of categories Two columns settle the whole question. Society answers rarely gain from a diagram, but a four-cell table costs three lines and replaces a paragraph.
bank: Census Act 1948
Confidentiality of individual returns is the statutory answer to the privacy objection — cite the Act, not the principle.
50% ceiling
Enumeration will produce demands to breach it; Janhit Abhiyan already unsettled the ceiling as an absolute.
Bihar survey
A State survey, not a census — upheld on the ground that a survey for policy is within State competence.
Rohini Commission
Constituted to answer exactly the intra-OBC stratification question; its report remains unpublished.
Women’s reservation
The 106th Amendment’s OBC sub-quota demand turns on precisely this data.
Beyond reservation
Data can target scholarships, credit and health rather than only quotas — the least-argued and highest-value line.

topics.q: The shift from self-identification to certification in the legal recognition of gender identity raises questions of dignity and autonomy. Examine.
body: NALSA (2014) recognised transgender persons as a third gender and held identity rests on self-identification as an aspect of dignity under Article 21. The Transgender Persons Act 2019 then required a District Magistrate’s certificate — replacing self-identification with certification.
Why the shift matters
• A change of gender to male or female requires proof of surgery, medically certified.
• Recognition therefore turns on an oﬀicer’s satisfaction and a medical procedure — the very gatekeeping NALSA rejected. Refusal has no clear appeal.
The countervailing argument, and its weakness
• Certification is defended as preventing misuse and giving the document evidentiary value.

• But the risk is speculative against a documented harm; identity documents elsewhere rest on declaration; and the Act provides no reservation, so the feared misuse does not exist. Section 18 penalties are also lower than general provisions.
topics.position: Restore self-declaration by aﬀidavit with penalties for false declaration; remove the surgery requirement; and extend horizontal reservation as several High Courts have directed. Recognition that requires permission is not recognition of identity but of a claim — NALSA located dignity in self-determination, and the statute has misplaced it in a file.
topics.draw: Two boxes with an arrow between — ‘NALSA 2014: self-identification’ → ‘2019 Act: certification by DM + surgery for binary’. Label the arrow ‘the shift’, and write ‘dignity, autonomy, Art 21’ under the first box only.
bank: Horizontal reservation
Karnataka and several High Courts have directed it; a vertical category would displace existing beneficiaries, so horizontal is the workable form.
Health
Gender-aﬀirming care is excluded from most insurance; PM-JAY inclusion is the concrete ask.
Comparative
Argentina and Ireland permit self-declaration without medical evidence — the direct international counterpoint.
Marriage / family
Recognition without a marriage or succession framework leaves civil rights unsettled; Supriyo (2023) left this to Parliament.
Data
Census undercounting means schemes are designed without a denominator — the same problem as disability.
Employment
Non-discrimination under Section 3 is unenforced without a designated complaint oﬀicer in every establishment.

topics.q: A decline in income poverty does not by itself signify a decline in deprivation. Discuss the implications for the measurement of poverty and for the design of welfare.
body: Income poverty measures a shortfall against a consumption line; deprivation measures absent capabilities. India’s Multidimensional Poverty Index has fallen sharply — but neither measure captures vulnerability.
Why the two must be read together
• A household can cross the income line while lacking sanitation, schooling or clean fuel.

• MPI gains concentrate in indicators public provision moves quickly — toilets, cooking gas, bank accounts — assets and access, not income and security. A household counted non-poor may have no stable earning.
Why vulnerability persists after poverty falls

• Employment is informal and uninsured, so illness removes income at once; health is the principal impoverishing shock, and hospitalisation insurance does not cover the outpatient costs that cause it.
• Climate and agrarian shocks strike households with no buffer; informal debt turns one shock into permanent liability; and caste, gender and disability compound each.
topics.position: Shift the target from crossing the line to staying above it — a vulnerability index alongside the headcount; portable social protection; and outpatient cover. India has become good at lifting households over the line and not much better at stopping them falling back — the next reduction must be measured in resilience.
topics.draw: Two overlapping circles — ‘income poor’ and ‘multidimensionally deprived’ — with a third dashed circle overlapping both labelled ‘vulnerable: informal, uninsured, one shock away’. The dashed circle is the answer.
bank: Tendulkar / Rangarajan
No oﬀicial poverty line has been updated since; the absence of a line is itself a measurement problem.
Consumption survey
The 2022-23 HCES ended a long gap; without it, poverty estimates were being made from proxies.
Global comparison
World Bank extreme-poverty estimates and the national MPI move differently — explain the methodology, do not pick one.
Urban poverty
MPI indicators are rural-weighted; urban deprivation is about tenure and portability, which the index barely captures.
Ayushman Bharat
Covers hospitalisation, not outpatient — the single largest gap between poverty reduction and financial protection.
Targeting
Deprivation-based targeting needs a dynamic, appealable registry, not a 2011 base — link to welfare-registry reform.

topics.q: India has solved availability and access in food security but not absorption. Examine why calories have not become nutrition, and the reforms required.
body: Food security is availability, access and absorption. India solved availability through buffer stocks and the NFSA 2013. It has not solved absorption — which is why undernutrition persists alongside record procurement.
Why calories have not become nutrition
• The PDS is calibrated to cereals where the deficiency is protein, micronutrient and dietary diversity — so an eﬀicient PDS delivers an inadequate basket.
• Absorption depends on non-food determinants: sanitation, since enteric infection prevents uptake; maternal nutrition, since low birth weight begins the cycle before birth; and birth spacing.
• NFHS-5 records stunting and anaemia inconsistent with India’s income.
The delivery architecture and its gaps
• POSHAN Abhiyaan, PM POSHAN and Anaemia Mukt Bharat converge nutrition, school meals and supplementation.
• The gaps are the first thousand days, where the anganwadi worker is overloaded; migrants outside its residence-based reach; and take-home ration quality.
topics.position: Diversify the PDS basket to pulses and millets through decentralised procurement; fortify staples; converge nutrition with sanitation; and extend anganwadi services to migrants. India feeds its population and does not yet nourish it — the remaining gap is not in the grain but in the water, the mother and the first two years.
topics.draw: Three stacked bands — availability (buffer stocks, NFSA), access (PDS, ONORC), absorption (WASH, maternal health, birth spacing). Tick the first two, cross the third. That is the whole argument.
bank: Global Hunger Index
India contests the methodology; the defensible domestic metric is the NFHS stunting and anaemia trend.
Millets / Shree Anna
Millets answer calorie, water and micronutrient objectives together, but need processing and taste recovery.
ONORC
Portability solved food for migrants; health, housing and schooling remain domicile-tied.
Fortification debate
Rice fortification is contested on iron-overload grounds in thalassaemia-prone populations — note the caveat, do not ignore it.
Anganwadi worker
Honorarium-based ‘volunteers’ performing public functions — a labour-rights question inside a nutrition programme.
Climate
Heat stress lowers grain protein and zinc content — climate change is a nutrition threat, not only a yield threat.

topics.t: Neighbourhood First and Domestic Political Transitions
topics.q: India’s neighbourhood policy is tested less by external hostility than by domestic political transitions in neighbouring States. Examine.
body: Neighbourhood First is tested less by external hostility than by domestic political change in neighbouring States. A policy built on incumbents is hostage to their survival — and every neighbour has changed government or regime in a decade.
Why transitions destabilise the relationship
• India engages the government of the day, not the spectrum, so a change of regime reads as a change of alignment, and an ‘India card’ is available to any opposition.
• Project delays convert goodwill into grievance, and rivals offer rapid finance precisely at moments of transition.
The record
• Bangladesh: the 2024 change disturbed a relationship built on one political axis; minority security, water and connectivity are under renegotiation.
• Maldives:   an ‘India Out’ campaign preceded the 2023 change, followed by personnel withdrawal and recovery through swap and budget support.
• Sri Lanka: $4 billion in credit lines during the 2022 collapse marked a shift to first-responder diplomacy. Nepal adds map disputes.
topics.position: Engage the political spectrum — parties, parliaments, provincial leaders; complete projects on schedule, since a finished project survives a government. Influence that depends on who is in oﬀice is not influence but access.
topics.draw: A horizontal timeline of transitions — Nepal, Maldives 2023, Sri Lanka 2022, Bangladesh 2024, Myanmar 2021 — with two parallel lines below: ‘access (incumbent-dependent)’ and ‘influence (project- and people-based)’.
bank: Gujral Doctrine
Asymmetric generosity — the larger neighbour must not seek reciprocity; the core insight worth naming.
China factor
Rapid unconditional finance is the competing offer; India’s counter is delivery speed, not matching terms.
Connectivity
BBIN, Kaladan and the Trilateral Highway are the instruments; each is delayed on the far side of the border.
Water
Teesta, Mahakali and Indus each convert a technical question into a domestic political one in the neighbour.
Diaspora / people
Scholarships, medical treatment and disaster relief survive regime change — the cheapest durable investment.
SAARC / BIMSTEC
SAARC is paralysed by one member; BIMSTEC is the workaround, and it needs a secretariat with resources.

topics.q: India–EU relations are moving beyond trade towards technology, security and strategic coordination. Discuss the significance of this shift for India.
body: The India–EU relationship was long unrealised potential — a Strategic Partnership since 2004, an FTA stalled in 2013 and resumed in 2022. The 2026 summit and the concluded trade negotiation mark a shift to technology, security and strategic coordination.
Why the relationship is deepening now
• Both hedge against dependence on single suppliers, and face the same coercion instruments.
• The Global Gateway offers an alternative infrastructure channel, and the Trade and Technology Council — India one of only two EU partners — covers semiconductors, AI and connectivity standards.
The implementation tests
• CBAM entered its definitive phase on 1 January 2026, imposing a carbon cost on steel, aluminium and cement exports; deforestation and due-diligence rules burden small exporters similarly.
• Data adequacy under GDPR is unresolved; mobility of professionals is India’s core ask and the EU’s hardest concession.
topics.position: Convert the FTA into utilisation — workable rules of origin, mutual recognition of standards, and MRV capacity so exporters claim actual rather than default carbon values. The partnership has moved from potential to interdependence; whether it becomes strategic depends on whether the EU’s regulatory instruments are negotiated with India or applied to it.
topics.draw: Three pillars under one roof — trade (FTA, CBAM), technology (TTC, data adequacy), security (Indo-Pacific, defence-industrial) — with ‘IMEC / Global Gateway’ as the base connecting them.
bank: CBAM detail
Certificate purchase from 1 Jan 2026; verified MRV yields the actual, lower value — default values are the penalty for weak data.
Mode 4 / mobility
Migration and mobility partnerships with Germany, France, Austria and Portugal are the concrete instrument.
Strategic autonomy
Europe’s own autonomy debate is an opportunity for India and a constraint — it narrows convergence on Russia.
Standards
EU regulation is exported globally; participating in standard-setting is worth more than tariff concessions.
Defence
Co-development with France and Germany, and naval exercises in the Indian Ocean, are the security content.
Comparison with US
The EU offers rules and regulation, the US offers technology and capital — India needs both, differently.

topics.t: The WTO after MC14 and the E-Transmission Moratorium
topics.q: The lapse of the moratorium on customs duties on electronic transmissions alters the terms of India’s engagement with the multilateral trading system. Examine.
body: The WTO is in a dual crisis — of adjudication, the Appellate Body non-functional since 2019, and of negotiation, consensus among 160-plus members producing few agreements. MC14 confirmed both.
The moratorium and its lapse
• In place since 1998 and renewed at each ministerial, it barred customs duties on digital products.
• Developing countries argued they were forgoing revenue as trade shifted to downloads, and that the scope of ‘electronic transmission’ was never settled. India and South Africa led that argument.
• The counter-case: duties raise input costs, are hard to administer without a border crossing, and would harm India’s own services exports.
India’s other standing positions

• A permanent solution on public stockholding, the Bali peace clause being interim; special and differential treatment as a right; fisheries disciplines protecting artisanal fishers; and binding dispute settlement restored.
topics.position: Prioritise restoring dispute settlement, since without adjudication every commitment is voluntary and a middle power loses most; and secure the permanent stockholding solution. A rules-based system is worth most to those who cannot coerce — which is why India’s interest lies in repairing the WTO, not accepting its irrelevance.
topics.draw: Two boxes labelled ‘adjudication crisis (Appellate Body, 2019–)’ and ‘negotiation crisis (consensus, MC14)’, with ‘moratorium lapse’ sitting on the line between them — it is a symptom of both.
bank: MPIA
An interim appeal arrangement India has not joined — explain the choice: joining legitimises a substitute for the real thing.
Public stockholding
The Bali peace clause shields NFSA procurement from challenge; a permanent solution is India’s single largest ask.
Fisheries
Disciplines must exempt artisanal and small-scale fishing — a livelihood, not a subsidy, argument.
Plurilaterals
Investment facilitation and e-commerce plurilaterals bypass consensus; India objects on process, not only substance.
CBAM / unilateralism
Regulatory extraterritoriality fills the vacuum a paralysed WTO leaves — link the two crises explicitly.
Digital trade
Data localisation and cross-border data flow rules are the next front; India’s DPDP framework is its negotiating position.

topics.q: Examine the significance of India’s maritime outreach in the Indian Ocean for its claim to be the region’s preferred security partner.
body: SAGAR (2015) framed India as Indian Ocean net security provider. MAHASAGAR (2025) broadens this to co-owned growth and resilience, extending it to Africa and the Global South.
What underpins the claim
• Capability: the Navy as first responder in humanitarian assistance, anti-piracy and anti-drone escort in the Gulf of Aden, and hydrographic survey support.

• Domain awareness: the Information Fusion Centre–Indian Ocean Region at Gurugram hosts partner liaison oﬀicers; white-shipping agreements and radar chains gifted to Mauritius, Seychelles and the Maldives.
• Institutions: IORA, the Colombo Security Conclave, IONS; access at Duqm, Chabahar and Agalega.
The implementation challenges
• Project delivery is slower than announcement, while competing infrastructure finance is faster and less conditional.

• Political transitions in island states can reverse access; naval capacity is stretched by a submarine shortfall; and ‘security provider’ framing reads as hegemonic — which MAHASAGAR’s co-owned language answers.
topics.position: Deliver — complete pending projects, since credibility is cumulative; convert the doctrine into instruments through maritime development finance and port cooperation. Preference is earned by being the partner who arrives first and finishes what was promised — the doctrine names the ambition; delivery decides the claim.
topics.draw: A map sketch of the Indian Ocean with three layers marked — capability (Navy, HADR), awareness (IFC-IOR, radar chains), institutions (IORA, Colombo Conclave). Mark access points at Duqm, Chabahar, Sabang, Agalega.
bank: China factor
Port investments and PLAN deployments are the competing presence — name capability, not intent.
Blue economy
Fisheries, seabed minerals and shipping are the growth half of ‘security and growth’ — MAHASAGAR’s actual novelty.
Island states
Mauritius, Seychelles and the Maldives each show access depends on domestic politics, not on capability.
Indo-Pacific link
IPOI and the Quad’s IPMDA extend the same domain-awareness logic eastward.
Capacity gap
Submarine and MCMV shortfalls constrain the claim; naval expansion plans are the honest caveat.
Africa outreach
MAHASAGAR’s extension to Africa converts an Indian Ocean doctrine into a Global South one.

topics.q: The WHO Pandemic Agreement seeks to reconcile the rapid sharing of pathogens with equitable access to the products derived from them. Discuss the institutional challenge involved.
body: Adopted at the World Health Assembly in May 2025, the Agreement reconciles two things COVID-19 showed to be in tension: rapid sharing of pathogens and sequence data, and equitable access to the products derived.
The institutional problem
• Sharing is immediate, by outbreak countries; benefit is deferred, delivered by countries with manufacturing capacity.
• Without an enforceable link the first group withholds — as Indonesia’s ‘viral sovereignty’ stand on H5N1 showed.

• The answer is Pathogen Access and Benefit-Sharing (PABS): manufacturers commit 20% of real-time production, split between donation and at-cost supply, to WHO. The details sit in an annex still being negotiated.
The unresolved questions
• Whether PABS binds manufacturers who are not party; whether technology transfer is genuinely voluntary, in which case manufacturing stays concentrated; and how it interacts with the amended IHR.
topics.position: India is both a likely early-outbreak country and the largest vaccine manufacturer, so it should press for a PABS annex with binding obligations and invest in genomic surveillance. An agreement that obliges sharing without guaranteeing benefit will be complied with slowly — and slowly is the one thing a pandemic does not permit.
topics.draw: Four boxes in a loop; draw the return arrow as a broken line and label it ‘the enforceable link that does not yet exist’.
topics.figure: ◆ The pandemic bargain outbreak country shares                  manufacturer develops pathogen + sequence                       countermeasure allocation back                PABS: 20% of real-time to the sharer                  production to WHO sharing is immediate, benefit is deferred — without an enforceable return leg the first country withholds A loop with a weak return arrow. Drawing the asymmetry is the institutional problem the question asks you to explain.
bank: IHR amendments
The 2024 IHR amendments create a ‘pandemic emergency’ category and a States Parties committee — the parallel instrument.
Nagoya interaction
Sovereign rights over genetic resources are the legal basis for withholding — PABS must displace it, not coexist.
Digital sequence information
The hardest question: a sequence can be transmitted without the sample, so physical-access rules can be bypassed.
India as manufacturer
Serum Institute and Bharat Biotech make India a duty-bearer, not only a claimant — state this honestly.
One Health
Detection capacity is what makes India a contributor rather than a claimant — invest in surveillance, not only in access.
Financing
The Pandemic Fund is under-capitalised; obligations without financing shift cost to the least able.

topics.t: Global AI Governance and the India AI Impact Summit
topics.q: The India AI Impact Summit, 2026 sought to move global AI governance from a safety debate to inclusive development. Evaluate India’s bridge-building role and the agenda that must follow.
body: Global AI governance ran through Bletchley Park (2023), Seoul (2024) and Paris (2025) — and the India AI Impact Summit (2026), which moved the agenda from safety to inclusive development.
Why the reframing matters
• The safety-first frame centres frontier-model risk among a few firms.
• For most of the world the risks are bias, exclusion, displacement and language coverage — that AI widens rather than narrows the gap.
• India’s bridging position rests on real assets: technical capacity, a DPI record others want to replicate, and no stake in either model.
The unresolved agenda

• Compute access is concentrated with no mechanism to distribute it; data sovereignty — most languages are poorly represented; interoperability , since the EU AI Act and China’s regime fragment the market; and enforcement , there being no AI equivalent of the IAEA.
topics.position: Build on the summit rather than bank it — press for a compute-access facility for the Global South, fund Indian-language datasets as public goods, and export DPI-plus-AI. India’s value is that it speaks for the majority of users without rivalling either producer — an advantage lasting only as long as it also builds capability.
topics.draw: Three summit boxes in sequence — Bletchley (safety) → Seoul → Paris (action) → India (inclusive development) — with four unresolved items listed beneath the last: compute, data, standards, enforcement.
bank: Domestic frame
IndiaAI Mission, AIKosh datasets and the AI Safety Institute are the credibility base — name them.
Algorithmic accountability
The four duties — notice, reasons, audit, appeal — are India’s constitutional contribution to the debate.
Compute
GPU access is the binding constraint for the Global South; a shared facility is the concrete ask.
EU AI Act
Risk-tiered regulation is the most developed model; India’s guidelines are deliberately lighter-touch.
Labour
Displacement in IT-enabled services is India’s specific exposure — the reason it cannot only be a bridge.
Military AI
Autonomous weapons and lethal decision-making sit outside these summits entirely — a gap worth naming.

topics.t: Skilled Mobility, Mode 4 and the Diaspora
topics.q: Restrictions on skilled mobility in developed economies affect India’s services economy more than they affect its diaspora. Critically examine.
body: Restrictions on skilled mobility — H-1B fees and caps, UK salary thresholds, tighter post-study work rights — are usually read as a diaspora issue. They are better understood as a trade issue, restricting India’s services economy far more than the diaspora.
Why the services economy bears the cost
• India’s services exports rest on Mode 4 supply — temporary movement of natural persons — for onsite delivery and project management.
• Visa restriction raises delivery cost, forces local hiring at higher wages and accelerates offshoring; the effect concentrates on mid-sized firms.
• The settled diaspora — over 32 million PIO and NRI, the world’s largest — is largely unaffected, being already inside.
The countervailing points
• Restriction also affects future diaspora formation and student flows; ageing labour markets in Japan, Germany and the Gulf create demand India can meet.
topics.position: Treat mobility as trade — press Mode 4 commitments and social-security totalisation in every FTA, since Indian workers contribute to foreign social security they cannot claim; and secure mutual recognition of qualifications. Visa policy abroad is industrial policy for India’s largest export sector — which is why it belongs in trade negotiations and not only in consular representation.
topics.draw: Two columns — ‘settled diaspora (32 mn, remittances, already inside)’ against ‘services economy (Mode 4, onsite delivery, margins)’. Draw the restriction arrow hitting only the second column.
bank: Totalisation
India has agreements with about twenty countries but not the United States — the single largest uncompensated contribution.
Remittances
India is the world’s largest recipient; the flow is counter-cyclical and stabilises the current account.
Student mobility
Post-study work rights determine student flows, which determine future diaspora — the long-run channel.
Gulf
Kafala reform, wage protection and eMigrate registration matter for the largest and most vulnerable cohort.
Brain drain
Reframe as brain circulation — return migration and diaspora investment need a domestic research environment to attract.
GATS
Mode 4 commitments are the weakest in the GATS schedule; that asymmetry is India’s standing WTO grievance. PART II ◆ 30 FIFTEEN-MARK TOPICS

topics.q: The Governor’s power over State Bills cannot become either an absolute veto or a judicially administered legislative timetable. Critically examine in the light of the Supreme Court’s 2025 rulings.
body: Article 200 gives the Governor four courses — assent, withhold, return a non-Money Bill, or reserve for the President; Article 201 gives the President three. Neither prescribes a period, and that omission is the whole controversy.
The two-stage judicial position
• In State of Tamil Nadu (8 April 2025) a two-judge bench prescribed timelines and declared ten Bills deemed assented under Art 142.

• On the Article 143 reference, a five-judge bench led by CJI B. R. Gavai on 20 November 2025 overruled it: courts cannot prescribe timelines under Art 200; deemed assent has no constitutional existence and Art 142 cannot manufacture it; and decisions under Arts 200–201 are not justiciable pre-enactment.
What survives the check
• A narrow remedy survives: where inaction is prolonged, unexplained and indefinite, a court may act to prevent gridlock — a mandamus to decide, not on how to decide.
• Article 361 grants personal immunity but does not immunise the oﬀice from that oversight.
• The convention remains:                the Governor acts on ministerial advice under Art 163 except in genuine discretion (Shamsher Singh (1974)).
Reform

• Sarkaria and Punchhi supply what the Court declined to impose: appointment in consultation with the Chief Minister from outside active politics; a fixed tenure removable only for cause; a convention of decision within a stated period, reasons recorded; and reservation confined to genuine repugnancy.
topics.position: The Court has correctly refused to legislate a deadline into a deliberate silence — the answer to a political abuse of discretion is a political convention, enforced by transparency rather than by decree.
topics.draw: Draw the fan of four first — the four courses are the marks — then the dashed box. If space is short, draw the fan and write the 20 Nov 2025 holding beside it in three words: no timelines, no deemed assent.
topics.figure: ◆ Articles 200 and 201 — the courses and the limit Bill presented to the Governor, Art 200 assent              withhold              return                   reserve for (non-Money)                the President No time limit prescribed. 20 Nov 2025: no judicial Arttime201: President’s lines, no deemed assent, non-justiciable pre-enactmentthree courses — except prolonged, unexplained, indefinite inaction Four boxes from one node, then the dashed limit. Drawing the four courses proves you know the provision; the dashed box carries the 2025 holding that most answers will get wrong.
bank: Federal friction
Kerala, Punjab, Telangana and Tamil Nadu litigation — the pattern is Opposition-ruled States, which is the political fact behind the legal one.
Article 361
Personal immunity does not bar review of the oﬀice’s inaction — the distinction the 2025 opinion turns on.
Article 143 critique
A five-judge advisory opinion effectively overruling an inter partes judgment is itself contested — link to the Art 143 answer.
Assembly’s remedy
A Bill returned and re-passed must receive assent under the second proviso — the legislature’s own answer to withholding.
Comparative
The UK monarch’s assent is a formality by convention; India wrote discretion into the text and then relied on convention to contain it.
Chief Minister’s role
Punchhi’s proposal that the Governor be appointed in consultation with the CM is the single most consequential unimplemented recommendation.

topics.t: Basic Structure and the Limits of Amendment
topics.q: Article 368 confers a power to amend but not a power to destroy. Critically examine the basic structure doctrine, the objections to it, and its consequences.
body: Article 368 confers a power to amend but, since Kesavananda Bharati (1973), not to destroy the basic structure. It is a judicially crafted implied limitation — nowhere stated in the text, which is both its strength and the ground of every criticism.
How it was arrived at
• Shankari Prasad (1951) and Sajjan Singh (1965) held ‘law’ in Art 13 excluded an amendment; Golaknath (1967) reversed this, making Fundamental Rights unamendable — an untenable absolute.
• Kesavananda’s thirteen judges replaced the absolute with a limit: all is amendable, nothing to the point of destroying identity.
How it has been applied

• Indira Nehru Gandhi (1975) struck down Art 329A; Minerva Mills (1980) struck down Art 368(4) and (5), holding limited amending power and the Part III–IV balance basic features; Waman Rao (1981) fixed 24 April 1973 as the Ninth Schedule cut-off, confirmed in I. R. Coelho (2007).
• It protects judicial review, free and fair elections, federalism, secularism (Bommai (1994)), rule of law and judicial independence (NJAC (2015)).
The objection, and the defence
• The counter-case is real: the content is judge-declared and open-ended, and it allowed the Court to strike down an amendment passed unanimously and ratified by the States.
• The defence is that an unamendable core is the only guard against constitutional self-destruction by a transient majority.
topics.position: The doctrine has been adopted in Bangladesh, Pakistan, Kenya and Uganda and rejected in Singapore and Malaysia — India’s most exported constitutional idea. Basic structure is not a limit on what Parliament may change but on what it may become — a distinction the Constitution’s own silences made necessary.
topics.draw: A vertical timeline of six cases — Shankari Prasad 1951, Golaknath 1967, Kesavananda 1973, Indira Gandhi 1975, Minerva Mills 1980, I. R. Coelho 2007 — with a horizontal line at 1973 marked ‘the limit is set’. Chronology drawn is chronology remembered.
bank: NJAC 2015
The most recent application — judicial primacy in appointments held part of independence, itself a basic feature.
Ninth Schedule
Post-1973 entries are reviewable on basic-structure grounds (I. R. Coelho) — immunity is no longer absolute.
Federalism
Basic structure is the strongest available check on centralising amendments — the federal use of a rights-born doctrine.
Countermajoritarian objection
An unelected court limiting a unanimous Parliament is the sharpest democratic objection — state it, then answer it.
Ordinary legislation
Basic structure does not apply to ordinary laws (Kuldip Nayar, State of AP) — a common error worth avoiding.
Comparative
Germany’s Article 79(3) eternity clause does textually what India’s doctrine does judicially — the cleanest comparison.

topics.q: Judicial independence is not secured by appointments alone; the administrative and financial autonomy of the courts is equally material. Critically examine with reference to the district judiciary.
body: Judicial independence is a basic feature, secured through Arts 124 and 217 on appointment, Arts 125 and 221 on charged salaries, and Arts 124(4) and 218 on removal. But working independence is decided far more by administrative and financial autonomy than by the appointment method that dominates debate.
Appointments — the unresolved half
• Second Judges (1993) and Third Judges (1998) created the collegium; NJAC (2015) struck down the 99th Amendment for compromising judicial primacy.
• The Memorandum of Procedure remains unsettled, so appointments turn on correspondence rather than a published standard — the collegium’s opacity being the strongest argument against it.
Why the district judiciary is the real test
• It carries the bulk of litigation yet depends on the State for buildings, staff and budget — constitutionally independent, administratively helpless.
• Vacancies persist against sanctioned strength; the All India Judges Association litigation has directed pay, cadre and infrastructure reform.
• The dependence is structural:    High Court budgets are cut by the State finance department, and no chargedexpenditure protection covers the subordinate judiciary.
Internal accountability

• Removal under Art 124(4) has never succeeded, so the only working mechanism is the non-statutory, unpublished in-house procedure. The Judicial Standards and Accountability Bill lapsed; the Restatement of Values (1997) is voluntary.
topics.position: A published Memorandum of Procedure with criteria and timelines; a collegium secretariat recording reasons; an All India Judicial Service under Art 312; and a charged, non-lapsable judicial infrastructure fund routed to High Courts. Independence contested only at appointment leaves the daily dependence untouched — a judge appointed impeccably still sits in a courtroom the executive builds and funds.
topics.draw: Reproduce the two-column table. Writing ‘secured’ and ‘unsecured’ as headings does more work than a paragraph of assertion.
topics.figure: ◆ Judicial independence — four legs, two secured secured                                      unsecured salary charged, Arts 125, 221                court budget voted by the State removal by special majority                  no working internal accountability collegium primacy (NJAC, 2015)               MoP unsettled; staff and infrastructure with the State Four rows, two columns. The argument is the right column — independence contested only at appointment leaves the daily dependence untouched.
bank: Pendency
Over five crore cases; judge-population ratio far below the Law Commission’s 50 per million — infrastructure is the binding constraint.
AIJS
Opposed by States and some High Courts on federal and language grounds — state the objection, not only the proposal.
Post-retirement
Post-retirement appointments are the standing conflict-of-interest critique — a cooling-off period is the standard answer.
Tribunalisation
L. Chandra Kumar (1997) preserved High Court review under Arts 226/227 as a basic feature no tribunal may oust.
Transparency
Collegium resolutions are now published, but reasons for supersession are not — the gap that sustains the criticism.
Contempt power
An unbounded contempt jurisdiction sits uneasily with accountability — the honest tension to name.

topics.t: Separation of Powers and the Regulatory State
topics.q: Statutory regulators increasingly combine rule-making, investigation and adjudication within a single body. Examine the safeguards that the separation of powers demands.
body: India follows a functional, not rigid, separation of powers — Ram Jawaya Kapur (1955) treats it as a basic feature without an American-style division. The diﬀiculty is the statutory regulator, which combines rule-making, investigation and adjudication: the same body writes the rule, prosecutes its breach and decides the case.
Why the combination is tolerated
• Regulated sectors are technical and fast-moving: a legislature cannot write spectrum or securities-disclosure rules in time, and a generalist court cannot adjudicate them competently.
• So SEBI, TRAI, CCI, IRDAI and the Data Protection Board get all three functions, with expertise as the justification.
What separation of powers then demands

• Functional separation inside the body: the investigating wing must not decide; and L. Chandra Kumar (1997) preserved High Court review under Articles 226 and 227 as a basic feature no tribunal may oust.

• Independence of appointment and tenure: Madras Bar Association and Rojer Mathew (2019) struck down rules giving the executive dominance in selection and short, renewable terms — renewability being the standing threat.

• Reasoned orders and transparent rule-making: mandatory consultation, publication of comments and a regulatory impact assessment, since a rule made without notice is legislation without a legislature.
• Appellate separation: an independent appellate tribunal, and laying of regulations before Parliament.
topics.position: The Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission draft code is the template — statutory consultation, cost-benefit analysis, reasoned decisions, a separated adjudicatory wing, performance reporting to Parliament, and plural appointment with fixed non-renewable tenure. Concentrating three functions is a price paid for expertise — legitimate only where procedure supplies the separation the structure has surrendered.
topics.draw: Three spokes from one hub, then the dashed remedy box. Write L. Chandra Kumar and Rojer Mathew inside the dashed box — the two cases are the safeguard.
topics.figure: ◆ A regulator’s three hats makes the rule                             investigates breach Regulator adjudicates the case separation must be supplied by procedure: consultation + reasons ◆ separated adjudicatory wing ◆ fixed non-renewable tenure ◆ appeal + Art 226 review (L. Chandra Kumar) Three spokes and a dashed remedy box. It states the constitutional problem and its answer in one figure — which is what a 15-marker on the regulatory State wants.
bank: Data Protection Board
The newest instance — and the weakest, since it adjudicates without rule-making or suo motu power.
Tribunalisation
Tribunals Reforms Act 2021 re-enacted struck-down provisions — a legislative-judicial standoff worth naming.
Delegated legislation
Regulators’ regulations often escape laying before Parliament — the largest unscrutinised body of rules.
Competition law
CCI combines investigation (DG) and adjudication; the DG’s functional separation is the standard defence.
Comparative
The US Administrative Procedure Act codifies notice-and-comment and separates administrative law judges — the model FSLRC borrowed.
Federalism
Central regulators over Concurrent or State subjects (electricity, education) raise a separate federal objection.

topics.t: Right to Information and Informational Privacy
topics.q: Informational privacy and the citizen’s right to know are complementary checks on power, yet the post-DPDP framework risks treating them as competing absolutes. Critically analyse and propose a reconciliation.
body: Both check arbitrary power from the same source — the right to know from Art 19(1)(a), aﬀirmed in Raj Narain (1975) and S. P.
Gupta (1981), and privacy from Art 21, declared fundamental in Puttaswamy (2017). Complementary in principle, they are in tension in statute.
Where the statutes diverge
• Section 8(1)(j) of the RTI Act 2005 exempted personal information unless disclosure served a larger public interest, and allowed anything not deniable to Parliament — a built-in balancing test.
• Section 44(3) of the DPDP Act 2023 amended it to exempt all personal information without qualification, removing both the public-interest override and the parliamentary-disclosure proviso.
• The consequence is practical: beneficiary lists, muster rolls, asset declarations and recruitment marks are all ‘personal information’.
The two positions
• For the amendment: Puttaswamy makes personal data a fundamental right, so an oﬀicer applying an ad hoc test is an inadequate guardian; RTI has been used for harassment.

• Against: transparency in public life is a corruption safeguard, and oﬀicial conduct is not private — Girish Ramchandra Deshpande (2012) had already narrowed disclosure; s.44(3) completes the closure.
• Both rest on the same weak enforcement — Commission vacancies and an executive-appointed Data Protection Board.
topics.position: Restore the public-interest override with a structured proportionality test rather than oﬀicer discretion; distinguish oﬀicial conduct from personal life; adopt an anonymisation-first duty so aggregates are released even where identifiers are withheld; and fill Commission vacancies within a statutory deadline. Privacy and transparency limit power in the same direction — treating them as rivals is a drafting failure, not a constitutional necessity.
topics.draw: Two arrows pointing the same way at a box labelled ‘arbitrary power’ — one from ‘right to know, Art 19(1)(a)’, one from ‘privacy, Art 21’. Below, a wedge labelled ‘s.44(3) DPDP’ driven between them.
bank: Proportionality test
Legality, legitimate aim, necessity, balancing — the four limbs are the reconciliation tool, so name them.
Electoral transparency
ADR (2024) on electoral bonds treated donor identity as public-interest information — the counter-authority to s.44(3).
Information Commissions
Vacancies and delayed appointments make the right unenforceable; Anjali Bhardwaj (2019) directed timely appointment.
Public servants
Asset declarations under the Lokpal Act were diluted; s.44(3) closes the RTI route to the same information.
Comparative
The EU balances GDPR against access-to-documents regulations through a public-interest test — the model India removed.
Journalism
No journalistic exemption exists in the DPDP Act, unlike GDPR Article 85 — a significant and under-argued gap.

topics.t: Article 356 and President’s Rule after Bommai
topics.q: Bommai converted a political weapon into a justiciable act. Examine how far Article 356 has been disciplined, and where the pressure on federalism has shifted.
body: Article 356 permits Union takeover where the President is satisfied, on the Governor’s report or otherwise, that government cannot be carried on constitutionally. Invoked over a hundred times before 1994, it was the most abused federal provision — and judicial, not legislative, action disciplined it.
What Bommai settled
• S. R. Bommai (1994) held the proclamation justiciable for mala fides or wholly extraneous material.
• The floor of the House is the only test of a government’s majority, not the Governor’s subjective assessment.
• The Assembly may be dissolved only after both Houses approve under Art 356(3); a government acting against secularism may be dismissed; and a wrongly dismissed government may be restored.
Why it has held, and where the pressure shifted
• Parliamentary approval within two months, the floor test and the restoration remedy removed the profit from the manoeuvre — proclamations have fallen sharply.

• Rameshwar Prasad (2006) struck down dissolution of the Bihar Assembly on a report about apprehended defections; Nabam Rebia (2016) restricted the Governor’s power to advance a session or act against advice.
• Pressure has migrated to the Governor’s other powers — assent under Art 200, the timing of a floor test, the discretion to invite.
topics.position: Sarkaria and Punchhi recommend Art 356 as a last resort after warning; localised breakdown met by targeted rather than State-wide proclamation; a speaking Governor’s report laid before Parliament; and a floor-test timetable prescribed by law. Bommai converted a political weapon into a justiciable act — the remaining federal risk now sits not in Article 356 but in the discretions that surround it.
topics.draw: A funnel narrowing from ‘100+ invocations before 1994’ to ‘rare after Bommai’, with three arrows leaking sideways out of the narrow end labelled ‘Art 200 assent’, ‘timing of floor test’, ‘discretion to invite’. The leaks are the argument.
bank: Art 355
The Union’s duty to protect States is the constitutional basis for lesser, targeted intervention short of 356.
Emergency provisions
The 44th Amendment disciplined Art 352 textually; Art 356 was disciplined judicially — the contrast is the point.
Governor’s report
Publishing it is the cheapest discipline; Sarkaria asked for it in 1988 and it is still not the norm.
Anti-defection link
Defection-driven government collapse is the modern route to instability, not proclamation — Subhash Desai (2023).
Delhi / UT question
Art 239AA disputes show a parallel federal contest where the Governor analogue is the Lieutenant Governor.
Comparative
US federalism has no analogue — State governments cannot be dismissed, which sharpens the Indian anomaly.

topics.t: The Tenth Schedule — the Adjudication Gap
topics.q: Vesting the adjudication of defection in a presiding oﬀicer who retains party aﬀiliation places the object of the Tenth Schedule at risk. Examine the case for reform.
body: The Tenth Schedule (52nd Amendment, 1985) disqualifies a member who gives up party membership or votes against a whip; the 91st Amendment (2003) removed the split exception, leaving only a two-thirds merger. It bought stability with the legislator’s deliberative independence.
What it achieved, and what it cost
• It ended the Aaya Ram Gaya Ram era of retail defection, and made the mandate meaningful, since a voter chooses a party as much as a person.

• But the whip applies to every vote, so a member cannot dissent without losing the seat — the House becomes a device for counting parties. Kihoto Hollohan (1992) upheld the Schedule but read down Paragraph 7 to preserve review, noting the object was defection, not honest dissent.
The adjudication problem
• The decision rests with the Speaker, who retains party aﬀiliation and whose ruling decides whether a government survives.

• The Schedule prescribes no time limit, so delay achieves what a decision could not. Keisham Meghachandra Singh (2020) urged an independent tribunal and three-month disposal; Subhash Desai (2023) re-exposed the gap.
• Wholesale defection survives through merger engineering and mass resignation.
topics.position: Transfer adjudication to an independent tribunal, or to the President or Governor on the Election Commission’s advice, as Dinesh Goswami and the Law Commission’s 170th Report recommend; confine the whip to confidence and money votes; and impose a statutory three-month deadline. A law meant to stop the sale of loyalty now suppresses its honest exercise — narrow the whip and move the umpire off the field.
topics.draw: Five boxes and the dashed reform box. Circle ‘no time limit’. If you draw nothing else in the paper, draw this — it converts a description into an indictment.
topics.figure: ◆ Anti-defection — the adjudication gap member votes            petition to         Speaker decides against whip             Speaker             — no time limit government survives             judicial review meanwhile                  only after (Kihoto) Reform: independent tribunal (Keisham Meghachandra); threemonth deadline; whip limited to confidence and money votes The figure’s whole value is the box marked ‘no time limit’ — delay achieves what a decision could not, and that is the reform case.
bank: Kihoto qualification
Review lies only after the order, so delay is the effective immunity — the single sharpest line available.
Merger route
Two-thirds merger is now the standard device; wholesale defection is lawful where retail defection is not.
Party democracy
The whip presupposes internal party democracy that the Representation of the People Act does not require.
Comparative
The UK has no anti-defection law; floor-crossing is lawful and disciplined by the electorate.
Speaker’s neutrality
Link to the India–UK Speaker comparison — resignation from party is the structural fix.
Constitutional morality
Subhash Desai (2023) held the whip is appointed by the party, not the legislature party — a significant clarification.

topics.q: The freezing of the allocation of seats among the States was a federal compromise; its unwinding is a federal problem. Critically examine the constitutional and political choices.
body: Article 81 requires Lok Sabha seats allocated by population and readjusted after each census (Art 82). The 42nd Amendment (1976) froze allocation to 1971 and the 84th (2001) extended it to the first census after 2026 — so States pursuing family planning would not lose weight.
Why unwinding is a federal problem
• Fertility decline has been uneven, so strict proportionality would transfer seats from the south and west to the northern belt.
• States that met a national policy objective would be penalised for it — the perverse incentive at the heart of the dispute.
• The 16th Finance Commission retains a demographic performance criterion to offset this fiscally; representation has no equivalent.
The constitutional choices
• Extend the freeze: simple, but entrenches malapportionment and offends one person, one vote.
• Full proportionality: constitutionally orthodox, politically destabilising.
• Expand the House: increase total seats so no State loses in absolute terms even as relative shares shift — Article 81(1)(a) permits up to 550.
• Weight the second chamber: a weighted rather than proportional Rajya Sabha, requiring a Fourth Schedule amendment.
Sequencing
• The 106th Amendment conditions women’s reservation on delimitation, so the two questions move together.
topics.position: A statutory Delimitation Commission with State representation and published criteria; a formula combining population with a demographic-performance weight; expansion rather than redistribution; and settlement before the census — a rule agreed in advance is a compromise, one agreed afterwards is a contest. Delimitation is arithmetic only if the federal bargain is ignored — the task is to keep representation proportionate without making demographic success a political liability.
topics.draw: Four boxes fanned from one, and bold the third. Write ‘Art 81: up to 550’ and ‘106th Amdt’ beneath — two provisions carry the whole answer.
topics.figure: ◆ Delimitation — the four choices Freeze ends: first census after 2026 (84th Amdt) extend                 full                    expand              weight the the freeze          proportionality            the House             Rajya Sabha only (c) avoids a State losing seats in absolute terms — Art 81 permits up to 550 106th Amendment ties women’s reservation to this Four options from one node with the workable one in bold. Presenting the choice set is what turns a description of the problem into an evaluation of it.
bank: One person, one vote
Malapportionment now runs several-fold between constituencies — the equality argument for unfreezing.
Second chamber
Weighting the Rajya Sabha needs a Fourth Schedule amendment; link to the Rajya Sabha–Senate comparison.
Women’s reservation
The 106th Amendment cannot operate until delimitation happens — a political incentive to delay both.
Union Territories / J&K
Delimitation there proceeded separately — a precedent both sides cite.
Language and region
The dispute maps onto the older north–south political cleavage; treat it as federal, not communal.
Comparative
The US caps the House at 435 and reapportions decennially; the cap is what makes each census a zero-sum contest.

topics.q: Cooperative federalism requires institutionalised consultation rather than episodic political accommodation. Critically evaluate the adequacy of India’s intergovernmental forums.
body: Cooperative federalism requires institutionalised consultation — a standing forum with a secretariat, an agenda and a record — not episodic accommodation at summits. India’s forums exist; their working is the problem.
The institutional map and its weaknesses
• The Inter-State Council (Art 263), established in 1990 on Sarkaria’s recommendation, is recommendatory and has met rarely.
• Zonal Councils are chaired by the Union Home Minister and largely advisory.
• NITI Aayog’s Governing Council replaced the Planning Commission’s transfer function with a convening one, so it advises without resources.

• The GST Council (Art 279A) is the outlier — weighted voting producing binding outcomes — but Mohit Minerals (2022) held its recommendations persuasive, and the Centre’s one-third bloc is an effective veto.
• River-water disputes go to tribunals under the 1956 Act, which are slow and whose awards are contested.
Why episodic accommodation fails
• Without a secretariat, issues are raised and lost; without a record, positions are deniable; without an agenda cycle, only crises reach the table.
• So genuinely federal questions — delimitation, devolution, All India Service deputation, Delhi’s services — are settled by litigation, which produces a winner rather than a bargain.
topics.position: The Punchhi Commission prescription: a permanent Inter-State Council with a full-time secretariat, three meetings a year and published minutes; referral of Concurrent List Bills to it before introduction; a standing dispute-resolution mechanism on the GST Council model; and a single permanent river-water tribunal. Federalism works where bargaining is continuous and recorded — India litigates because it has not built the table at which it would otherwise negotiate.
topics.draw: A table with four chairs labelled Inter-State Council, Zonal Councils, NITI Governing Council, GST Council. Tick only the GST Council and write ‘binding, weighted, constitutional’ beside it; write ‘no secretariat, no record, no cycle’ across the other three.
bank: Art 263
The Council may investigate and advise on disputes — a power never used, which is itself the finding.
All India Services
Cadre rules amendments and deputation disputes are the sharpest current friction; Art 312 is the anchor.
Delhi / Art 239AA
Services control litigation and the 2023 Act show the cost of settling federal questions in court.
Fiscal side
Read with the Finance Commission and GST answers — the divisible pool is the fiscal half of the same bargain.
Comparative
Australia’s Council of Australian Governments and Germany’s Bundesrat institutionalise exactly what the ISC does not.
Centrally sponsored schemes
Design without State consent converts cooperation into conditionality — consolidate and untie.

topics.t: The Rajya Sabha and the United States Senate
topics.q: Compare the Rajya Sabha and the Senate of the United States as instruments of federal representation. Does the Indian scheme adequately protect less populous States? Both are second chambers for federal representation, differing on what matters most: the Senate gives equal representation to every State, the Rajya Sabha seats by population under the Fourth Schedule. India’s second chamber reproduces, rather than corrects, the asymmetry of the first.
body: The structural comparison
• Composition: Senate — two per State, directly elected since 1913. Rajya Sabha — elected by MLAs through STV, twelve nominated under Art 80(3).

• Powers: the Senate is co-equal, with exclusive treaty-ratification and confirmation powers. The Rajya Sabha cannot amend or reject a Money Bill (Art 109) and is outvoted in a joint sitting (Art 108).
• Distinctive Indian powers: Art 249 authorises legislation on a State List entry and Art 312 an All India Service — powers the Lok Sabha lacks.
Does the Indian scheme protect smaller States?
• Only weakly. Uttar Pradesh returns thirty-one members while several north-eastern States return one — a dominant State is dominant in both chambers.
• Removal of domicile in 2003, upheld in Kuldip Nayar (2006), loosened the member–State link further.
• Against this: its federal weight lies less in arithmetic than in Arts 249 and 312 and in revision — and the Senate’s equality is itself criticised as a democratic distortion.
topics.position: Federal protection runs through the Finance Commission, the GST Council and the courts rather than the second chamber.
topics.conc: A weighted formula and restored domicile would strengthen it — but the Rajya Sabha was designed as a chamber of revision with federal features, not as a federal veto — which is why delimitation is a federal question, not an arithmetical one.
topics.draw: Reproduce the four rows. The first row is the thesis and the last row is the redemption — draw both even if you drop the middle two.
topics.figure: ◆ Rajya Sabha and the US Senate Rajya Sabha                                   Senate seats by population (Fourth                   two per State, equal Schedule) indirect, MLAs, STV; 12 nominated             direct since the 17th Amdt, 1913 no Money Bill power; outvoted in              co-equal; treaties and confirmations joint sitting Arts 249 and 312 unique to it                 no equivalent A comparison table is the correct form for any ‘compare with another country’ question — four attributes, both columns, no prose needed.
bank: Joint sitting
Held three times; the Lok Sabha’s numbers always prevail — the structural asymmetry in one fact.
Nominated members
Art 80(3) intends expertise; the practice is contested — a short, fair line either way.
Anti-defection
Applies to Rajya Sabha members too, so the chamber of revision is also whipped.
Money Bill link
Certification under Art 110(3) is how the second chamber is bypassed — connect the two answers.
German Bundesrat
State governments are represented directly with weighted votes — the model India’s ‘weighted’ option borrows.
Delimitation
Weighting the Rajya Sabha is the fourth delimitation option — the two answers are one argument.

topics.q: Uncodified privileges preserve legislative autonomy but leave the rights of citizens uncertain. Examine the case for and against codification under Articles 105 and 194.
body: Articles 105 and 194 confer freedom of speech in the House and immunity for anything said or voted, and provide that other privileges shall be ‘as defined by Parliament by law’ — until then, those of the House of Commons in 1950. Parliament has never legislated, so privileges remain uncodified and their limits unknown.
The case for leaving them uncodified
• Codification invites judicial construction of every clause, drawing courts into the House’s internal working.
• Articles 122 and 212 bar review of procedural irregularity for that reason.
• Flexibility lets the House meet obstruction it could not anticipate, and its own restraint has kept punishment rare.
The case against
• A citizen — typically a journalist — faces a power of unascertainable content, exercised by a body that is complainant, prosecutor and judge, with no appeal and no defined penalty.

• Keshav Singh (1965) exposed the conflict with Article 21 without resolving it; Raja Ram Pal (2007) held privilege reviewable for illegality though not for procedure; and Sita Soren (2024), overruling P. V. Narasimha Rao (1998), held a legislator taking a bribe to vote enjoys no immunity under Art 105(2) — immunity protects the deliberative function, not its corruption.
topics.position: The workable middle is calibrated codification — define only the punitive edge: the offences constituting contempt, the maximum penalty, and procedure including notice, hearing and appeal, leaving deliberative privileges uncodified, as the National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution recommended. The choice is not between autonomy and rights — it is between a punitive power with known limits and one with none.
topics.draw: Two columns — ‘deliberative privileges: leave uncodified’ and ‘punitive power: codify offences, penalty, procedure, appeal’. The split is the answer; a single column is not.
bank: Sita Soren 2024
A seven-judge bench overruling a 1998 precedent — the most citable recent development in the area.
Media
Reporting of proceedings is protected by the Parliamentary Proceedings (Protection of Publication) Act 1977.
Procedural irregularity is non-justiciable; illegality is not — the distinction that governs the whole field.
State legislatures
Art 194 privileges are exercised more frequently and with less restraint than in Parliament.
UK comparison
The Commons has itself moved away from penal jurisdiction; India inherited a power the original has abandoned.
Expulsion
Raja Ram Pal upheld expulsion in the cash-for-query case while asserting reviewability — both halves matter.

topics.q: The 74th Amendment gave cities elections without giving them government. Critically examine the devolution of functions, finances and functionaries.
body: The 74th Amendment (1992) gave municipalities constitutional status, a five-year term, State Finance Commissions under Art 243Y and a Twelfth Schedule of eighteen functions. It did not mandate devolution: Art 243W leaves it to the State legislature ‘as it may by law’ — creating bodies without guaranteeing them power.
The three missing devolutions

• Functions:  the Twelfth Schedule is illustrative, and core services — water, sewerage, transport, planning — are retained by State parastatals, so the elected mayor does not control the service the voter holds him responsible for.
• Finances: own-source revenue is thin, property tax far below potential because valuation is outdated, and municipalities depend on transfers and grants that are tied.
• Functionaries: staff are State cadre, appointed and transferred by the State, so accountability runs upward rather than to the council.
The structural weaknesses
• The mayor is mostly indirectly elected for a short term with a ceremonial role, while the State-appointed commissioner holds executive power — an inversion of accountability.
• Metropolitan and District Planning Committees under Arts 243ZD and 243ZE are largely unconstituted, so no body plans at the scale cities function at; and elections are frequently delayed.
topics.position: Statutory activity mapping assigning each Twelfth Schedule function to a tier with matching funds and staff; directly elected mayors with executive authority; GIS-based property tax with a floor rate; Metropolitan Planning Committees with real powers; and untied grants linked to own-revenue performance. India created a third tier and withheld the third set of powers — the 74th Amendment gave cities elections without giving them government.
topics.draw: Three columns — Functions, Finances, Functionaries — each with an arrow that stops short of the municipality box. The three truncated arrows are the answer.
bank: Art 243W
‘As the legislature may by law’ is the permissive clause that makes the whole Amendment conditional — quote it.
State Finance Commissions
Constituted late and reports rarely acted on; no constitutional consequence follows.
Municipal bonds
Borrowing needs a rated revenue stream, which needs property tax reform first — the sequence matters.
Parastatals
Water boards and development authorities are the real urban government; naming them is the sharpest point.
Urban poverty
Non-portable services and rental insecurity are municipal failures — connect to the urban poverty answer.
Comparative
Directly elected executive mayors in London and New York are the model; India’s commissioner system is colonial in origin.

topics.q: The generalist–specialist debate is a false binary unless recruitment, tenure, learning and accountability are reformed together. Discuss.
body: The debate is posed as a binary — a generalist moving between departments against a specialist who stays. It is false, because both failures have a common cause: tenure. A generalist who stays two years learns nothing; a specialist who cannot rise has no reason to stay.
The case for each
• The generalist supplies coordination across silos, political judgement and the weighing of competing interests — skills an expert is not selected for.
• The specialist supplies depth in domains now genuinely technical — financial regulation, spectrum, public health.
The Second ARC recommended oﬀicers choose a domain after general service and senior posts be filled against domain requirements.
Why neither works at present

• Tenure is short and transfers arbitrary — the largest destroyer of both continuity and expertise, which T. S. R. Subramanian (2013) met by directing a two-year minimum tenure and a Civil Services Board.

• Promotion is seniority-dominated, so specialisation carries no return; lateral entry supplies specialists but raises reservation and institutional-memory questions; and post-retirement assignments distort incentives.
• Accountability rests on the annual appraisal and Art 311, making removal for non-performance effectively unavailable.
topics.position: Reform recruitment, tenure, learning and accountability together: domain allocation after the first field tenure; a statutory minimum tenure enforced by a Civil Services Board; Mission Karmayogi competencies tied to posting eligibility; and a mid-career filter with real consequences. The choice is not between the generalist and the specialist but between an oﬀicer who stays long enough to learn the job and one who does not.
topics.draw: Two columns, generalist and specialist, converging on a single box below labelled ‘common cause: short, arbitrary tenure’. Drawing the convergence is what proves the binary is false.
bank: Art 311
Constitutional protection was designed against political victimisation; it now shields non-performance — state both halves.
Prakash Singh 2006
Police reform’s fixed tenure and State Security Commission is the same design applied to one service.
Lateral entry
Reservation in single-post recruitment is the live legal objection; a cadre-wide scheme would attract it.
Federal dimension
State cadres deliver most citizen-facing service; reform confined to the AIS misses where capacity actually binds.
Gender and diversity
Representation in senior posts remains skewed; domain allocation must not reproduce it.
Comparative
Singapore and the UK Fast Stream both stream by domain early while retaining a coordinating generalist core.

topics.q: AI can make public services anticipatory and accessible, but it may also automate administrative opacity. Analyse the governance framework required for responsible use by the State.
body: AI can make public services anticipatory — identifying the eligible before they apply, triaging health risk — and simultaneously opaque, automating discretion beyond the reach of the person it affects. The governance question is how to capture the first without conceding the second.
Where the gains are real
• Proactive delivery from linked registries, so a benefit reaches a household without an application.
• Multilingual, voice-first interfaces reaching the non-literate through Bhashini.
• Predictive maintenance and fraud detection that free scarce inspection capacity, and decision support where expert supply is the binding constraint.
Where it automates opacity
• The model’s reasons are not the oﬀicial’s, so a reasoned order becomes a formality — and vendor proprietary claims block audit of logic the State is accountable for.
• Training data encodes historical exclusion, so the system repeats past error with new authority.
• Error at scale differs in kind from error in a file: one misconfigured rule denies a hundred thousand people silently.
Inclusion as a design obligation

• Language, disability, connectivity and explainability must be procurement requirements, not later additions — an interface built for English on a smartphone excludes by design. The India AI Governance Guidelines adopt this framing.
topics.position: A published algorithmic impact assessment before deployment in any rights-affecting domain; notice of automation and reasons in the person’s language; retained logs with independent bias audits; a human appeal on a statutory clock; procurement standards barring unauditable systems; and a named accountable oﬀicer for every deployed system. Anticipatory government is worth having only if the citizen can still ask why — automation must expand the reasons available, not retire them.
topics.draw: Reuse the four-duties fan from the algorithmic-fairness answer — notice, reasons, audit, human appeal — and add a fifth box, ‘named accountable oﬀicer’. One figure serves both questions.
bank: Constitutional anchor
Arts 14 and 21, Maneka on reasons, Puttaswamy on proportionality — the doctrinal spine of the answer.
Welfare exclusion
Aadhaar seeding mismatch is the commonest automated denial — the concrete Indian example.
Policing
Facial recognition and predictive policing engage Art 21 liberty with the weakest safeguards of any use case.
Data protection
The DPDP Act has no equivalent of GDPR Art 22 on automated decision-making — a nameable statutory gap.
Capacity
The State cannot audit what it cannot understand; in-house technical capacity is the binding constraint.
Global governance
Link to the India AI Impact Summit — domestic practice is what makes the international position credible.

topics.q: Schemes designed for saturation and schemes designed for targeting fail in characteristically different ways. Examine, and assess what integrated registries add and risk.
body: Saturation covers everyone in a defined category; targeting reaches only the deserving. They are not degrees of one approach — they fail in characteristically different ways, and integrated registries change the failure mode of both.
How each fails

• Saturation fails by inclusion: fiscal cost, benefit to those who do not need it, and a category definition that is itself the rationing device. It also stops at the last mile — ‘saturation’ is declared on the registry, while those never registered stay invisible by construction.

• Targeting fails by exclusion: proxy means tests misclassify at the margin, income is unobservable in an informal economy, and the burden of proof falls on those least able to bear it. Exclusion error is the graver failure and is invisible in savings figures.
What integrated registries add, and risk
• Linked databases enable portable and proactive entitlement — a migrant drawing rations under ONORC, or a benefit pushed without an application.

• The risks mirror this: digital exclusion, since authentication failure and seeding mismatch deny at the point of delivery; function creep, as a welfare database becomes surveillance infrastructure; and opacity, since a denial by mismatch has no author to appeal to.
topics.position: Publish and audit exclusion error alongside coverage; retain offline channels with a statutory grievance route; enforce purpose limitation under the DPDP Act; replace the 2011 base with a dynamic, appealable registry; and choose saturation where exclusion is costlier than inclusion. The measure of a welfare system is not how many it reached but who it could not see.
topics.draw: Reproduce the two-column table and underline ‘invisible in savings figures’. That phrase is the analytical core of the whole answer.
topics.figure: ◆ Saturation and targeting fail differently saturation                                    targeting fails by inclusion — fiscal cost              fails by exclusion — invisible in savings the category is the rationing device          proxy means test misclassifies ‘saturated’ on the registry only              burden of proof on the applicant Two failure modes side by side. The same table answers welfare design, poverty measurement and the digital-registry question alike.
bank: PMGKAY / NFSA
Free foodgrain to two-thirds is saturation within a targeted category — both logics operating together.
Ayushman Bharat
SECC-2011-based targeting with a stale base is the clearest live example of the exclusion problem.
Puttaswamy (Aadhaar)
No benefit may be denied for authentication failure — the constitutional answer to digital exclusion.
Fiscal argument
Universalising a small benefit can cost less to administer than targeting it — compare delivery cost, not just outlay.
Urban gap
Registries are residence-anchored; the urban poor and migrants are excluded by the unit of enrolment itself.
Social audit
Individually verifiable registries are auditable by beneficiaries — pair the two answers.

topics.t: A Single Regulator for Higher Education
topics.q: A single higher-education regulator may reduce fragmentation, but centralisation is not the same as autonomy. Critically examine the Viksit Bharat Shiksha Adhishthan Bill, 2025.
body: Higher education is regulated by the UGC, the AICTE, the NCTE and a dozen professional councils — overlapping mandates, duplicated compliance, no coherent quality regime. NEP 2020 proposed a single Higher Education Commission of India with four verticals; the Viksit Bharat Shiksha Adhishthan Bill 2025 is the vehicle.
The case for consolidation

• Separating the four functions — regulation, accreditation, funding, academic standard-setting — into distinct verticals removes the central conflict in which the same body funds an institution and judges it.

• Single-window compliance reduces paperwork that falls hardest on small institutions; a common accreditation framework makes quality comparable; and graded autonomy becomes possible only once accreditation is credible.
The case against, which is about federalism and diversity
• Education is Concurrent and States run most institutions and students, so a centralised regulator shifts control without shifting financing responsibility.
• Uniform standards can flatten institutional diversity — a tribal-area college and a research university judged on one scale.

• Concentrating rule-making, accreditation and enforcement raises the same separation-of-powers question as any regulator. And centralisation is not autonomy — one regulator can be more intrusive than four if its powers are wider.
topics.position: Functional separation with distinct boards and no cross-membership; State representation and a defined sphere left to State regulators; accreditation by multiple independent agencies rather than a monopoly; autonomy graded to accreditation outcome; and published reasons and appeal against every regulatory decision. Fragmentation and centralisation are both failures of regulatory design — the object is a small number of clearly separated functions, not a single large authority.
topics.draw: Four boxes — regulation, accreditation, funding, standards — currently overlapping, redrawn as four separated boxes under one roof. Draw the ‘before’ and ‘after’ side by side; the separation is the reform.
bank: NAAC reform
Binary accreditation and multiple agencies address the credibility problem that graded autonomy depends on.
Foreign universities
UGC regulations permitting foreign campuses need a regulator with clear standard-setting authority.
Professional councils
Medical and legal education have their own statutes; a single regulator must reconcile or exclude them.
Funding vertical
A separate funding body is the key anti-conflict reform; without it consolidation is cosmetic.
Autonomy in practice
Institutional autonomy means academic and financial freedom, not exemption from accountability.
Comparative
England’s Oﬀice for Students separates regulation from research funding — the model the four-vertical design borrows.

topics.t: Parliament’s Deliberative Capacity and the Standing Committees
topics.q: Parliament’s authority rests on deliberation. Examine the evidence of its decline and the role of Department-related Standing Committees in arresting it.
body: Parliament’s authority rests on the assumption that a Bill is improved by scrutiny before it becomes law. That has weakened along four measurable dimensions — sitting days, legislative time, disruption, and instruments that bypass debate.
The four indicators
• Sitting days have fallen far below early levels, and no minimum exists — Art 85 requires only six months not elapse between sessions.
• Legislative time: many Bills pass with brief debate, and Demands for Grants are largely guillotined.
• Disruption is now routine, because debate the government wins on numbers offers no leverage.
• Bypass instruments:      ordinances under Art 123, re-promulgation condemned in Krishna Kumar Singh (2017); Money Bill certification; and skeletal statutes leaving substance to rules.
Why the Standing Committees matter

• The twenty-four Department-related Standing Committees (1993) examine demands for grants, Bills referred to them and policy. They meet in private and are not televised — which is why they remain the one place the House deliberates across party lines.

• Their influence is uneven because referral is discretionary and the share of Bills referred has fallen sharply; recommendations are not binding; and membership rotates annually, defeating the expertise the design assumes.
topics.position: A statutory minimum of sitting days — NCRWC suggested 120 and 100; a calendar fixed in advance; a defined share of time for the opposition; mandatory committee referral with a recorded reason for exemption; and committee tenure of two to three years with a research unit. A legislature that neither sits nor scrutinises transfers authority to the executive by default — no amendment is needed for Parliament to become marginal.
topics.draw: Four descending bars — sitting days, legislative time, Bills referred to committees, private members’ Bills passed — with ‘disruption’ and ‘ordinances’ drawn as two arrows bypassing the House entirely.
bank: Committee success
PAC and the Estimates and Public Undertakings Committees are chaired by the opposition by convention — it works, so extend it.
Pre-legislative consultation
The 2014 policy requiring publication of draft Bills is advisory and unevenly observed.
Anti-defection link
The whip removes the individual member’s voice, so debate cannot change an outcome — the incentive behind disruption.
Private members’ Bills
Almost none pass; a guaranteed slot and a vote would restore a channel of individual initiative.
Question Hour
