Its suspension during the pandemic showed how easily accountability instruments are set aside.
Comparative
The UK’s opposition-day convention and Westminster Hall debates give the minority guaranteed floor time.

topics.t: Universal Health Coverage and Primary Care
topics.q: The expansion of publicly financed health insurance does not by itself amount to universal health coverage. Analyse the roles of primary care, public-health capacity and financial protection.
body: Universal health coverage means everyone receives the services they need, of adequate quality, without financial hardship. Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY covers hospitalisation up to ₹5 lakh for the bottom two-fifths — one of the three dimensions.
Why insurance alone does not close the gap
• The largest share of out-of-pocket expenditure is outpatient — consultation, diagnostics and medicines for chronic disease — none of it covered.
• Insurance is demand-side: it pays for care but creates no facility, so where supply is weak the entitlement is unusable.
• It also incentivises hospitalisation over prevention, since only the expensive event is reimbursed.
• Public health spending remains near 2% of GDP against the National Health Policy 2017 target of 2.5%.
The three legs that must move together

• Primary care: Ayushman Arogya Mandirs with an expanded package covering NCD screening, mental health and elderly care, staffed by a Community Health Oﬀicer — primary care both prevents hospitalisation and rations it.
• Public health capacity: surveillance, epidemiology, laboratory networks and the public health cadre most States lack — a population function no insurance product supplies.
• Financial protection: cover for outpatient care and medicines, where impoverishment occurs, with free essential drugs on the Tamil Nadu model.
topics.position: Gatekeeping so PM-JAY is reachable only through primary care; a public health cadre in every State; free essential medicines as an entitlement; strategic purchasing with quality-linked rates; mid-level providers at scale; and a national floor for public health expenditure. Insurance buys treatment; only primary care and public health buy health — and only the two together produce financial protection.
topics.draw: Three stacked boxes and one arrow from ‘PM-JAY’ touching only the middle. Draw the two untouched legs boldly — the omission is the argument.
topics.figure: ◆ Insurance is not universal health coverage primary care prevents and rations public health                                PM-JAY covers hossurveillance, cadre                             pitalisation only financial protection OPD + medicines largest OOP share is outpatient ◆ public health spend 2% of GDP against the 2.5% NHP 2017 target Three stacked legs with the insurance box reaching only one. The gap between the box and the other two legs is the answer.
bank: Human resources
Doctor and nurse density below WHO norms; mid-level providers are the only scalable answer.
Private sector
Most outpatient care is private and unregulated; the Clinical Establishments Act is unadopted in many States.
Federalism
Health is a State subject; PM-JAY is a centrally designed insurance product States must co-finance.
NCDs
The disease burden has shifted to chronic conditions needing continuing care, which the system was not built for.
Mental health
The Mental Healthcare Act 2017 creates a right to treatment with almost no service capacity behind it.
Ageing
Geriatric and palliative care is the fastest-growing unmet need — link to the care-economy answer.

topics.t: Population Ageing and the Care Economy
topics.q: India must move from treating population ageing as family welfare to building a rights-based care economy. Analyse the emerging challenges and policy priorities.
body: India’s elderly will approach a fifth of the population by 2050. The risk is one of sequence: India is ageing at a lower income level and before pension, health and care systems exist. The frame must shift from family welfare to a rights-based care economy.
Why the traditional arrangement is failing
• The joint family was the de facto pension and care system; migration has thinned it.
• Ageing is feminised — women live longer, marry older men and are more often widowed, producing a large elderly female population with no independent income.
• Rural elderly remain in agriculture with no retirement while children have migrated. Most worked informally, so have no contributory pension, and the NSAP pension is small in real terms.
The health and care gap
• Morbidity shifts to degenerative disease requiring continuing care — which a system built around maternal, child and acute care cannot deliver.
• Geriatrics is barely present in medical training, palliative care scarce outside Kerala, and chronic-illness expenditure a leading cause of impoverishment.
• The Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act 2007 places a maintenance duty on children, enforceable through a tribunal but weakly implemented.
topics.position: Expand and index the NSAP pension; build home-based geriatric care through ASHAs rather than institutionalisation; train, certify and pay caregivers, so care becomes recognised employment; and make Ayushman Bharat cover chronic outpatient costs.
topics.conc: The question is not whether India can afford care for the old, but whether it builds the system before the cohort arrives — and it is already arriving.
topics.draw: A population pyramid inverting over time, with three arrows from the widening top — pension, health, care — each hitting a box marked ‘not yet built’. The sequence, not the number, is the argument.
bank: Care economy as employment
Paid care work is among the largest potential sources of women’s formal employment — an FLFP argument.
Fiscal
Ageing raises pension and health costs exactly as the dependency ratio worsens — the window is the 2040s.
State variation
Kerala and Tamil Nadu are ageing decades ahead of the northern States — policy must be State-differentiated.
Old Pension Scheme debate
Reverting to defined benefit shifts cost to future taxpayers; the Unified Pension Scheme is the compromise.
Elder abuse
Tribunals under the 2007 Act are under-used; awareness and a designated oﬀicer are the practical fix.
Technology
Tele-medicine and remote monitoring suit continuing care, but assume connectivity the elderly least possess.

topics.t: Portable Social Security for Unorganised and Migrant Workers
topics.q: A registration portal is a gateway, not social security. Evaluate India’s framework for unorganised and migrant workers and suggest how portability can become an enforceable entitlement.
body: Over nine-tenths of India’s workforce is informal, and its defining policy feature is mobility — between employers, sectors and States. Any entitlement tied to one employer or one State fails by design. e-Shram is a registration portal — a gateway, not social security.
What registration does and does not achieve
• It creates a unique identity and a denominator — a real advance over neither.
• But registration confers no benefit: the worker must still be enrolled, contributions collected, and a benefit claimable at the destination. Registration numbers rise while coverage does not.
The design problems in making entitlement portable
• Financing: most have no identifiable employer, so contributions must come from the worker, the State or a levy — the aggregator contribution of 1–2% of turnover under the Code on Social Security.

• Federal division: welfare boards, ration, health and housing are State-administered, so the destination State bears the cost of a person on the origin State’s rolls. ONORC solved this for food by making the entitlement travel with the person; extend the model to health, housing and pension.
• Enforcement: the construction workers’ cess has large unspent balances — collecting money is easier than delivering a benefit.
topics.position: Seed e-Shram universally and auto-link a defined floor package — accident, health, maternity, pension — vesting with days worked rather than an employer; a national contribution ledger; destination-State delivery with inter-State settlement; a statutory deadline for cess utilisation; and enforceable rental housing, shelter being the first failure of migration. Portability is a settlement architecture, not a registration exercise — the entitlement must move as easily as the worker does.
topics.draw: Six boxes in a loop with box one shaded. If short of time draw boxes one, four and five — registration, ledger, destination delivery — and the argument still lands.
topics.figure: ◆ Portability — from registration to entitlement contribution: e-Shram            floor package           worker, State, registration            defined               aggregator inter-State           destination           national ledger settlement           State delivers          accumulates ONORC proves the model for food — the gap is health, housing, schooling and pension A registration portal is box one of six. Drawing the remaining five is the whole point: ‘a gateway, not social security’.
bank: Labour Codes
The Code on Social Security 2020 creates the legal basis for aggregator contributions and a national board.
Gig work
Platform workers are statutorily recognised for the first time; the contribution is capped at 5% of payments to workers.
BOCW cess
Large unspent balances are the single most citable evidence that collection is not delivery.
Inter-State Migrant Workmen Act
The 1979 Act was subsumed into the Codes; its registration requirement was never enforced.
Pandemic lesson
The 2020 reverse migration exposed the absence of a destination-side entitlement — the origin of ONORC’s extension.
Urban link
Rental insecurity and non-portable services are the same problem seen from the city — pair the answers.

topics.q: Urban poverty is increasingly a problem of insecure work, rental housing and exclusion from portable basic services, not merely of slum residence. Analyse.
body: Urban poverty has been addressed through residence — the slum as the unit of intervention. That framing is inadequate: the urban poor are defined by insecure work, rental tenure and exclusion from portable services rather than by living in a notified slum.
Why residence is the wrong unit
• Many live outside notified slums — unrecognised settlements, construction sites, shared rental rooms, the street — so slum-linked entitlements miss them by definition.
• Many are circular migrants whose documents are anchored to the origin State, so they are invisible in destination records.
• Upgrading a slum in situ does nothing for a worker who moves each season.
The three real deprivations
• Insecure work: casual construction, street vending, domestic and platform labour — daily earnings, no contract, no protection against a lost day.
• Rental insecurity: the poor rent informally and without agreement, so eviction is instantaneous and no scheme built around ownership reaches them — PMAY-Urban’s design assumption is the diﬀiculty.
• Non-portable services: ration, health, schooling and social security tied to a domicile the migrant lacks.
topics.position: Shift targeting from settlement to household and worker using e-Shram and ONORC; scale Affordable Rental Housing Complexes and a workable Model Tenancy Act so informal renting is documented; implement the Street Vendors Act 2014, which most cities have not; extend health and schooling entitlements on residence rather than domicile; and create an urban employment guarantee, since the urban poor have no MGNREGS. The urban poor are not primarily people who live badly but people who work insecurely and rent without rights — policy addressed to the dwelling keeps missing them.
topics.draw: Three columns — work, rent, services — each with a box ‘slum-based scheme’ that fails to reach the person below it. Draw the person outside the notified-slum boundary; that placement is the argument.
bank: Street Vendors Act 2014
A rights-based statute almost universally unimplemented — the sharpest single example of urban policy failure.
PMAY-U 2.0
Includes a rental component; whether it reaches informal renters depends on documentation, not on finance.
Migrant data
No destination-side enumeration exists; the Census is residence-based and misses circular migrants.
Urban MGNREGS
Kerala’s Ayyankali and Odisha’s UWEP are State precedents for an urban employment guarantee.
74th Amendment link
Municipalities lack the functions and funds to deliver any of this — pair with the local government answer.
Heat and climate
Informal settlements bear the highest heat and flood exposure — the disaster dimension of urban poverty.

topics.t: Disability — Accommodation as an Equality Guarantee
topics.q: For persons with disabilities, reasonable accommodation and universal accessibility are enforceable equality guarantees, not matters of charity. Discuss.
body: The social model, adopted in the UNCRPD and the RPwD Act 2016, holds that disability arises from an impairment meeting a disabling environment — a wheelchair user is disabled by the staircase, not the chair. The Act expanded recognised conditions from seven to twenty-one and made reasonable accommodation and accessibility enforceable equality guarantees, not charity.
What the law requires
• Section 3 prohibits discrimination and defines denial of reasonable accommodation as discrimination; Sections 40–46 mandate accessibility standards for the built environment, transport and ICT.
• Four per cent reservation in government employment and five per cent in higher education.

• Vikash Kumar v. UPSC (2021) held reasonable accommodation — a scribe for a candidate with dysgraphia — a facet of equality that rigid rule cannot deny; Rajive Raturi (2024) held accessibility standards mandatory, not aspirational, and directed enforceable rules.
Why implementation lags
• The Accessible India Campaign’s targets have slipped, and UDID certification is onerous with entitlements gated behind it.

• Inclusive education is nominal for want of trained special educators; private-sector obligations are incentives rather than duties; digital services routinely fail accessibility standards; and Census undercounting leaves planning without an accurate denominator.
topics.position: Make accessibility a condition of occupancy certificate, licence and public procurement rather than a target; enforce Rajive Raturi through binding rules with penalties; simplify and make the UDID interoperable; fund special educators and assistive technology; and extend accommodation duties to large private employers. India has legislated the social model and administers the medical one — the gap between them is where disability is produced.
topics.draw: Two facing boxes — ‘medical model: impairment in the person’ and ‘social model: barrier in the environment’ — with a staircase drawn between a wheelchair and a doorway. Label the staircase, not the chair.
bank: UNCRPD
India ratified in 2007; the 2016 Act is the domestic implementing statute — state the sequence.
Employment
Backlog vacancies in the 4% quota persist; identification of suitable posts is the administrative bottleneck.
Digital accessibility
Government apps and websites frequently fail WCAG standards — accessibility must be a procurement condition.
Mental illness
The Mental Healthcare Act 2017 and the RPwD Act overlap; capacity and guardianship remain unresolved.
Data
Census undercounting understates prevalence, so budgets are set against a wrong denominator.
Disaster management
Evacuation and shelter design rarely account for disability — a concrete, under-used example.

topics.t: Self-Help Groups — from Thrift to Service Delivery
topics.q: Self-Help Groups have moved from thrift and credit towards enterprise and the delivery of public services. Examine whether this shift has strengthened or diluted their transformative potential.
body: Self-Help Groups began as savings-and-credit collectives of women, linked to banks through NABARD SHG–Bank Linkage and federated under the National Rural Livelihoods Mission. They now deliver public services — banking correspondents, ration dealers, Krishi and Bank Sakhis. Whether that strengthens or dilutes them is the live question.
The case that it strengthens
• Service delivery brings a reliable income, freeing the group from micro-enterprise margins.
• It creates a formal interface with the State, raising standing and bargaining position.
• It converts women’s collectives into visible economic actors — how Lakhpati Didi operates.
The case that it dilutes
• The original purpose was collective agency — a forum in which women deliberated on their own priorities, including against local power. A delivery contractor takes its agenda from the department.
• Dependence on government contracts creates capture: a federation that criticises a programme risks losing the work.

• Elite capture intensifies when there is a contract to allocate. And the State gains a low-cost delivery arm without employment protection — women performing public functions as ‘volunteers’, the undervaluation that runs through ASHA and anganwadi work.
topics.position: Keep the two functions distinct — the SHG a member body, a separate federation the contractor; pay honorarium cadres a minimum wage with social security; ring-fence federation income for member priorities; and evaluate SHGs by member income and voice, not scheme targets. An SHG that delivers services is more powerful and less free — the task is to keep the collective’s agenda its own while it works for the State.
topics.draw: One circle labelled ‘SHG: member body, collective agency’ and a second labelled ‘federation: commercial contractor’, joined by a dotted line. Drawing them as separate circles is the recommendation.
bank: Lakhpati Didi
Asset creation and income targets are the current frame; measure member income, not enrolment.
ASHA / anganwadi
The same undervaluation — public functions performed at honorarium rates without employment status.
Financial inclusion
SHG–bank linkage remains the most successful collateral-free lending model India has built.
Microfinance contrast
For-profit MFIs lend to individuals without the collective; over-lending stress is the counter-example.
Political agency
SHG federations have contested local elections in several States — collective agency’s natural endpoint.
Urban SHGs
DAY-NULM’s urban SHGs are far weaker; the model has not transferred to insecure urban livelihoods.

topics.q: The weaponisation of trade, finance and technology has blurred the distinction between economic policy and national security. Examine the implications for India’s strategic autonomy.
body: Trade, finance and technology are now instruments of statecraft — tariffs, sanctions, export controls, chokepoints, payment exclusion.
The distinction between economic policy and national security has dissolved, so strategic autonomy requires economic capability as much as diplomatic flexibility.
The instruments and India’s exposure
• Tariffs and reciprocity replacing rules-based access, the WTO Appellate Body being paralysed.
• Export controls on advanced semiconductors and dual-use technology — which India needs and does not make.
• Chokepoint dependence: rare-earth magnets, active pharmaceutical ingredients, electronics components and solar cells, concentrated in a single supplier.
• Financial instruments: secondary sanctions and payment exclusion, constraining India’s Russian energy and defence ties.
• Regulatory extraterritoriality: CBAM and due-diligence directives functioning as market-access conditions.
What capability actually consists of
• Resilience of supply: ISM 2.0, the National Critical Mineral Mission and rare-earth magnet scheme, PLI in electronics and pharmaceuticals, petroleum reserves.
• Diversification: FTAs with the UAE, Australia, EFTA, the UK and the EU; IMEC and INSTC as alternative corridors.
• Financial insulation: local-currency settlement, rupee vostro accounts, UPI internationalisation, gold reserves.
• Technological depth: indigenous defence production, space and AI capability, standard-setting participation, and WTO coalitions.
topics.position: Autonomy is bought, not declared: reduce dependence at identified chokepoints, since blanket substitution taxes exports; keep multiple partnerships live so none is decisive; build the market that makes India worth not coercing; and invest in writing the new rules, since a rule India helped write constrains the coercer too. Strategic autonomy was once the freedom to choose partners; it is now the capability to survive the consequences of the choice.
topics.draw: Reproduce the two-column table. Writing the answer beside each instrument is what converts a list of threats into a strategy.
topics.figure: ◆ Strategic autonomy — the coercion instruments instrument                              India’s answer export controls, chokepoints            ISM 2.0, National Critical Mineral Mission, REPM scheme sanctions, payment exclusion            rupee vostro, local-currency settlement, UPI internationalisation tariffs, CBAM, due diligence            FTAs, IMEC, MRV capacity, WTO repair Instrument against answer, three rows. It demonstrates that autonomy is a capability question — which is the thesis a 15-marker wants argued, not asserted.
bank: Russia oil / CAATSA
The clearest live case of secondary-sanction exposure — and of India’s insulation working.
China dependence
APIs, electronics components and magnets are the named chokepoints; substitution must be selective.
Semiconductors
Export controls on advanced nodes are the sharpest technology-denial instrument — link to ISM.
WTO
Restoring binding dispute settlement is the multilateral half of autonomy — coercion fills an adjudication vacuum.
Digital sovereignty
Data localisation and payments infrastructure are autonomy instruments as much as regulatory ones.
Non-alignment contrast
Then it meant abstention; now it means capability — state the shift explicitly.

topics.t: India and China — the Present Phase
topics.q: Normalisation of relations with China cannot run ahead of peace and tranquillity in the border areas. Examine the possibilities and constraints of the present phase.
body: The relationship has three layers moving at different speeds: the border, where Galwan 2020 ended three decades of calm; economics, with record trade and a large deficit; and the systemic, where Indo-Pacific alignments are opposed. Normalisation on the second cannot durably run ahead of the first.
What has moved

• The October 2024 patrolling understanding at Depsang and Demchok enabled the first leaders’ meeting in five years at Kazan, resumed Special Representatives talks, restored direct flights and the Kailash Mansarovar Yatra.
• This is disengagement, not de-escalation: forces remain forward-deployed, buffer zones restrict patrolling, and deinduction has not begun.
The constraints that persist
• The boundary question is unsettled and the 1993, 1996 and 2005 agreements proved insuﬀicient; LAC infrastructure asymmetry persists.

• The deficit is structural and concentrated in APIs, components, solar cells and rare-earth magnets — the inputs of India’s manufacturing ambition — so dependence deepened even as politics soured, and export controls demonstrated the leverage.
• Ties with Pakistan, CPEC through territory India claims, damming of the Yarlung Tsangpo and Indian Ocean positioning are unchanged.
topics.position: Calibrated engagement — restore normalcy where estrangement costs India more, while insisting that de-escalation follow disengagement and patrolling rights be codified rather than left to informal buffer zones; continue border infrastructure and Vibrant Villages; reduce chokepoint dependence selectively; and maintain Indo-Pacific engagement without converting it into an alliance.
topics.conc: Peace and tranquillity in the border areas is not a precondition India invented — it is the term on which the post-1988 relationship was built, and must be restored before normalisation can be called that.
topics.draw: Three stacked bars of different lengths, longest for economics and shortest for the border. The unequal lengths carry the thesis without a sentence.
topics.figure: ◆ India–China — three layers, three speeds border — disengagement done; de-escalation and de-induction not begun economic — record trade; deficit in APIs, components, magnets systemic — Pakistan, CPEC, Indian Ocean, Brahmaputra normalisation on layer 2 cannot durably run ahead of layer 1 — peace and tranquillity is the post-1988 term of the relationship Three stacked bands. Separating the layers is what prevents the common error of treating restored flights as normalisation.
bank: Buffer zones
They restrict Indian patrolling in areas previously patrolled — a concession, not a settlement.
Trade remedies
Anti-dumping and Press Note 3 investment screening are the operative instruments, not tariffs.
Brahmaputra
The Medog/Yarlung Tsangpo project is an upstream leverage question with no treaty to govern it.
Multilateral
India and China cooperate in BRICS, SCO and on climate while contesting bilaterally — name the compartments.
Taiwan / Indo-Pacific
India’s position is deliberately understated; strategic ambiguity is itself a policy choice.
Border infrastructure
Vibrant Villages, ICBR roads and tunnels are the material answer to asymmetry — delivery, not declaration.

topics.q: Enlargement has increased the representational weight of BRICS while making internal coherence harder to sustain. Evaluate the priorities before India as Chair in 2026.
body: BRICS has expanded to include Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, the UAE and Indonesia, with a wider partner tier — raising its share of world population and output and its representational claim. Enlargement has increased weight and reduced coherence, and India chairs it in 2026 at that inflection.
What enlargement changed
• It now contains members in active rivalry and members under Western sanction, so consensus is harder and the agenda drifts to the lowest common denominator.
• It has also sharpened the framing question: whether BRICS is a platform for reform of global governance or a bloc against the West.

• India’s position is consistent — non-Western, not anti-Western — and de-dollarisation is the sharpest test: a common currency is neither feasible nor in India’s interest, while local-currency settlement is.
The institutional assets worth building on

• The New Development Bank, with growing local-currency lending; the Contingent Reserve Arrangement as a liquidity backstop; and working groups on agriculture, health, counter-terrorism and vaccines — functional and free of the political fault lines.
topics.position: Steer BRICS towards deliverables not declarations: expand NDB local-currency lending; press IMF quota realignment and UNSC reform where positions overlap; build payment interoperability without a common currency; deliver on counter-terrorism and the pending Comprehensive Convention; advance vaccine and pharmaceutical cooperation where India’s capacity is the asset; and resist framing that makes membership a choice against the West. An enlarged BRICS is worth chairing only if it produces cooperation rather than communiqués — India’s task is to keep it a reform coalition and not let it become a bloc.
topics.draw: One circle expanding outward with new members added, and two arrows leaving it labelled ‘reform of global governance’ and ‘bloc against the West’. Mark India’s position on the first arrow.
bank: De-dollarisation
Local-currency settlement is practical; a common currency requires fiscal union no member will accept.
NDB
Local-currency lending insulates borrowers from dollar cycles — the most concrete deliverable available.
China’s weight
Enlargement increased China’s relative influence; India’s counterweight is agenda-setting, not membership vetoes.
G20 comparison
India’s G20 presidency delivered the African Union’s admission — the template for chairship as delivery.
Iran / sanctions
Members under sanction constrain what the grouping can agree on financially — a real coherence cost.
Global South
BRICS competes with the G77 and the Voice of the Global South Summit as a representative platform.

topics.t: The Quad and Regional Public Goods
topics.q: The durability of the Quad will depend upon its capacity to deliver regional public goods without losing strategic coherence. Discuss.
body: The Quad — India, the United States, Japan and Australia — was revived in 2017 and elevated to leaders’ level in 2021. Its character is deliberate: not an alliance but a coalition delivering regional public goods. Its durability depends on doing that without militarising or dissipating.
The public goods it has attempted
• The pandemic vaccine partnership; and IPMDA, using commercial satellite data to give partner states a picture of dark shipping and illegal fishing — the most tangible deliverable.
• Working groups on semiconductors, telecom standards and undersea cables; clean energy supply chains; and disaster relief, exercised after the Tonga eruption.
The tensions in the model
• Goods versus coherence: the wider the agenda, the more it resembles a donor forum and the less it deters.
• Divergent threats: the maritime Indo-Pacific is the shared theatre, but India’s primary problem is a continental land border — and India is the only member without a US treaty alliance.
• Delivery: announcements outpace disbursement, and ASEAN centrality requires the Quad add to, not displace, regional institutions.
• Political durability: three of four have had changes of government, and there is no secretariat or standing budget.
topics.position: Keep the Quad non-military in form while deepening interoperability bilaterally — foundational agreements, Malabar, reciprocal logistics — so capability grows without alliance commitment; prioritise a few visibly delivered goods, IPMDA above all, over a broad agenda; anchor it in ASEAN centrality; and preserve strategic autonomy, since India’s value to the grouping lies partly in not being an ally. The Quad’s credibility rests on what arrives in the region, not what is declared at the summit.
topics.draw: Hub with five spokes and the footer line. The footer — no secretariat, no treaty, India the only non-ally — is where the analysis sits.
topics.figure: ◆ The Quad as public goods, not alliance IPMDA — dark shipping, IUU fishing vaccines,                                      critical and health security             Quad emerging tech HADR, climate,           undersea cables, fellowship               connectivity no secretariat, no treaty, no budget ◆ ASEAN centrality ◆ India the only member without a US alliance Hub-and-spoke is correct here because the deliverables are simultaneous, not sequential. The footer line is the strategic point.
bank: AUKUS contrast
An explicitly military arrangement India is not part of — the comparison that defines the Quad’s character.
ASEAN centrality
Southeast Asian states resist bloc formation; the Quad must add to regional institutions, not replace them.
China framing
The Quad avoids naming China; whether that is prudence or evasion is a fair line either way.
IPMDA
Commercial satellite data given to partner states is the model deliverable — concrete, non-military, wanted.
India’s constraint
A continental land border means India cannot subordinate continental defence to a maritime coalition.
Quad Plus
Extension to South Korea, New Zealand and Indian Ocean states dilutes coherence but widens delivery.

topics.q: The India–US relationship is described as a comprehensive global strategic partnership. Examine what holds it together, what strains it, and how India should manage it.
body: The relationship has moved from estrangement to a comprehensive global strategic partnership — anchored in the 2005 civil nuclear agreement, the foundational defence agreements (LEMOA 2016, COMCASA 2018, BECA 2020), the 2+2 dialogue, iCET and the Quad. It is India’s most consequential and least predictable partnership.
What holds it together
• A shared assessment of the Indo-Pacific balance; defence trade and co-production in jet engines, armed drones and maritime systems, India being a Major Defence Partner with STA-1 status.
• Technology cooperation in semiconductors, space and critical minerals; a diaspora of over four million; and deep services and pharmaceutical trade, the US being India’s largest export market.
What strains it
• Trade: reciprocal tariffs, agriculture and dairy market access, data localisation, and no comprehensive trade agreement.
• Russia: India’s energy purchases and legacy defence dependence, with CAATSA sanctions a standing risk.
• Immigration: H-1B restrictions and visa backlogs, affecting India’s services economy directly.
• Autonomy: India will not join an alliance, and US expectations periodically exceed that limit.
• Domestic politics on both sides, with electoral cycles and periodic criticism of democratic backsliding.
topics.position: Deepen where interests are structurally aligned — defence co-production with technology transfer rather than off-the-shelf purchase, semiconductors, critical minerals and maritime domain awareness; insulate trade from strategy through a phased trade agreement; diversify procurement so no supplier is decisive; and be explicit that partnership is not alignment. This is a partnership of converging interests rather than shared commitments — its durability depends on both sides continuing to want it for their own reasons.
topics.draw: Two columns — ‘holds it together’ (Indo-Pacific balance, defence co-production, technology, diaspora, trade) against ‘strains it’ (tariffs, Russia, immigration, autonomy, domestic politics). Five rows each; the symmetry is the point.
bank: iCET / TRUST
Technology frameworks are the newest layer; delivery on jet engines and semiconductors is the test.
Nuclear deal
The 2005 agreement opened everything else; the SHANTI Act 2025 finally removed the liability obstacle.
Indo-Pacific
Convergence is maritime; India’s continental problem is not shared — the structural asymmetry.
Trade
India’s services surplus and goods position with the US make it uniquely exposed to reciprocal tariffs.
Democracy criticism
Periodic Congressional and media criticism is a recurring irritant — treat it as structural, not episodic.
Comparison
The US offers technology and capital, the EU offers rules and regulation — India needs both, differently.

topics.q: India’s Russia policy is often described as nostalgia. Examine what still binds the relationship, what is eroding it, and how India should manage the transition.
body: The relationship rests on defence dependence built over six decades, an annual summit, and a record of Soviet and Russian vetoes on Kashmir at the Security Council. It is a partnership of legacy and hedging at a time when Russia’s own alignments have narrowed towards China.
What still binds it

• Defence: a very large share of India’s inventory is Russian — the S-400, licensed T-90 production, the BrahMos joint venture, submarine leasing. Spares and upgrades alone make abrupt separation impossible.
• Energy: discounted crude since 2022 made Russia a leading supplier.
• Nuclear and multilateral: Kudankulam; coordination in BRICS, the SCO and RIC; Russian support in the Nuclear Suppliers Group.
• Connectivity: INSTC, the Chennai–Vladivostok corridor, Far East resource cooperation.
What is eroding it
• Russia’s dependence on China constrains its willingness and ability to balance, and defence technology-sharing with Pakistan has begun where it did not exist.
• Sanctions complicate payment, insurance and shipping; CAATSA exposure persists; and deliveries have slipped as Russian industry serves its own war.
• Trade is one-sided and Indian exports small, so the relationship lacks commercial ballast; and Russia’s technological base has narrowed.
topics.position: Manage the transition rather than announce it — diversify new procurement while sustaining spares for the existing fleet; move from buyer to co-producer where technology transfer is available; build vostro settlement to insulate payments; and expand Indian exports to correct the imbalance. India’s Russia policy is not nostalgia but insurance — and the task is to reduce dependence without discarding the option, since a Russia entirely dependent on China is not in India’s interest.
topics.draw: Two arrows of unequal thickness — a thick one for defence and energy dependence, a thin one for trade — with a third arrow labelled ‘Russia → China’ drawn pulling away. The asymmetry is the argument.
bank: CAATSA
Secondary-sanction exposure on the S-400 is the sharpest live risk — and the clearest test of autonomy.
Payments
Rupee–rouble settlement built surplus rouble balances Russia could not spend — the practical limit of the workaround.
Defence indigenisation
Every rupee of domestic production reduces the dependence that constrains policy — link to Atmanirbhar Bharat.
RIC format
Its revival is contingent on India–China normalisation — the three relationships are linked.
Arctic / Far East
Energy and shipping-route cooperation is the growth area least affected by sanctions.
Ukraine position
India’s abstentions are consistent with strategic autonomy; state the principle, not a partisan case.

topics.t: UN Reform, Multilateralism and the Global South
topics.q: The multilateral order is failing at both ends. Examine India’s strategy of pressing reform while building coalitions outside the formal institutions.
body: The multilateral order is failing at both ends — the Security Council reflects the balance of 1945, and WTO dispute settlement has been paralysed since 2019. India presses reformed multilateralism while building coalitions outside the formal institutions.
The reform agenda and why it stalls
• Expansion in both categories — India, Brazil, Germany and Japan as the G4, and the AU’s Ezulwini Consensus demanding two permanent African seats.

• It stalls because Uniting for Consensus opposes new permanent members; the veto is unresolved; Article 108 requires all five permanent members to ratify a Charter amendment; and the Intergovernmental Negotiations have run a decade without a text.
• Beyond the Council: IMF quota realignment lags world output, and climate finance commitments have fallen short.
India’s Global South strategy
• The Voice of the Global South Summit series as a convening platform; and the African Union’s admission to the G20 during India’s 2023 presidency — the most concrete institutional outcome.

• Issue-based coalitions — the International Solar Alliance, Global Biofuels Alliance, CDRI; capacity demonstrated through Vaccine Maitri and disaster relief; and development partnership through credit lines and ITEC.
topics.position: Pursue reform and workaround simultaneously — press the IGN towards an actual negotiating text while building plurilaterals that deliver without Charter amendment; restore WTO dispute settlement, since a rules-based order protects a middle power from coercion; convert Global South convening into standing weight through the G20 and BRICS; and offer development partnership on a demand-driven, non-conditional model. India’s claim on the high table rests on being indispensable to solving problems rather than on the justice of its case.
topics.draw: Four blocking boxes and the workaround line beneath. Write Article 108 inside its box — it is the provision most answers omit.
topics.figure: ◆ UN reform — why it stalls G4 + Ezulwini: expand both categories Uniting for          veto question           Art 108:               IGN has Consensus opposes        unresolved          P5 must ratify             no text so India pursues the workaround: G20, BRICS, ISA, GBA, Voice of the Global South ◆ AU into the G20, 2023 Four blocking factors from one node. Naming Article 108 is the specific that separates a serious answer from a general one.
bank: Veto reform
France and the UK support restraint on veto use in mass-atrocity situations — a partial reform that needs no amendment.
UNSC non-permanent
India has served eight terms; the case is capability and contribution, not entitlement.
Peacekeeping
India is among the largest troop contributors — the strongest single claim to a larger role.
Bretton Woods
IMF quota realignment and World Bank capital adequacy reform are the financial half of the same agenda.
Climate
Loss and damage and adaptation finance are where Global South coalition-building has the sharpest edge.
Comprehensive Convention

India’s CCIT proposal has been pending since 1996 — definitional disputes over ‘terrorism’ block it. PART III ◆ SYLLABUS FILLERS — the lines none of the three papers covered Compressed notes, not model answers. Each entry is the minimum you must be able to write if the paper turns to a syllabus line outside the sixty topics: the provision or institution, the one analytical point that earns the mark, and the reform where one exists. A ◆ CONSTITUTION, JUDICIARY, RIGHTS Comparison with other constitutions Parliamentary executive and rule of law from the UK; Fundamental Rights, judicial review and an independent judiciary from the US; Directive Principles from Ireland; Emergency provisions from Weimar Germany; Concurrent List and joint sitting from Aus- tralia; a strong Centre with residuary powers from Canada; amendment procedure and Fundamental Duties from the USSR; procedure established by law from Japan. The analytical point: India borrowed institutions but adapted them to a diverse, unequal and federal society — hence a federal structure with unitary features, and a judiciary with wider remedial power than any of its sources. Emergency provisions Art 352 national emergency — ‘armed rebellion’ since the 44th Amendment (1978), written Cabinet advice required, par- liamentary approval by special majority within one month, six-monthly renewal. Art 356 State emergency (see Part II topic 6). Art 360 financial emergency, never invoked. Art 359 cannot suspend Arts 20 and 21 after the 44th Amendment — the direct legislative answer to ADM Jabalpur (1976), overruled in Puttaswamy (2017). Asymmetric federalism Art 370 (abrogated 2019, upheld in In re Art 370, 2023); Arts 371 to 371J for Maharashtra, Gujarat, Nagaland, Assam, Manipur, Andhra, Sikkim, Mizoram, Arunachal, Goa, Karnataka; the Fifth Schedule (Scheduled Areas, Tribes Advisory Councils, Governor’s power to modify laws) and the Sixth Schedule (Autonomous District Councils in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram). Point: India’s federalism is asymmetric by design — accommodation is a constitutional technique, not an exception. Tribunals and dispute redressal Arts 323A and 323B; L. Chandra Kumar (1997) — High Court review under Arts 226/227 is a basic feature no tribunal may oust; Madras Bar Association and Rojer Mathew (2019) on selection and tenure; Tribunals Reforms Act 2021. Alternative dispute resolution: Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996 (amended 2015, 2019, 2021), Mediation Act 2023, Lok Adalats and permanent Lok Adalats under the Legal Services Authorities Act 1987, NALSA and Art 39A free legal aid, Gram Nyayalayas Act 2008. Point: pendency is a capacity problem; ADR diverts flow but does not fix the judge–population ratio. Criminal justice Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (in force 1 July 2024) replace the IPC, CrPC and Evidence Act — new offences of organised crime and terrorism, timelines for investigation and judgment, mandatory forensics for offences above seven years, electronic and audio-video procedure, community service as a sentence. Police reform: Prakash Singh (2006) — State Security Commission, fixed two-year tenure for DGP and SHOs, separation of investigation from law and order, Police Establishment Board, Police Complaints Authority; compliance remains partial. Prisons: Model Prisons Act 2023; overcrowding and undertrial proportion are the standing indictment; Hussainara Khatoon (1979) on speedy trial. Anti-corruption architecture Prevention of Corruption Act 1988, amended 2018 — bribe-giving criminalised, prior approval required to investigate a public servant; CVC given statutory status by Vineet Narain (1997); CBI under the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act 1946, general consent withdrawn by several States — a live federal question; Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act 2013; Benami Transactions Act; Fugitive Economic Offenders Act 2018. B ◆ PARLIAMENT, ELECTIONS, LOCAL GOVERNMENT Representation of the People Acts RPA 1950 — qualification of voters and allocation of seats; RPA 1951 — conduct of elections, qualifications and disqualifications, corrupt practices, election petitions, registration of political parties (s.29A), disqualification on conviction (s.8). Lily Thomas (2013) struck down s.8(4), so conviction disqualifies immediately. ADR (2002) and PUCL (2003) — disclosure of assets and criminal antecedents is part of Art 19(1)(a); PUCL (2013) created NOTA; ADR v. Union (2024) struck down the electoral bond scheme. Reform agenda: state funding of elections, decriminalisation through disqualification on framing of charges for grave offences, a cap on party (not merely candidate) expenditure, and internal party democracy. Parliamentary financial procedure Arts 112–117 — Annual Financial Statement, charged expenditure, Demands for Grants, Appropriation and Finance Bills; Art 114(3) no expenditure without appropriation; Art 266 Consolidated Fund, Art 267 Contingency Fund, Public Account. Cut motions — policy, economy, token. Vote on account, supplementary and excess grants. Financial committees: Public Accounts, Estimates, Public Undertakings. Point: the guillotine means most Demands are voted without discussion — financial control is formal. Panchayati Raj — the 73rd Amendment Part IX, Eleventh Schedule (29 subjects), Art 243B three tiers above 20 lakh population, 243D reservation for SC/ST and one-third for women (many States now half), 243E five-year term, 243I State Finance Commission, 243K State Election Commission. Same three failures as the 74th: functions illustrative, funds tied, functionaries State cadre. Add: parallel bodies bypass panchayats; the ‘sarpanch pati’ phenomenon; PESA 1996 for Fifth Schedule areas requiring gram sabha consent, largely unimplemented. Constitutional, statutory and regulatory bodies Constitutional — Election Commission (324), UPSC and State PSCs (315–323), Finance Commission (280), CAG (148), Attorney General (76), Advocate General (165), NCSC (338), NCST (338A), NCBC (338B, 102nd Amendment), Special Oﬀicer for Linguistic Minorities (350B), GST Council (279A). Statutory — NHRC and State HRCs (Protection of Human Rights Act 1993), NCW, NCPCR, CIC, Lokpal, CVC, NGT, Law Commission (executive resolution, not statutory). Regulatory — SEBI, RBI, TRAI, IRDAI, PFRDA, CCI, CERC, FSSAI, Data Protection Board. Quasi-judicial — NGT, CAT, NCLT, TDSAT, consumer commissions. C ◆ GOVERNANCE, DEVELOPMENT PROCESSES, VULNERABLE SECTIONS Pressure groups and the development industry Delivery in India runs through voluntary organisations, self-help federations, CSR funds, philan- thropies and bilateral donors — they exercise public functions without public mandates. What they supply: reach into populations the administration does not serve; pilots that later become policy (SEWA on informal work, Pratham on learning, MKSS on the right to information, which produced the RTI Act); representation for groups without electoral weight; and independent verification. The regulatory turn: FCRA 2010 as amended in 2020 — registration and renewal, a ban on sub-granting, administrative expenditure capped at 20%, Aadhaar for oﬀice bearers, all receipts through one designated SBI branch in New Delhi; upheld in Noel Harper (2022), holding that receiving foreign contribution is not a right. Effect: the sub-granting ban dismantled the intermediary model through which large organisations funded small grassroots ones, consolidating the sector towards larger, compliance-capable entities. CSR: s.135 Companies Act 2013, 2% of average net profit — the world’s first such mandate, but flows disproportion- ately to already-developed districts and visible sectors. Reform: a graded FCRA regime distinguishing security-sensitive from ordinary development funding, with reasons and an appeal; regulated sub-granting through audited intermediaries; a domestic philanthropy framework and social stock exchange; publication of CSR spending by district. Women — laws and institutions Arts 15(3), 39(a) and (d), 42, 51A(e), 243D and 243T. Statutes: Dowry Prohibition 1961, PCPNDT 1994, Domestic Violence 2005, PoSH 2013 (following Vishaka, 1997), Criminal Law Amendments 2013 and 2018, Maternity Benefit Amendment 2017, Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) 2019, Prohibition of Child Marriage 2006. Judicial: Joseph Shine (2018) adultery, Navtej Johar (2018), Shayara Bano (2017) triple talaq, Sabarimala (2018), Vishaka. 106th Amendment — one-third reservation, conditional on delimitation after the census. Point: the deficit is enforcement and social norms, not statute. Children Arts 21A, 24, 39(e)–(f), 45. RTE Act 2009; Juvenile Justice Act 2015 (16–18 in heinous offences); POCSO 2012; Child Labour Amendment 2016; Mission Vatsalya, Mission Shakti, Poshan 2.0, PM POSHAN. Point: institutional care remains the default despite the JJ Act’s preference for family-based care. Minorities and SC/ST Arts 29 and 30 (TMA Pai, 2002; Aligarh Muslim University, 2024 on minority status); National Commission for Minorities Act 1992; SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act 1989 as amended 2018 after Subhash Kashinath Mahajan; Forest Rights Act 2006; PESA 1996; Prohibition of Employment as Manual Scavengers Act 2013 and the NAMASTE scheme. Point: atrocity conviction rates and FRA title rejection rates are the two most citable implementation failures. D ◆ HEALTH, EDUCATION, HUMAN RESOURCES Health architecture National Health Mission (NRHM 2005, NUHM 2013); Ayushman Bharat — Arogya Mandirs, PM-JAY, ABDM digital mission; National Health Policy 2017 (2.5% of GDP, not met); Clinical Establishments Act 2010, adopted unevenly; NMC Act 2019 replacing the Medical Council; Drugs Price Control Order and NPPA; Jan Aushadhi; Epidemic Diseases Act 1897 and the Public Health Bill; National Medical Devices Policy 2023; One Health mission for zoonoses. Point: India’s health system is strong on programmes and weak on primary care and public health capacity — the two things no insurance scheme can buy. Education Art 21A and RTE 2009 (age 6–14, 25% EWS admission in private schools upheld in Society for Unaided Private Schools, 2012); NEP 2020; NIPUN Bharat; Samagra Shiksha; PM SHRI; higher education — NAAC, NIRF, ABC credit bank, four-year UG, Institutions of Eminence, foreign campuses. Skilling — Skill India, PMKVY, National Apprenticeship Promotion Scheme, NSQF. Point: the sector’s binding constraints are teacher quality at school level and employability at tertiary level, neither of which structural reform alone addresses. Human resources and labour Four Labour Codes (Wages 2019; Industrial Relations, Social Security, OSH 2020) in force 21 November 2025 — con- solidating 29 laws, statutory recognition of gig and platform workers, aggregator contribution capped at 5%, threshold for standing orders and retrenchment approval raised to 300 workers. Point: flexibility in hiring is defensible only if paired with enforceable portable social security — otherwise risk is simply transferred to the worker. E ◆ INTERNATIONAL RELATIONS — NEIGHBOURS, GROUPINGS, INSTITUTIONS Neighbours, one line each Nepal — 1950 Treaty revision demand, Kalapani/Lipulekh map dispute, Agnipath and Gorkha recruitment, hydropower and power trade, open border. Bangladesh — post-2024 transition, Teesta and the 1996 Ganga Treaty due for renewal in 2026, minority security, transit and connectivity, CAA sensitivities. Sri Lanka — 2022 crisis and India’s $4 bn first response, 13th Amendment and provincial devolution, fishermen and Katchatheevu, Trincomalee and Colombo terminals. Maldives — ‘India Out’, personnel withdrawal, currency swap and budget support, Uthuru Thila Falhu. Bhutan — hydropower, Doklam, Gelephu Mindfulness City, China boundary talks. Myanmar — coup, Free Move- ment Regime curtailed, Kaladan project, refugee inflow. Afghanistan — technical mission, humanitarian wheat, Chabahar route, non-recognition. Pakistan — Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance, terrorism as the precondition, trade suspended. Groupings SAARC paralysed by one member; BIMSTEC the working substitute with a charter since 2022; IORA, IONS, Colombo Security Conclave; SCO (security and connectivity, India resists BRI endorsement); G20 (India’s 2023 presidency, AU admission, New Delhi Declaration); G7 outreach; ASEAN centrality, Act East, RCEP declined; IMEC, INSTC, Chabahar, BBIN, Trilateral Highway; I2U2 (India, Israel, UAE, US); IBSA; Indo-Pacific Oceans Initiative; ISA, CDRI, Global Biofuels Alliance, IPEF (India outside the trade pillar). International institutions UN system — General Assembly, Security Council (Art 108 amendment rule), ECOSOC, ICJ, ILO, UNESCO, WHO (IHR 2005 as amended 2024, Pandemic Agreement 2025); Bretton Woods — IMF (quota realignment, SDRs), World Bank, and the newer NDB and AIIB; WTO (Appellate Body vacancy, MPIA, MC14, e-transmission moratorium lapse, public stockholding); FATF (grey and black lists, mutual evaluation, travel rule); IAEA and the NSG (India outside the NPT, 2008 waiver); ICC (India not a party); UNCLOS and the BBNJ Agreement; UNFCCC, Paris Agreement Art 6, Loss and Damage Fund; UNHRC and UPR. Diaspora Over 32 million PIO and NRI — the world’s largest, and the largest recipient of remittances. Instruments: Pravasi Bharatiya Divas, OCI cardholders (with periodic restrictions), Know India Programme, eMigrate for emigration clearance, Indian Community Welfare Fund, Mode 4 commitments and social-security totalisation agreements, migration and mobility partnerships with Germany, France, Austria and Portugal. Two analytical points: the diaspora is an asset for soft power and remittances but a constraint when host-country politics turn; and visa policy abroad is industrial policy for India’s largest export sector. PART IV ◆ RECALL — case law, provisions, committees, value additions One line each, and the line is the holding you would actually cite. An unexplained case name earns nothing; a case with its year placed at the point of argument is GS-2’s highest-yield value addition. 1 ◆ THE CASE-LAW BANK BASIC STRUCTURE AND AMENDMENT Shankari Prasad (1951) ‘Law’ in Art 13 does not include a constitutional amendment. Sajjan Singh (1965) Aﬀirmed Shankari Prasad; doubts recorded in dissent. Golaknath (1967) Fundamental Rights unamendable — the untenable absolute. Kesavananda Bharati (1973) Amending power under Art 368 cannot damage or destroy the basic structure. Thirteen judges. Indira Nehru Gandhi (1975) Art 329A struck down; free and fair elections a basic feature. Minerva Mills (1980) Art 368(4) and (5) struck down; limited amending power and the Part III–Part IV balance are basic features. Waman Rao (1981) Ninth Schedule immunity only for laws added before 24 April 1973. I. R. Coelho (2007) Post-1973 Ninth Schedule entries reviewable on basic-structure grounds. In re Delhi Laws Act (1951) Essential legislative function cannot be delegated. EXECUTIVE, GOVERNOR, FEDERALISM Shamsher Singh (1974) President and Governor act on the aid and advice of ministers; discretion is narrow. S. R. Bommai (1994) Art 356 proclamation justiciable; floor test the only test of majority; Assembly dissolved only after both Houses approve; secularism a basic feature. Rameshwar Prasad (2006) Dissolution of the Bihar Assembly on a Governor’s report about apprehended defections struck down. Nabam Rebia (2016) Governor cannot advance an Assembly session or act on his own discretion contrary to ministerial advice. State of Tamil Nadu v. Governor (8 April 2025) Two judges prescribed timelines under Art 200 and declared ten Bills deemed assented under Art 142 — overruled. In re Assent, Presidential Reference (20 Nov 2025)  Five judges, CJI Gavai: courts cannot prescribe timelines under Art 200; deemed assent has no constitutional existence; Arts 200–201 decisions not justiciable pre-enactment; remedy only for prolonged, unexplained, indefinite inaction. Mohit Minerals (2022) GST Council recommendations persuasive, not binding; Union and States have simultaneous power. Kuldip Nayar (2006) Removal of the domicile requirement for Rajya Sabha upheld. In re Article 370 (2023) Abrogation upheld; Art 370 held a temporary provision. PARLIAMENT, PRIVILEGE, DEFECTION Kihoto Hollohan (1992) Tenth Schedule upheld; Para 7 read down to preserve judicial review; the Speaker acts as a tribunal. Keisham Meghachandra Singh (2020) A Speaker belonging to a party should not decide defection; independent tribunal urged; three-month disposal. Subhash Desai (2023) The whip is appointed by the political party, not the legislature party; Governor erred in calling a floor test. Raja Ram Pal (2007) ‘Finality’ does not oust review for illegality or unconstitutionality; expulsion power upheld. Keshav Singh (1965) Privilege versus Art 21 — conflict exposed, not resolved. Sita Soren (2024) Seven judges, overruling P. V. Narasimha Rao (1998): no Art 105(2) immunity for a legislator who takes a bribe to vote. Krishna Kumar Singh (2017) Re-promulgation of ordinances is a fraud on the Constitution; laying before the House is mandatory. Puttaswamy (Aadhaar) (2018) Money Bill certification of the Aadhaar Act upheld by majority; strong Chandrachud dissent. Rojer Mathew (2019) Doubted the Aadhaar money-bill reasoning; scope of ‘only’ in Art 110 referred to seven judges, still undecided. Tribunal rules struck down for executive dominance. RIGHTS, REVIEW, TRIBUNALS A. K. Gopalan (1950) → Maneka Gandhi (1978) Procedure under Art 21 must be just, fair and reasonable; Arts 14, 19 and 21 read together. E. P. Royappa (1974) Arbitrariness is the antithesis of equality under Art 14. K. S. Puttaswamy (2017) Privacy a fundamental right under Art 21; four-part proportionality — legality, legitimate aim, necessity, balancing. L. Chandra Kumar (1997) High Court review under Arts 226/227 is a basic feature; no tribunal may oust it. NJAC / Supreme Court AoR (2015) 99th Amendment struck down; judicial primacy in appointments part of independence. Second Judges (1993), Third Judges (1998) Collegium created; the CJI’s opinion means collegium opinion. Prem Chand Garg (1963); A. R. Antulay (1988) Art 142 cannot override express statutory provisions or fundamental rights. Supreme Court Bar Association (1998) Art 142 cannot build a new edifice ignoring substantive law. Shilpa Sailesh (2023) Art 142 may dissolve a marriage on irretrievable breakdown. Berubari (1960) Cession of territory requires a constitutional amendment (Art 143 reference). Anita Kushwaha (2016) Access to justice is a facet of Art 21. ADM Jabalpur (1976) Art 21 suspendable during emergency — expressly overruled in Puttaswamy; 44th Amendment is the legislative answer. EQUALITY, RESERVATION, SOCIAL JUSTICE Indra Sawhney (1992) Caste may identify a class; creamy layer excluded from OBC benefit; 50% ceiling; no reservation in promotion; quantifiable data required. M. Nagaraj (2006), as modified by Jarnail Singh (2018) Promotion quota needs data on inadequacy of representation; backwardness data not required for SC/ST; creamy layer applies. Janhit Abhiyan (2022) 103rd Amendment upheld — EWS reservation valid; the 50% ceiling is not inviolable. State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh (2024) Overruled E. V. Chinnaiah (2005): States may sub-classify Scheduled Castes on quantifiable data. NALSA (2014) Transgender persons recognised; gender identity rests on self-identification. Vikash Kumar v. UPSC (2021) Reasonable accommodation is a facet of equality; a scribe cannot be denied by rigid rule. Rajive Raturi (2024) Accessibility standards under the RPwD Act are mandatory, not aspirational. Girish Ramchandra Deshpande (2012) Service records of a public servant largely ‘personal information’ under RTI s.8(1)(j). Vishaka (1997) → PoSH Act 2013 Judicial guidelines converted into statute — the model of directive-to-legislation. ELECTIONS AND THE COMMISSION Mohinder Singh Gill (1978) Art 324 is a reservoir of power where the law is silent; orders must stand on their own reasons. Anoop Baranwal (2023) EC appointment by PM, Leader of the Opposition and CJI until Parliament legislates — superseded by the CEC Act 2023. ADR v. ECI (2025) Special Intensive Revision upheld; Art 324 is not a dead letter; Aadhaar admitted as a twelfth identity document; omitted-elector list to be published. ADR (2002), PUCL (2003) Disclosure of assets and criminal antecedents is part of Art 19(1)(a). Lily Thomas (2013) RPA s.8(4) struck down — conviction disqualifies immediately. ADR v. Union (2024) Electoral bond scheme struck down as violating the right to information. Art 329(b) No judicial interference once the electoral process has begun; the election petition is the sole remedy. GOVERNANCE, REGULATION, CIVIL SERVICE Ram Jawaya Kapur (1955) Functional, not rigid, separation of powers in India. Noel Harper (2022) FCRA 2020 amendments upheld; receiving foreign contribution is not a right. T. S. R. Subramanian (2013) Civil Services Board; minimum two-year tenure; oral instructions to be recorded in writing. Vineet Narain (1997) CVC given statutory status; fixed tenure for the CBI Director; insulation of investigation. Prakash Singh (2006) State Security Commission, fixed DGP and SHO tenure, separation of investigation from law and order, Police Complaints Authority. All India Judges Association Successive directions on district judiciary pay, cadre strength and infrastructure. Anjali Bhardwaj (2019) Directions on timely appointment to Information Commissions. Madras Bar Association (2014, 2020, 2021) Tribunal member selection and short renewable tenures struck down repeatedly. 2 ◆ ARTICLE INDEX — provision to content 13, 32, 226, 227 Laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights void; constitutional remedies; High Court writ and superintendence. 14, 15, 16, 17 Equality; 15(4)/(5) and 16(4) enable reservation; 15(6)/16(6) EWS; abolition of untouchability. 19(1)(a), 21, 21A Speech — source of the right to know; life and liberty — source of privacy; right to education. 32, 136, 141, 142, 143 Writ jurisdiction; special leave; law declared binding; complete justice (remedial, not legislative); Presidential reference. 80, 81, 82, 108, 109, 110 Rajya Sabha composition (Fourth Schedule); Lok Sabha composition; readjustment after census; joint sitting; Money Bill procedure; Money Bill defined exhaustively, 110(3) certification final. 85, 105, 112–117, 122, 123 Six months maximum between sessions — no minimum sitting days; privileges; financial procedure; procedural irregularity not justiciable; ordinances. 124, 124(4), 125, 148, 151, 217, 218, 221, 312 Appointment and removal of judges; charged salaries; CAG; audit reports laid before Parliament; All India Services. 163, 200, 201, 213, 356, 361 Governor’s Council of Ministers and discretion; assent — four courses; President’s three courses; State ordinances; President’s Rule; personal immunity. 243–243ZG Panchayats (Part IX, Eleventh Schedule) and Municipalities (Part IXA, Twelfth Schedule); 243I and 243Y State Finance Commissions; 243K and 243ZA State Election Commissions; 243ZD and 243ZE planning committees. 249, 263, 270, 275, 279A, 280, 281, 282 Rajya Sabha resolution on a State List entry; Inter-State Council; distribution of taxes — cesses not shareable; grants-in-aid; GST Council; Finance Commission; report laid with action-taken memorandum; discretionary grants. 324, 326, 329(b), 368 Superintendence of elections; adult suffrage — citizenship, age, ordinary residence; bar on judicial interference; amending power, limited by basic structure. Schedules Fourth — Rajya Sabha seats; Fifth and Sixth — tribal areas; Ninth — immunity, only pre-1973; Tenth — anti-defection; Eleventh and Twelfth — panchayat and municipal functions. Amendments to name 42nd (1976) freeze on seats, ‘secular’; 44th (1978) Art 352 ‘armed rebellion’, Arts 20 and 21 non-suspendable; 52nd (1985) Tenth Schedule; 73rd and 74th (1992); 84th (2001) freeze to first census after 2026; 91st (2003) split exception removed; 99th (2015) NJAC, struck down; 101st (2016) GST; 103rd (2019) EWS; 106th (2023) women’s reservation, conditional on delimitation. 3 ◆ COMMITTEES AND COMMISSIONS — the recommendation worth citing Sarkaria (1988) Governor from outside active politics, appointed in consultation with the Chief Minister; Art 356 as a last resort; Inter-State Council under Art 263. Punchhi (2010)  Fixed five-year gubernatorial tenure removable only for cause; localised emergency instead of State-wide; permanent Inter-State Council with a secretariat; Concurrent List Bills referred to it. Tarkunde (1975), Dinesh Goswami (1990) Parity of removal protection for all Election Commissioners; defection adjudication by the President or Governor on the Election Commission’s advice. Law Commission 170th Report (1999) Anti-defection — restrict the whip to confidence motions and money bills. Second ARC (2005–09) Social audit; statutory citizen’s charters with penalties; domain specialisation in the civil services; RTI as the first report; Sevottam framework. National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution (2002) Define contempt of the House without a comprehensive privilege code; minimum sitting days — 120 Lok Sabha, 100 Rajya Sabha. T. S. R. Subramanian (2013) Civil Services Board; minimum two-year tenure; written instructions. FSLRC (2013) Statutory duties of consultation, cost-benefit analysis and reasoned orders for regulators; separated adjudication. Rohini Commission (2017–) Sub-categorisation of OBCs — report submitted, not published. Justice Verma (2013) Criminal law reform after the 2012 Delhi case — the basis of the 2013 amendments. Kelkar (2015) PPP renegotiation must be institutionalised, not criminalised. 16th Finance Commission (2026–31)  Chair Arvind Panagariya. Devolution 41%; income distance 42.5%, population (2011) 17.5%, demographic performance 10%, area 10%, forest 10%, contribution to GDP 10%; local bodies ₹7.91 lakh crore; disaster ₹1.55 lakh crore; Centre 3.5% deficit by 2030-31, States 3% of GSDP. Mandal (1980), Balwant Rai Mehta (1957), Ashok Mehta (1978) OBC reservation; three-tier panchayati raj; two-tier with political parties — the lineage of decentralisation. 4 ◆ VALUE ADDITIONS — data, doctrines, instruments Numbers worth carrying Public health spending 2% of GDP against the NHP 2017 target of 2.5%; research intensity 0.65% of GDP; education target 6% of GDP, unmet since 1968; over nine-tenths of the workforce informal; FLFP 23% (2017-18) → over 40% (2023-24), urban still near 25%; DPDP penalties up to ₹250 crore; PM-JAY cover ₹5 lakh; diaspora 32 million; RPwD reservation 4% employment, 5% higher education; Twelfth Schedule 18 functions, Eleventh Schedule 29. Dates worth carrying DPDP Act 2023, s.44(3) amending RTI; Labour Codes in force 21 Nov 2025; three criminal codes in force 1 July 2024; In re Assent 20 Nov 2025; SHANTI Act 22 Dec 2025; CBAM definitive phase 1 Jan 2026; BBNJ in force Jan 2026; WHO Pandemic Agreement adopted May 2025; UN Convention against Cybercrime opened Hanoi, Oct 2025; delimitation freeze ends at the first census after 2026. Doctrines and principles Basic structure; proportionality (four limbs); reasonable accommodation; the social model of disability; cooperative and asymmetric federalism; subsidiarity; Gujral Doctrine — asymmetric generosity, the larger neighbour seeks no reciprocity; SAGAR → MAHASAGAR; strategic autonomy as capability, not abstention; non-Western, not anti-Western.
Phrases that carry an argument

‘A promise without a right’ (citizen’s charters); ‘a gateway, not social security’ (e-Shram); ‘centralisation is not autonomy’ (higher-education regulator); ‘insurance buys treatment, primary care buys health’; ‘saturation fails by inclusion, targeting by exclu- sion’; ‘elections without government’ (74th Amendment); ‘the pool, not the percentage, is the federal question’; ‘coordination without command’ (intelligence and intergovernmental forums); ‘disengagement is not de-escalation’; ‘delivered, not declared’. The turn every GS-2 answer needs Name the reform — the committee, the statutory change or the procedural safeguard — not a general aspiration. ‘Independence is a property of design, not of character’ is a position; ‘there should be more independence’ is not.

topics.q: What is a Farmer Producer Organisation? Discuss its role in agricultural marketing and examine the constraints that limit its effectiveness.
body: An FPO is a registered producer collective — a Producer Company under Part IXA or a cooperative — aggregating smallholders, who hold 86% of operational holdings. With the 10,000-FPO target achieved, the question is now commercial viability, not formation.
Role in agricultural marketing
• Scale: aggregation converts the scale disadvantage into bargaining power; direct sale to processors compresses intermediary layers.
• Access: grading, storage, e-NAM and ONDC linkage; warehouse-receipt finance replaces distress sale with deferred sale.
• Value capture: primary processing, branding and PDS procurement preference turn a price-taker into a pricenegotiator.
Constraints

• Organisational: dependence on the promoting institution, a single hired CEO, low member equity; members sidesell when spot prices are marginally better — exactly when the FPO needs volume to honour a contract.
• Financial: no collateral or credit history; working capital is scarcest at procurement; equity-grant caps and delayed subsidy release persist despite the Credit Guarantee Fund.
• Scale: most stay below the turnover at which processing is viable.
CONCLUSION Shared-services management, blended finance and FPO federations are the remedy. FPOs must be judged by member price realisation, not by registrations.
topics.draw: Hub-and-spoke — smallholders and inputs → FPO → processor / e-NAM / warehouse receipt; hang the three failure modes (governance, equity, working capital) below the hub.
bank: Doubling farmer income
FPOs shift income from yield to margin — the same tonnage sold graded and aggregated fetches a higher farm-gate share.
Women / SHG angle
Lakhpati Didi and SHG–producer-collective convergence gives women cultivators a market identity that land records deny them.
Contract farming
An FPO is the only counterparty that makes contract farming enforceable at smallholder scale — it internalises default risk.
Cooperative comparison
Producer Companies escape State cooperative-law interference but lose the deposit and patronage base cooperatives enjoy.
Digital / ONDC
ONDC lowers the fixed cost of market discovery, the single largest entry barrier for a sub-₹2 crore FPO.
Allied sectors
Dairy and fishery FPOs generate weekly cash flow, so they stabilise working capital in a way crop FPOs structurally cannot.

topics.t: Cyber-enabled Financial Crime and Mule Accounts
topics.q: Cyber-enabled financial crime relies on social engineering, mule accounts and transnational payment infrastructure. Trace the crime chain and evaluate India’s response.
body: Cyber-enabled financial crime uses digital channels for ordinary acquisitive crime. Its distinguishing feature is speed and distance — funds are layered across dozens of accounts and jurisdictions within minutes, while legal process remains designed for physical crime.
The crime chain
• Data: leaked databases, brokers and social-media profiling.
• Deception: impersonation of banks, police and courts; ‘digital arrest’ confinement; task-based job, investment and romance fraud.
• Access: phishing, SIM swap, malicious apps, OTP interception, remote-access tools.
• Layering: fan-out across mule accounts, wallets and prepaid instruments; conversion to virtual digital assets; crossborder transfer.
• Integration: cash withdrawal near borders, gold and trade-based laundering, much run from South-East Asian scam compounds.
India's response --- reach and limits
• Built: I4C as nodal body, the 1930 helpline and cybercrime reporting portal enabling transaction hold-back in the golden hour.
• Gaps: mule detection is bank-by-bank, prepaid KYC is loose, liability for loss is unallocated, and cross-border evidence moves slower than the money.
CONCLUSION Behavioural mule-detection shared across banks, NPCI negative-list sharing and a statutory liability rule are needed.
The decisive window is the first hour and the first mule account — after that, recovery becomes diplomacy.
topics.draw: Linear chain: data leak → social engineering → access (OTP/SIM swap) → mule accounts → VDA/cross-border → cash, gold, offshore. Mark the single intervention point at ‘mule accounts — 1930, golden-hour hold-back’.
bank: Digital arrest scams
The offence is impersonation of the State itself — so the counter-measure is public communication that no agency arrests over video.
Banking regulation
Tokenisation, cooling-off on new payees and transaction-limit tiering reduce the value extractable per compromised account.
Elderly / rural victims
Exclusion-adjacent victims lose most and complain least; assisted grievance redress through business correspondents must be built in.
International law
The UN Convention against Cybercrime (Hanoi, October 2025) offers 24/7 contacts and expedited preservation of volatile data.
Crypto link
Virtual asset service providers must be brought under the FATF travel rule so the layering step regains a paper trail.
Policing capacity
Conviction, not registration, is the metric — district cyber cells need forensic capability and trained prosecutors.

topics.q: How does dual-frequency synthetic aperture radar improve observation of change on the Earth’s surface? Explain its applications in agriculture and disaster management.
body: SAR uses the satellite’s own motion to synthesise a very large antenna. As an active microwave sensor it works through cloud and darkness — decisive where optical sensors are blocked through kharif. NISAR, the NASA–ISRO mission, is the first satellite carrying both L-band and S-band radar.
Why two frequencies improve observation
• Penetration scales with wavelength: L-band reaches through canopy and dry soil to sense biomass, soil moisture and ground; S-band reads surface roughness and crop structure.
• Disambiguation: using both separates vegetation change from ground change — an ambiguity single-frequency radar cannot resolve.
• Interferometry: repeat-pass InSAR detects displacement at centimetre scale.
Applications

• Agriculture: all-weather crop-area and growth-stage estimation through kharif; soil-moisture mapping for irrigation advisory and drought declaration; biomass yield modelling; objective crop-insurance damage assessment.

• Disaster management: Joshimath-type subsidence, landslide precursor movement, glacier and glacial-lake monitoring for GLOF risk, co-seismic displacement, flood extent under cloud, coastal erosion and oil-slick detection.

CONCLUSION Observation converts to outcome only when data reaches users — Bhuvan dissemination, PM Fasal Bima and NDMA integration. Dual-frequency SAR turns one-off observation into continuous monitoring — the basis of anticipatory rather than reactive management.
topics.draw: Section view: canopy over ground, with two arrows of different reach — S-band stopping at the canopy top, L-band penetrating to the soil. Label ‘both = vegetation change separated from ground change’.
bank: Space diplomacy
NISAR is the largest India–US civil space collaboration — a template for cost-shared, dual-badge Earth observation.
Climate change
Ice-sheet, permafrost and mangrove biomass monitoring feed directly into NDC accounting and blue-carbon credit verification.
Crop insurance
Radar-based area and damage estimates replace manual crop-cutting experiments, compressing PMFBY settlement time.
Infrastructure
InSAR monitors dam deformation, tunnel and metro subsidence and pipeline right-of-way — an asset-integrity tool.
Data policy
Free and open data multiplies value; the constraint is downstream analytics capacity in States, not satellite supply.
Security use
All-weather, night-capable imaging supports maritime domain awareness and change detection along contested frontiers.

topics.q: Revision of the base year of national accounts is necessary for statistical relevance, but does not by itself resolve the problems of measuring a changing economy.
body: Explain.
A base year fixes the price and structural reference for constant-price estimates. India has moved the National Accounts base from 2011-12 to 2022-23, with parallel revision of the IIP and CPI.
Why rebasing was necessary
• Obsolete weights: services, digital and platform activity had outgrown their shares, and an ageing consumption survey overstated the CPI food weight.
• Better sources: GST returns, MCA-21, e-way bills and the revamped PLFS improve coverage and timeliness.
• Consistency: Supply–Use Tables reconcile product supply with intermediate and final use.
What rebasing does not resolve
• Informal sector: still estimated from periodic surveys and formal-sector proxies rather than observed directly.
• Single deflation: wholesale-price-heavy deflators misstate real value added, sharply so in manufacturing — double deflation remains unadopted.
• Quality and free digital services: poorly captured, biasing measured productivity.
• Comparability: a methodological break shifts growth and sector shares without equivalent real change, so backseries splicing needs published assumptions and sensitivity checks.

CONCLUSION Annual supply–use tables, an updated enterprise-survey frame, double deflation and audited statistical independence are the real reforms. A new base year restores relevance; credibility depends on better primary data and methods, not on the rebasing itself.
topics.draw: Two-column grid — ‘What rebasing fixes’ (weights, sources, SUT) against ‘What it leaves’ (informal sector, single deflation, quality change, comparability break).
bank: Statistical governance
An independent National Statistical Commission with a statutory mandate is the institutional counterpart of methodological reform.
Poverty / inequality
Consumption-survey revision matters more than GDP rebasing for distributional statistics.
Employment data
The PLFS revamp gives monthly urban and quarterly rural estimates — frequency, not just accuracy, is the gain.
Fiscal ratios
Debt-to-GDP, tax-to-GDP and capex-to-GDP all shift mechanically on rebasing without any real change in policy.
International comparison
SNA compliance determines cross-country comparability; deviations must be documented, not silent.
Data trust
Publishing unit-level data with documented methods is the cheapest way to convert technical accuracy into public credibility.

topics.q: Digital public infrastructure in agriculture can reduce information and transaction costs, but may exclude tenants, women farmers and those with weak land records. Examine.
body: Agri-DPI — the Farmer Registry, village maps and Crop Sown Registry under AgriStack — creates a consent-based identity layer for advisory, credit, insurance and procurement. Bharat-VISTAAR adds validated ICAR advice.
The cost reductions are real
• Information: personalised multilingual advisory replaces generic extension at a fraction of the cost.
