• Transaction:  paperless KCC shortens credit turnaround; digital crop surveys replace crop-cutting experiments, speeding PM Fasal Bima settlement.
• Market: verified crop data lower buyers’ due-diligence cost and improve price discovery.
Why the exclusion is structural, not incidental
• Land-record anchoring: the Farmer ID is tied to ownership, so tenants, sharecroppers and oral lessees — a large unrecorded share of cultivators — fall outside credit, insurance and relief.
• Gender: women cultivate extensively but rarely hold title, so the registry reproduces exclusion digitally.
• Access and opacity: connectivity, literacy and gendered device ownership exclude a second group, opaque credit scoring a third — a denial cannot be contested if its basis is undisclosed.

CONCLUSION Recognise cultivator status independently of ownership through cultivator cards and model tenancy law; enforce purpose limitation and redress under the DPDP Act 2023. Digital infrastructure inherits the inequities of the land record it is built on.
topics.draw: One vertical spine — land record → Farmer ID → credit/insurance/relief — with a dashed branch (tenants, sharecroppers, oral lessees, women cultivators) falling outside it.
bank: Data protection
Consent, purpose limitation and a data-fiduciary duty must bind private agri-tech partners, not only the State.
AI advisory
Bharat-VISTAAR must augment, not replace, accountable extension workers — a model error at scale is an agronomic disaster.
Credit deepening
Cash-flow-based underwriting on crop-sown data can finally displace collateral, which is the actual exclusion mechanism.
Precision agriculture
Plot-level advisory reduces fertiliser and water use — an environmental gain, not merely an income gain.
Federal issue
Land records are a State subject, so AgriStack quality varies with State capacity; incentivise digitisation through grants.
Global comparison
Unlike private ag-data platforms abroad, DPI keeps the identity layer public — the value lies in interoperability, not the app.

topics.t: Early Warning Systems --- Cyclone, Flood and Heat
topics.q: Early warning systems have sharply reduced cyclone mortality in India. Examine why comparable gains have not been achieved for floods and heatwaves.
body: Cyclone mortality has fallen from over ten thousand in the 1999 Odisha super-cyclone to double digits today. The gain came from a complete warning chain, which breaks at its weakest link.
Why the cyclone chain succeeded
• Lead time: cyclones form over the sea across days, so track and landfall skill is high.
• A single unambiguous action: move to a designated shelter before landfall.
• Institutional clarity: IMD as sole authoritative source, rehearsed NDRF and volunteer protocols, purpose-built shelters.
Why floods and heat lag

• Floods: flash and urban floods develop within hours, leaving no evacuation window; responsibility is split across CWC, irrigation departments and municipalities, so reservoir release is not integrated with downstream warning; destinations are unclear and assets immovable, so compliance is low.
• Heat: the hazard is invisible and cumulative, protective action costs a daily wage, and heat is not a notified disaster, so no SDRF/NDRF funds are triggered.

CONCLUSION Mission Mausam and IMD’s AI/ML models now give seven-day advance prediction; couple this with impact-based forecasting, Common Alerting Protocol dissemination in local languages, single-source authority and post-event audit. Forecasting skill without a governance chain is measurement, not protection.
topics.draw: Six boxes in sequence — detect → forecast → disseminate → comprehend → act → recover. Mark ‘flood breaks here (no protective action)’ and ‘heat breaks here (acting costs a day’s wage)’.
bank: Sendai Framework
Target G — multi-hazard early warning availability — and the UN ‘Early Warnings for All’ 2027 goal give the benchmark.
Technology
Doppler radar density, AWS networks and cell-broadcast are inputs; the binding constraint is institutional, not instrumental.
Community role
Odisha’s cyclone volunteers show the last 500 metres is covered by people, not by systems.
GLOF / landslide
Himalayan hazards need instrumented, site-specific warning with minutes of lead time — a different design problem.
Insurance link
Parametric triggers convert a forecast into an automatic payout — the fastest recovery instrument available.
Urban flooding
Warning cannot substitute for drainage design and floodplain regulation — exposure control is the primary instrument.

topics.q: Small unmanned aircraft have converted low-cost technology into an asymmetric threat. Explain the elements of an effective counter-unmanned aircraft system architecture.
body: Small unmanned systems combine low cost, small radar cross-section, low-altitude flight and autonomy. Together these invert the cost-exchange ratio — a drone worth lakhs compels air defences costing far more.
The threat
• Cross-border delivery of narcotics, weapons and IED components along Punjab and Jammu, in the fence–radar gap.
• Armed and swarm attack, reconnaissance, and exposure of refineries, airports and grid substations — with deniability, since airframes are commercial.
A layered architecture
• Detect: fused radar, RF, EO/IR and acoustic sensing — no single sensor catches a low, slow, small target.
• Identify: Digital Sky and NPNT enforcement separate hostile from lawful flights.
• Decide: a unified command picture and common rules of engagement across Army, BSF, police and CISF.
• Defeat: graded to collateral risk — soft-kill jamming in urban settings, hard-kill directed energy or interceptors where safe.
• Exploit: chip-level attribution and network mapping to disrupt the supply chain.

CONCLUSION Statutory clarity on who may engage an aircraft over civil airspace, indigenous sensors and directed-energy systems at scale, and counter-UAS cover in every critical installation’s plan. Counter-drone capability is an architecture and a set of authorities, not a device.
topics.draw: Five stacked bands — DETECT (radar/RF/EO-IR/acoustic) → IDENTIFY (Digital Sky, NPNT) → DECIDE (unified picture, common RoE) → DEFEAT (soft-kill / hard-kill by risk) → EXPLOIT (forensics, network mapping).
bank: Drone as enabler
Kisan drones, Namo Drone Didi and survey drones mean regulation must be permissive by default and restrictive by exception.
Lessons from conflict
Ukraine and West Asia show attritable mass beats exquisite platforms — magazine depth matters more than interceptor quality.
Legal gap
The Aircraft Act framework does not clearly authorise a policeman to down an aircraft; a statutory power with safeguards is overdue.
Critical infrastructure
Extend the CISF security-plan template to include an airspace annexe for every refinery, port and grid node.
Indigenisation
iDEX and DRDO’s drone detection and interdiction system give a base; the gap is serial production and integration.
Maritime drones
Uncrewed surface and underwater vehicles extend the same cost-exchange logic to ports and the littoral.

topics.q: What is a Heat Action Plan? Examine its effectiveness in Indian cities and the institutional and financial constraints on implementation.
body: A Heat Action Plan links IMD forecasts to graded preparedness across health, water and labour services. Ahmedabad’s 2013 plan, the first in South Asia, cut summer mortality measurably. Urban heat is a compound disaster — warming, land use, housing and health inequality interact, so the same temperature kills unequally.
The risk chain
• Rising temperature meets the urban heat island of concrete and lost tree cover; night minima stay high, denying the body its recovery window — which is what kills.
• Tin-roofed, unventilated housing traps heat indoors; outdoor workers, the elderly and the ill have least reserve; power demand peaks when the grid is stressed.
Why plans underperform
• Design: plans copied without local vulnerability assessment achieve little; most use dry-bulb temperature alone, ignoring humidity and night minima.
• Institutional: municipal bodies lack disaster powers, and heat is not a notified disaster.
• Financial: heat mortality is under-measured, so cool roofs and water infrastructure stay unfunded.

CONCLUSION ‘HAP 2.0’ — statutory backing through urban disaster authorities, humidity-adjusted ward thresholds, wage-protected work–rest–water–shade protocols, and cool roofs in building codes. Heat plans must become year-round budgeted urban policy, not seasonal advisories.
topics.draw: Risk chain, not a list: warming + urban heat island → high night minima (no recovery) → tin roofs, density, no ventilation → outdoor workers, elderly, chronically ill → excess mortality.
bank: Labour / economy
Lost outdoor labour hours are the largest measurable economic cost; wage-protected rest is an income-security instrument.
Notified-disaster debate
Notification unlocks funds but requires a defensible mortality-attribution methodology first.
Urban planning
Blue-green infrastructure, canopy targets and building-envelope norms act on the hazard, not merely on exposure.
Cooling policy
The India Cooling Action Plan — passive design and eﬀicient appliances avoid the emissions-from-cooling feedback loop.
Health system
Heat–health surveillance and ward-level mortality reporting convert an invisible hazard into a governable one.
Rural heat
Agricultural workers face the same exposure with none of the plan coverage — HAPs are almost entirely urban instruments.

topics.t: Solid Waste Management and the Circular Economy
topics.q: The Solid Waste Management Rules, 2026 mandate four-stream segregation. Explain why segregation is necessary but insuﬀicient for a circular urban economy.
body: A circular economy designs waste out by keeping materials in use, disposal last. The SWM Rules 2026, in force from 1 April 2026, mandate four-stream segregation: wet, dry, sanitary and special-care waste.
Why segregation is necessary
• Segregation decides whether anything downstream is recoverable: mixed waste is contaminated waste, and wet organics destroy the dry fraction’s recyclability.
• It is also the cheapest intervention — value is lost irreversibly at the bin.
Why it is insuﬀicient

• Missing downstream: a segregated stream still needs a Material Recovery Facility, an off-taker and a composting route for wet waste. Absent these, waste is re-mixed in the truck — destroying public willingness to segregate.

• EPR’s own limits: fraudulent certificates; the informal sector does most actual recovery but is excluded from EPR value; weight-based targets are met through easy plastics while multi-layer packaging continues; and fees are too low to change design.

CONCLUSION Eco-modulate EPR fees so recyclable design pays less; integrate waste-pickers into MRFs; enforce Extended Bulk Waste Generator obligations; and price landfill so recovery becomes commercially rational. Circularity is decided at the design stage — everything after the bin is damage limitation.
topics.draw: Waste hierarchy pyramid — prevent / reuse–repair / recycle–compost / disposal (last resort). Mark ‘segregation acts here’ at the recycle band, three levels below where circularity is actually decided.
bank: Legacy waste
Bio-mining and capping of dumpsites under Swachh Bharat 2.0 recover land, but do not alter the daily inflow.
Waste-to-energy
Calorific value is low in Indian mixed waste; WTE competes with recycling for the dry fraction and needs a tipping fee.
E-waste
Producer responsibility plus a floor price for recyclers is needed because informal acid-leaching is cheaper than compliant recovery.
Construction waste
C&D debris is the largest volume stream; mandating recycled aggregate in public works creates the missing demand.
Climate link
Landfill methane is a short-lived climate pollutant — wet-waste diversion is mitigation, not merely sanitation.
Informal sector
Waste-pickers already deliver much of India’s recycling rate at zero public cost — formalising them is eﬀiciency, not welfare.

topics.t: Organised Crime and the Financing of Terrorism
topics.q: Discuss the linkages between organised crime and the financing of terrorism. Examine the effectiveness of India’s legal and institutional framework in disrupting them.
body: The crime–terror nexus converges profit-driven organised crime with ideological terrorism, sustained by shared infrastructure rather than shared belief — the same routes, documents, hawala channels and facilitators serve both. Ideology explains motive; logistics and finance explain capability.
The changing forms
• Narco-terrorism: along the western border, with drones replacing human couriers.
• Counterfeit currency and gold smuggling; extortion converted into political funding; illegal arms supply.
• Cyber-enabled finance: crowdfunding under charitable cover, virtual assets and mule accounts, which decouple the funder from the operation.
The framework and where it strains
• Built: UAPA Chapter IV-A on terror financing; PMLA 2002 attachment by the ED; NIA for scheduled offences; FIUIND for suspicious transaction reports; NDPS and State laws such as MCOCA.

• Strain: policing is a State subject while networks are transnational; convictions are few because the money trail is hard to prove; legal assistance is slower than transfer; virtual-asset regulation is immature.

CONCLUSION Follow the money first; build financial-investigation capacity inside State police; use beneficial-ownership registries and the travel rule for virtual asset providers. Terror networks are disrupted where their finance and logistics are, not where their ideology is.
topics.draw: Two overlapping circles — ‘organised crime’ and ‘terrorism’ — with the intersection labelled ‘routes, hawala, documents, facilitators’. Caption: shared infrastructure, not shared ideology.
bank: White-collar terrorism
Educated, socially integrated recruits use legitimate professional cover, which defeats profiling-based detection entirely.
FATF process
Grey-listing imposes measurable capital-flow costs — compliance is a strategic as well as a legal interest.
Left-wing extremism
Extortion from contractors and tendu/mining rents is the LWE analogue of terror finance — audit the contract chain.
Federal friction
NIA–State coordination and consent decide how fast a transnational case actually moves.
Human traﬀicking
Scam compounds in South-East Asia run on traﬀicked labour — a crime-finance node with a human-rights dimension.
Asset forfeiture
Non-conviction-based forfeiture disrupts capability faster than conviction does, but needs due-process safeguards.

topics.t: Carbon Markets and the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme
topics.q: India’s Carbon Credit Trading Scheme can lower mitigation costs only if credits possess environmental integrity. What safeguards are necessary? India’s CCTS, run by the Bureau of Energy Eﬀiciency, is an intensity-based baseline-and-credit system, not cap-and-trade. Obligations began 1 April 2025 for 490 entities in seven sectors, first compliance due 31 July 2026.
body: Why the design matters
• Targets are per unit of output, so growth is not penalised — but absolute emissions can still rise under full compliance: the scheme delivers eﬀiciency, not an emissions ceiling.
The four integrity conditions
• Additionality: a credit must represent abatement that would not have happened anyway; crediting business-as-usual creates paper reductions.
• Credible baselines: an inflated baseline manufactures surplus credits and collapses the price, as in earlier offset markets.
• Verification: accredited, rotated verifiers, since a verifier paid by the entity it audits faces a rating-agency conflict.
• No double counting: a credit sold abroad must be subtracted from India’s NDC through corresponding adjustments under Article 6.2 of the Paris Agreement.
CONCLUSION Tighten targets so a price signal emerges; publish an entity-level MRV registry; set a price floor; cover steel and fertiliser.
A carbon market’s value is entirely a function of the credibility of one tonne — without integrity it subsidises doing nothing.
topics.draw: Four sequential gates, one exit: claimed abatement → additional? → baseline credible? → independently verified? → no double counting? → ‘a real tonne’. Any gate failing → ‘a paper credit’.
bank: CBAM interaction
A credible domestic carbon price is the strongest argument for CBAM deductibility — integrity is a trade interest.
Voluntary market
The offset mechanism for non-obligated entities needs the same four gates, or it will discredit the compliance segment.
Just transition
Auction or levy revenue can fund coal-district diversification — recycling revenue is what buys political consent.
Comparison with EU ETS
A cap plus a Market Stability Reserve delivers certainty of quantity; India has chosen certainty of growth instead.
Agriculture / forestry
Soil carbon and afforestation credits face the hardest permanence and leakage tests — buffer pools are essential.
MSME impact
Obligated firms pass costs down an unregulated supply chain; support for MSME measurement prevents regressive incidence.

topics.t: Urban Disaster Management --- From Relief to Risk Governance
topics.q: The Disaster Management (Amendment) Act, 2025 provides for Urban Disaster Management Authorities and a National Disaster Database. Explain how these can improve risk-informed planning.
body: Relief responds after an event; risk governance manages the accumulation of risk before it. The DM (Amendment) Act 2025 provides for Urban Disaster Management Authorities in State capitals and municipal-corporation cities, and a National Disaster Database.
Why an urban authority was needed

• Urban risk is created by planning decisions — floodplain building, wetland filling, unregulated construction — taken by municipal authorities, while disaster powers sat with district authorities that do not control land use.
• A UDMA places prevention power and response duty in one institution, with one city plan covering flooding, heat, fire and industrial hazard.
What the database changes
• Risk-informed planning needs exposure and loss data India has never held centrally.
• Without it, mitigation funds are allocated politically rather than by risk, insurance cannot price exposure, and no one can show a mitigation rupee reduced loss.

CONCLUSION Only Karnataka has constituted a UDMA — implementation is the gap. Give UDMAs untied mitigation budgets; make the database mandatory for master-plan approval; use the 16th Finance Commission’s ₹1.55 lakh crore allocation to shift relief spending to mitigation. Risk governance is decided in the master plan, not in the relief camp.
topics.draw: Vertical flow — master plan (land use, building code) → UDMA (prevention + response in one body) → National Disaster Database (hazard, asset, loss) → risk-priced mitigation spending. Footnote the implementation gap.
bank: Municipal finance
A UDMA without an untied budget is an advisory committee; mitigation needs a dedicated municipal budget line.
74th Amendment link
Metropolitan Planning Committees remain unformed in most States — disaster powers float unless planning powers land.
Insurance
Municipal catastrophe cover and parametric products need the database to exist before they can be priced at all.
Cascading risk
Power is the common failure node; a city plan must map lifeline interdependencies, not just hazard zones.
Sendai / SDG 11
Local DRR strategies are a Sendai Target E commitment India reports against — UDMAs are the reporting unit.
Retrofitting
Existing building stock, not new construction, carries most seismic and flood risk — retrofit finance is the hardest gap.

topics.t: Free Trade Agreements --- A Double-Edged Instrument
topics.q: “FTAs are double-edged instruments; while they open access to foreign markets, they can also expose domestic sectors to unfair competition.” Discuss in the Indian context.
body: India has moved from FTA caution to FTA activism — CEPAs with the UAE and Australia, the India–EFTA TEPA with a $100 billion investment commitment, and agreements with the UK and EU.
Where FTAs open access
• Tariff access: duty-free entry for textiles, leather, gems and marine products, where competitors already enjoy preference.
• Value chains: tariff-free intermediates lower input cost and let firms plug into regional supply chains.
• Services and mobility: Mode 4 commitments, totalisation and digital-trade chapters, where India’s advantage lies.
• Rules: FTAs anchor regulatory predictability, which attracts FDI more reliably than tariffs alone.
Where they expose
• Import surge: after the India–ASEAN FTA imports outpaced exports, while Indian preference utilisation stayed low.
• Third-country routing: weak rules of origin allow trans-shipment, turning an FTA into a back door.
• Sensitive sectors: dairy and MSMEs face price suppression — the reason India stayed out of RCEP.
• Non-tariff cost: sanitary standards, carbon border measures and due-diligence rules penalise small exporters.

CONCLUSION   Strict rules-of-origin enforcement under CAROTAR, sensitive-list protection, PLI and logistics reform, and tradeadjustment assistance. An FTA must be judged by export competitiveness and quality employment, not by trade volume.
topics.draw: Two-column ledger — OPPORTUNITY (market access, GVC entry, Mode 4, FDI) against EXPOSURE (import surge, trans-shipment, sensitive sectors, NTBs) — with a bottom bar: ‘rules of origin + competitiveness = which side wins’.
bank: Agriculture defensive
Dairy and edible oil are livelihood, not trade, questions — a bound-tariff floor is a food-security instrument.
Labour / environment chapters
EU and UK agreements embed sustainability conditionality; capability to comply is the real negotiating asset.
WTO context
With the Appellate Body paralysed, bilateral dispute chapters substitute for multilateral adjudication.
MSME participation
Preference utilisation is low because certification cost is fixed; digitised origin certification lowers the barrier.
Services trade
Mobility and data-flow commitments matter more to India’s export basket than goods tariffs do.
Strategic dimension
FTAs with EFTA, the EU and UK are supply-chain de-risking instruments as much as commercial ones.

topics.t: The Shifting Global Trade Order and Imbalances
topics.q: The global trading order is shifting from multilateral liberalisation towards managed and reciprocal arrangements. Examine the implications for India’s exportoriented sectors and the policy responses available.
body: The order is shifting to managed and reciprocal arrangements — reciprocity tariffs, sustainability requirements, friend-shoring — while the WTO Appellate Body stays paralysed. The EU’s CBAM entered its definitive phase on 1 January 2026, converting reporting into certificate purchase.
Implications for India's export sectors
• Carbon-intensive exports: steel, aluminium and cement face a tariff proportional to embedded emissions, heaviest on exporters who cannot afford verified accounting.
• Labour-intensive exports: rules-of-origin and due-diligence compliance are fixed costs that penalise small firms.
• Rules to bargains: reciprocal tariffs make access contingent on bargaining, withdrawing predictability — the old order’s core public good.
• Imbalance: a merchandise deficit concentrated in China and energy, offset by services and remittances, leaves India exposed to tariff and currency shocks.
The opportunity within the shift
• Diversification away from a single hub opens a window in electronics, textiles and pharmaceuticals — but only for economies with low logistics cost, scale and predictable regulation.

CONCLUSION Build MRV capacity so exporters claim actual, not default, carbon values; conclude FTAs with services chapters; make the domestic carbon price creditable against CBAM. In a reciprocity-based order, leverage comes from indispensability in the chain, not market size.
topics.draw: CBAM cost transmission: Indian steel plant → embedded emissions → CBAM certificate → EU landed price rises. Branch: ‘verified MRV = actual, lower’ vs ‘no data = default value’.
bank: Trade deficit with China
Import dependence is concentrated in intermediates — substitution must be selective at chokepoints, not general.
Currency angle
Depreciation improves competitiveness only where import intensity is low; for electronics assembly it is largely neutral.
Export diversification
Product and market concentration ratios are the vulnerability metric — diversify destinations before diversifying products.
WTO reform
India’s interests lie in restoring binding dispute settlement, S&DT and a permanent solution on public stockholding.
Global South
India can position as a standards bridge — pressing for CBAM revenue recycling to fund developing-country decarbonisation.
Services resilience
Services exports and remittances are the shock absorber; digital-trade rules therefore matter more than tariff schedules.

topics.q: Self-reliance in pulses requires alignment of price support and procurement with seed systems, water use and cropping choice. Discuss the policy trade-offs involved.
body: India is the world’s largest producer and consumer of pulses, yet imports 2-3 million tonnes yearly. The Mission for Aatmanirbharta in Pulses (₹11,440 crore) treats this as a systems, not acreage, problem.
Why the deficit persists
• Agronomy: pulses are grown on rainfed, marginal land, so yields are low and variable.
• Seed: low seed replacement and a thin breeder-to-certified seed chain.
• Credibility: procurement is announced but thin, so the MSP floor is not believed and farmers revert to cereals.
• Policy signal: import liberalisation at price peaks depresses the sowing decision that would end the shortage.
The trade-offs to name
• Consumer versus producer: import easing calms retail inflation and destroys next season’s acreage.
• Ecology versus return: pulses fix nitrogen and use little water, so the ecological case is strongest where the private return is weakest.
• Fiscal: credible procurement means carrying stocks of a crop with no PDS obligation.

CONCLUSION  Announce assured NAFED and NCCF procurement before sowing; set a pre-announced import tariff path; expand seed hubs and short-duration varieties for rice-fallow areas. Self-reliance in pulses requires policy predictability more than new technology.
topics.draw: Decision loop — price rise → import easing → price falls → acreage falls next season → price rise. Break the loop at ‘pre-announced tariff path + procurement announced before sowing’.
bank: Nutrition link
Pulses are the primary protein source for vegetarian households — availability is a nutrition-security variable, not only a price one.
Cropping-pattern reform
Rice-fallow pulses in eastern India add a crop without additional water — the largest untapped area gain.
Edible oil parallel
The same import-dependence logic applies to oilseeds; a National Mission on Edible Oils runs on identical trade-offs.
Climate resilience
Pulses are heat-sensitive at flowering — terminal-heat-tolerant varieties are the key breeding target.
Market reform
Stock limits and export bans imposed mid-season are the single biggest deterrent to private storage investment.
Soil health
Legume rotation reduces synthetic nitrogen demand — a fertiliser-subsidy saving that is never credited to the pulses budget.

topics.q: India has achieved calorie security but not nutrition security. Examine the reasons and suggest reforms in the food-security architecture.
body: The NFSA 2013 covers roughly two-thirds of the population and PMGKAY provides free grain, so availability and access are largely solved. Yet NFHS-5 records persistent stunting and anaemia: the system is calibrated to calories in cereals in a country whose deficiency is now protein and micronutrient.
Why nutrition lags food security
• Basket design: an eﬀicient PDS delivering wheat and rice still delivers a nutritionally inadequate diet; pulses, millets and oil sit outside the entitlement.
• Non-food determinants: sanitation, safe water, maternal health and birth spacing drive stunting as much as intake does.
• Intra-household distribution: women and adolescent girls eat last and least; anaemia persists across income classes.
• Chain losses: cover-and-plinth storage and multiple handling points cause quality loss.
• Affordability of diversity: a nutritionally adequate diet costs several times the cereal-only diet, so relative prices bind, not absolute income.

CONCLUSION Diversify the basket toward millets and pulses; scale fortification; converge Poshan 2.0 and PM POSHAN with WASH; decentralise procurement; and protect migrants through One Nation One Ration Card. The food chain must be judged by nutrition delivered per rupee, not grain moved per tonne.
topics.draw: Funnel — production → procurement → storage → distribution → intake → absorption. Mark where each stage leaks: transport cost, cover-and-plinth loss, cereal-only basket, WASH-driven malabsorption.
bank: Hidden hunger
Biofortified varieties (zinc wheat, iron pearl millet) put nutrition into the seed rather than into the ration card.
Global Hunger Index critique
India contests the methodology; the defensible domestic metric is NFHS stunting and anaemia trends.
Cash versus kind
Cash assumes functioning markets; in remote and price-volatile areas in-kind provision remains protective.
Climate risk
Heat stress lowers grain protein and zinc content — climate change is a nutrition threat, not only a yield threat.
Millets / Shree Anna
Millets solve calorie, water and micronutrient objectives jointly, but need processing and taste-recovery investment.
Urban food insecurity
Migrants outside their ration domicile are the largest excluded group — portability is the fix that exists on paper.

topics.q: “Inclusive growth should be the focus rather than mere GDP growth in India.” Do you agree? Give reasons in support of your arguments.
body: India is the fastest-growing major economy, yet growth is services-led, capital-intensive and regionally uneven. GDP measures the economy’s size; inclusive growth measures whether size converts into capability, participation and security.
Limits of a GDP-centric focus
• Distribution is invisible: high growth can coexist with widening wealth concentration.
• Human development lags: India’s HDI rank remains far below its GDP rank; public health spending stays near 2% of GDP against the 2.5% policy goal.

• Employment quality: capital- and skill-intensive growth generates output faster than jobs — manufacturing employment has plateaued at 11-12% and agriculture’s share has been rising since 2019: structural retrogression.
• Gender and region: urban female participation is near 25%, and inter-State divergence widens.
• Ecological cost: groundwater depletion and air pollution are unpriced deductions from output.
Why inclusion is also the growth strategy

• Health, learning and skills raise output per worker; a broad consumer base sustains demand; welfare foundations buffer crises, as free foodgrain did during COVID-19. It is constitutionally anchored in the Directive Principles.
CONCLUSION  Growth and inclusion are sequential, not alternative — growth finances inclusion, inclusion sustains growth. The measure of success is earnings per worker, not the aggregate growth rate.
topics.draw: Hub-and-spoke: ‘Inclusive growth’ at the centre with eight spokes — employment (MGNREGS), agriculture (PM-KISAN, FPO), financial (PMJDY, JAM), human capital (NEP), health (PM-JAY), women (Lakhpati Didi), regional (Aspirational Districts), digital (DPI).
bank: Beyond-GDP measures
Multidimensional Poverty Index, HDI and green accounting supply what a single output number cannot.
Poverty decline
Multidimensional poverty has fallen sharply — credit this while noting it measures deprivation, not mobility.
Fiscal trade-off
Consolidation achieved by cutting capex, health and education is arithmetic, not consolidation.
Regional inequality
The 16th Finance Commission’s income-distance weight and City Economic Regions pull in opposite directions.
Jobless growth debate
The problem is not open unemployment but low earnings — an economy that cannot absorb labour productively.
Viksit Bharat 2047
Reaching high-income status requires raising the bottom of the distribution; growth alone is arithmetically insuﬀicient.

topics.t: The Platform Economy and Its Regulation
topics.q: “Platform-based digital economies are reshaping traditional markets.” Examine the regulatory issues they pose and suggest reforms.
body: Platforms intermediate transactions across e-commerce, ride-hailing, delivery and fintech, lowering search and transaction costs at scale. Gig and platform work is projected at 2.35 crore workers by 2029-30 (NITI Aayog), and the Code on Social Security gives them statutory recognition for the first time.
Regulatory issues
• Competition: network effects and deep discounting entrench dominance; self-preferencing forecloses rivals, and ex-post CCI action arrives after the market has tipped.
• Data asymmetry: behavioural data gives platforms market intelligence unavailable to the sellers who depend on them.
• Algorithmic opacity: surge pricing, ranking and deactivation are unexplained and uncontestable.
• Labour: tight algorithmic control without employer obligations — de facto employment without rights; multihoming makes benefits non-portable.
• Consumer harm: dark patterns, fake reviews and weak grievance redress.

CONCLUSION Move from reactive probes to ex-ante rules for designated gatekeepers; operationalise aggregator contributions under the Code on Social Security with e-Shram-seeded portability; mandate pay and deactivation transparency; enforce purpose limitation under the DPDP Act 2023; and scale ONDC so open protocols restore price-discovery transparency. Regulation must protect competition and workers without extinguishing the eﬀiciency that made platforms useful.
topics.draw: Hub-and-spoke: PLATFORM at the centre; inward spokes (e-commerce, ride-hailing, fintech, gig services); downward arrows split into ‘positive — lower transaction cost, wider access’ and ‘regulatory — competition, data, labour, consumer’.
bank: Digital Competition Bill
An ex-ante gatekeeper regime borrows from the EU DMA; the risk is over-inclusion of Indian start-ups.
State legislation
Rajasthan and Karnataka gig-worker welfare Acts show State-level boards will fragment unless a national ledger exists.
ONDC critique
Open protocols solve discovery, not logistics and trust — unbundling needs a fulfilment layer to work.
Taxation
Equalisation levy, GST on aggregators and permanent-establishment questions determine where platform value is taxed.
MSME impact
Platforms expand market reach for small sellers while compressing their margin — net effect depends on take rates.
AI pricing
Algorithmic collusion without communication is the emerging competition-law frontier the CCI is not yet equipped for.

topics.q: Distinguish genome editing from transgenic modification. Discuss its applications in climate-resilient agriculture and the biosafety and regulatory concerns it raises in India.
body: Transgenic modification inserts DNA from an unrelated organism. Genome editing (SDN-1, SDN-2) uses CRISPR-Cas for targeted edits within the plant’s own genome without foreign DNA — an outcome conventional breeding could have produced, only faster.
Why the distinction carries regulatory weight
• Because no foreign DNA persists, MoEFCC exempted SDN-1 and SDN-2 from the transgenic approval process, leaving GEAC oversight for SDN-3.

• India’s first genome-edited rice — DRR Dhan 100 (Kamala), edited at a cytokinin oxidase gene for a fifth higher yield and earlier maturity, and Pusa DST Rice 1 for salinity tolerance — came through this route.
Applications and concerns

• Applications: strongest where traits are polygenic and slow to breed — drought, salinity and heat tolerance, disease resistance, nutritional enhancement. Earlier maturity also cuts irrigation and residue burning.

• Concerns: off-target edits and absent long-term data; seed-sector concentration and farmers’ rights under the PPVFR Act 2001; no labelling for consumer choice; and whether ICAR retains publicly bred varieties.

CONCLUSION Published trial data, post-release monitoring, public germplasm ownership and clear liability rules. Genome editing offers the biotechnology dividend without the transgenic controversy — provided regulatory trust is built before the trait, not after.
topics.draw: Two chromosomes side by side — transgenic (foreign gene inserted, shaded block) versus edited (cut mark within own sequence, no foreign block). Label ‘SDN-1/2 exempt → ICAR route’ and ‘SDN-3 → GEAC’.
bank: Bt brinjal / GM mustard
Judicial and political contestation shows public trust, not science, is the binding constraint on transgenics.
Farmers' rights
Section 39 of the PPVFR Act protects seed saving — editing must not be used to build a technological seed lock.
Trade / labelling
EU treats edited crops restrictively; export markets may demand segregation India has not built.
Gene drives / health
The same tools apply to vector control and sickle-cell therapy — the biosafety frame must be trait-specific.
Regulatory reform
A single science-based biotechnology regulator with statutory independence resolves the GEAC credibility problem.
Public funding
Editing is cheap enough for public institutions — this is the first biotech where India need not license the platform.

topics.q: What are the principal pillars of the BBNJ Agreement? Discuss its significance for India’s interests in marine biodiversity beyond national jurisdiction.
body: The BBNJ Agreement — Biodiversity Beyond National Jurisdiction — is the third UNCLOS implementing agreement, governing the high seas and deep seabed — two-thirds of the ocean, until now ungoverned for conservation. It entered into force in January 2026.
The four pillars
• Marine genetic resources: equitable benefit-sharing including digital sequence information — the central North– South bargain.
• Area-based management tools: including high-seas marine protected areas, which no instrument previously allowed.
• Environmental impact assessment: for activities beyond national jurisdiction.
• Capacity building and marine technology transfer to developing States.
Significance for India
• India has a large EEZ, a deep-sea mining contract in the Central Indian Ocean Basin and the Deep Ocean Mission, so sits on both sides — claimant to benefit-sharing and actor the EIA regime governs.
• High-seas protected areas may constrain fishing and seabed access, but a rules-based ocean order protects India against unilateral exclusion by stronger powers.

CONCLUSION Ratify and legislate; strengthen marine science so India shares benefits as a contributor; coordinate with the Indian Ocean Rim and G-77. BBNJ closes the last governance gap in the global commons — the test is whether benefit-sharing proves real or declaratory.
topics.draw: Four boxes under one header ‘BBNJ (3rd UNCLOS implementing agreement, in force Jan 2026)’ — MGR + DSI, area-based tools/MPAs, EIA, capacity & technology transfer. Below: India = claimant + actor.
bank: Blue economy
India’s blue-economy strategy needs BBNJ compliance built in, or deep-sea projects will face later legal challenge.
Deep-sea mining
ISA’s Mining Code and BBNJ EIA must be reconciled; India’s CIOB contract sits precisely at that seam.
Climate link
The ocean absorbs a large share of excess heat and carbon — high-seas protection is climate policy by another name.
Fisheries
Illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing on the high seas depletes stocks that enter India’s EEZ — enforcement is the gap.
Technology transfer
The pillar most likely to under-deliver; India should press for measurable, time-bound obligations.
Comparison
BBNJ is to the ocean what the Nagoya Protocol is to terrestrial genetic resources — same bargain, weaker enforcement.

topics.t: Quantum Computing and the National Quantum Mission
topics.q: What is quantum computing? Discuss the objectives of India’s National Quantum Mission and the security implications of quantum technologies.
body: Quantum computing uses superposition and entanglement so states scale exponentially with qubits, making factoring, optimisation and molecular simulation tractable. The National Quantum Mission (₹6,003 crore, 2023-31) funds four hubs — computing, communication, sensing and materials.
Applications
• Computing: drug and materials discovery, logistics and grid optimisation.
• Communication: Quantum Key Distribution distributes a key such that interception is detected — informationtheoretic security.
• Sensing: gravimetry, GNSS-free navigation, submarine and underground detection — of defence value.
Security implications
• The break: a large enough quantum computer breaks public-key cryptography underlying banking, defence and government; ‘harvest now, decrypt later’ means data stolen today is already at risk.

• QKD’s limits: it protects the key exchange, not the data or endpoints; photon loss limits distance, so long links need trusted-node relays, each a classical vulnerability; and it cannot authenticate.
• The real requirement: post-quantum cryptography — a software migration that scales where QKD cannot.

CONCLUSION Publish a national PQC migration roadmap with a cryptographic bill of materials; use QKD selectively; build indigenous hardware so the trust anchor is not imported. The quantum threat arrives before the quantum computer does.
topics.draw: Timeline arrow — ‘data stolen today’ → ‘stored’ → ‘decrypted when CRQC arrives’. Below, two columns: QKD (hardware, key exchange only, distance-limited) vs PQC (software, scales, authenticates).
bank: Strategic autonomy
Cryptographic sovereignty means owning the algorithm and the hardware — an imported trust anchor is not sovereign.
Global race
NIST’s standardised PQC algorithms give a migration baseline; India’s contribution should be implementation and audit capacity.
Talent
Quantum is talent-bound, not capital-bound; hub-based fellowships and retention matter more than machine procurement.
Start-ups / industry
QNu Labs and similar firms show the ecosystem exists; public procurement is the missing demand certainty.
Satellite QKD
Space-based links avoid trusted-node relays — a natural ISRO–NQM convergence.
Sensing dividend
Quantum sensing is nearer to deployment than computing and has immediate ISR and mineral-exploration value.

topics.q: Mangroves are among the most cost-effective forms of coastal protection. Examine their ecological and economic value and the pressures they face.
body: Mangroves are salt-tolerant intertidal forests between land and sea. India has close to 5,000 sq km, roughly 3% of global cover, with the Sundarbans alone over 40% of the Indian total.
Ecological and economic value
• Coastal defence: they attenuate storm surge and wave energy — the most cost-effective coastal defence available, and the only one that grows.
• Shoreline stability: root systems trap sediment, countering erosion and saline ingress.
• Blue carbon: sequestration in waterlogged sediment at several times the rate of terrestrial forest; because the sediment is anaerobic the carbon stays stored for centuries.
• Livelihoods: nursery habitat for coastal fish and prawn stocks, so fishery income depends on them; also honey and ecotourism.
Pressures

• Conversion to aquaculture, salt pans and ports; upstream dams cutting freshwater and sediment, so deltas cannot keep pace with sea-level rise; pollution; and cyclone damage compounded by the erosion mangrove loss itself causes — a feedback loop.

CONCLUSION Enforce Coastal Regulation Zone protection; scale MISHTI with hydrology-first restoration rather than plantation drives; assign community management rights; use blue-carbon crediting to finance conservation. Mangroves are infrastructure — the cheapest sea wall India owns.
topics.draw: Cross-section of a coast — sea, mangrove belt, village. Arrows: storm surge attenuated, sediment trapped, carbon stored in sediment, fish nursery. Dashed arrows of pressure: aquaculture, port, upstream dam cutting freshwater.
bank: Sundarbans specifics
A transboundary delta with India and Bangladesh, tiger habitat and the highest human exposure — governance is bilateral.
Blue carbon finance
Permanence and community benefit-sharing are the two credibility tests any mangrove credit must pass.
Restoration failures
Monoculture plantation on unsuitable hydrology has high mortality — restore the tidal regime before planting.
Ramsar / MPA
Designation gives prestige but little domestic enforcement power unless backed by notified State rules.
Disaster link
Post-cyclone damage assessments consistently show lower losses behind intact mangrove belts — quantify and publish this.
Aquaculture trade-off
Shrimp exports earn foreign exchange while destroying the nursery that sustains capture fishery — price the externality.

topics.q: What is the Space Docking Experiment (SpaDeX)? Explain why docking capability is technologically demanding and what it unlocks for India’s space programme.
body: SpaDeX placed two small satellites in orbit on PSLV-C60 in December 2024 and, on 16 January 2025, docked them autonomously — making India the fourth country with docking capability. It then transferred power between the craft and undocked successfully.
Why docking is technologically demanding
• It requires millimetre-level control at orbital velocity between two independently moving bodies.

• Elements: a rendezvous sequence using differential orbit-raising; sensors — laser range finder, rendezvous camera, proximity sensor — working against a moving Earth; an androgynous mechanism tolerant of misalignment; autonomous guidance; and control of the combined body after capture, when mass properties change instantly.
What the capability unlocks
• Assembly of the Bharatiya Antariksh Station (2035), which cannot be launched in one piece.
• The Chandrayaan-4 lunar sample return, needing orbital transfer between modules.
• Crew and cargo transfer; on-orbit refuelling and satellite life extension; and active debris removal — docking with a tumbling target.

CONCLUSION Standardise the docking interface across Indian and commercial spacecraft; extend it to non-cooperative targets; and open servicing missions to private operators through IN-SPACe. Docking converts a launch programme into a space programme — nothing permanent can be built in orbit without it.
topics.draw: Sequence of boxes — differential orbit raising → far-range rendezvous → proximity sensors → capture / hard dock → combined-body control → power and crew transfer.
bank: Human spaceflight
Gaganyaan to BAS 2035 to a crewed lunar landing by 2040 all presuppose rendezvous and docking.
Commercial space
On-orbit servicing is a market, not just a capability — IN-SPACe authorisation makes it investable.
Space debris
Active debris removal is docking with a tumbling target — technically harder and legally unsettled on liability.
Strategic
Rendezvous and proximity operations are dual-use; transparency measures matter for space-security stability.
Cost frugality
SpaDeX used two 220 kg satellites on an existing PSLV — capability demonstrated at a fraction of comparable cost.
Indigenous tech
Bharatiya Docking System is an indigenous androgynous design, so the interface standard itself is Indian-owned.

topics.q: What are directed energy weapons? Examine their operational advantages and the limitations that constrain their deployment in the Indian context.
body: Directed energy weapons deliver concentrated electromagnetic energy — laser, microwave or particle beams — not kinetic mass.
India demonstrated a 30 kW laser (Mk-II(A), ‘Sahastra Shakti’) in 2025.
Operational advantages
• Cost exchange: a shot costs hundreds of rupees against a missile costing crores — decisive against swarms that exhaust magazine depth.
• Speed and precision: engagement at light speed with no lead computation; graduated effects from dazzle to burnthrough, without fragmentation over cities.
• Logistics: a magazine limited by power, not resupply.
Limitations
• Atmospheric: fog, dust, rain and thermal blooming scatter the beam — it fails in exactly the weather an adversary will choose.
• Power and thermal: high electrical draw and heat rejection limit sustained mobile operation.
• Dwell time: the beam must hold one aim point for seconds, so swarms can exceed the engagement rate.
• Countermeasures and law: ablative coatings raise required power; CCW Protocol IV bans blinding lasers.

CONCLUSION Treat DEW as one layer of mixed air defence, scale thermal management, and transfer technology to industry for serial production. Directed energy changes the economics of defence, not the requirement for layered defence.
topics.draw: Cost-exchange bar chart, hand-drawn: attacker’s drone (low bar) versus interceptor missile (tall bar) versus DEW shot (near-zero bar). Beside it, a limitation column: weather, power, dwell time, saturation.
bank: Counter-UAS link
DEW is the ‘hard-kill’ band of the layered counter-drone architecture — always place it inside that stack.
Naval application
Shipborne DEW has power and cooling available from the platform — the most deployable near-term use case.
Space / ASAT
Ground-based lasers can dazzle satellite optics without debris — a reversible counterspace option with escalation questions.
High-power microwave
HPM defeats swarms and electronics area-wide, complementing lasers which are single-target.
Indigenisation
Beam directors, optics and thermal management are the import-dependent subsystems, not the laser source.
Ethics / law
Autonomy in engagement decisions raises the same accountability question as lethal autonomous weapon systems.

topics.q: Examine the sources and impacts of marine oil pollution in India’s waters and evaluate the adequacy of the institutional response.
body: India’s coast sits astride one of the world’s densest tanker routes; the MSC ELSA 3 sinking off Kerala (May 2025) showed how fast a shipping casualty becomes a livelihood emergency.
Sources and impacts

• Sources: accidental — collision, grounding, rig failure; operational — tank washing and bilge discharge, small individually but larger cumulatively; and land-based refinery effluent and urban runoff, largest by volume.
• Ecological: a surface film blocks light and gas exchange, killing plankton; oil smothers mangrove roots and coral; aromatics persist in sediment for years.
• Livelihood: fishing bans, catch rejection, tourism loss and port shutdown — costs fall on the least insured.
The institutional response
• The Indian Coast Guard coordinates under the National Oil Spill Disaster Contingency Plan; India is party to MARPOL, OPRC and the Civil Liability Convention.
• Gaps: State plans are untested; equipment sits in a few ports; hazardous cargo spills fall outside a plan written for oil; and fisher compensation is slow.

CONCLUSION Pre-position tier-wise equipment, rehearse State and port plans, map sensitive shorelines, and fast-track fisher compensation. Spill response is judged in hours — preparedness must be local even when authority is central.
topics.draw: Coastal cross-section — ship → slick → arrows to mangrove, coral, fishery, beach/tourism. Side ladder: Tier 1 (port) → Tier 2 (regional ICG) → Tier 3 (national/international assistance).
bank: Ship recycling
Alang’s yards are a chronic oil and hazardous-waste source — the Hong Kong Convention is the governing instrument.
Blue economy
Fisheries and coastal tourism are the exposed assets; marine spatial planning should treat spill risk as a zoning input.
Climate / Arctic
New shipping routes and heavier traﬀic raise spill probability in ecologically slow-recovering waters.
Technology
Bioremediation using indigenous oil-degrading consortia (NIOT/TERI Oilzapper) suits tropical shorelines better than dispersants.
Liability regime
India’s accession to the HNS Convention would close the hazardous-cargo compensation gap ELSA 3 exposed.
Disaster classification
A marine spill is not a notified disaster, so SDRF funds are not automatically available to coastal States.

topics.q: Female labour force participation in India has risen in recent years, yet remains low relative to educational attainment. Examine the reasons for this divergence and the measures needed to sustain participation.
body: FLFP rose from about 23% in 2017-18 to over 40% by 2023-24, yet remains low relative to women’s education and below comparable economies. The rise is compositionally weak — largely rural, self-employed and unpaid family work, with urban FLFP still near 25%.
Why attainment has not converted into participation
• The U-shaped relationship: as household incomes rise, women withdraw from distress work before white-collar opportunities open, so education first reduces measured participation.
• Unpaid care work: among the highest gender gaps in the world — an unpriced constraint no wage can offset.
• Enabling conditions: deficits in safe transport, hostels and childcare bind independently of demand.
• Occupational segregation: concentration in a narrow band of low-wage sectors compresses the return to education.
• Measurement: subsistence and home-based work is undercounted, so the statistic understates work while accurately reporting paid work.

CONCLUSION Expand labour-intensive manufacturing and formal services where women’s employment elasticity is highest; universalise crèches under the Code on Social Security; enforce equal-remuneration and safety provisions of the Labour Codes; support SHG enterprise; and improve time-use surveys. Participation will not be sustained by opportunity alone until the care burden is socialised.
topics.draw: U-shaped curve — household income on the x-axis, FLFP on the y-axis, with India marked at the trough. Annotate the three levers that flatten the left arm: care infrastructure, safe mobility, formal-sector demand.
bank: Agriculture feminisation
Male out-migration has raised women’s field role without raising their titles, credit access or decision rights.
Gig / platform work
Flexible hours suit care constraints but offer no maternity cover — portability must include maternity benefit.
Demographic dividend
The dividend is arithmetically unreachable at current FLFP — this is a growth argument, not only an equity one.
Global comparison
Bangladesh’s garment sector shows a single labour-intensive export industry can move national FLFP by itself.
Safety / law
PoSH Act compliance and public transport safety determine whether jobs that exist are actually takeable.
Skilling
Skill India enrolment is high but placement is low for women — the gap is mobility and hostels, not training. PART II ◆ 27 FIFTEEN-MARK TOPICS

topics.t: Small Modular Reactors and India's Nuclear Strategy
topics.q: The SHANTI Act, 2025 removes the legal and financial constraints on nuclear expansion. Examine India’s nuclear strategy after the Act, and the place of SMRs within it.
body: Nuclear supplies firm, low-carbon baseload renewables and current storage cannot replace. India has 8-9 GW against a 100 GW by 2047 goal; the binding constraints were legal and financial. The SHANTI Act (22 December 2025) removes both.
What the Act changes
• Ends the state monopoly, allowing private ownership and operation for the first time since the Atomic Energy Act 1962.
• Removes the operator’s right of recourse against suppliers — old Section 17(b), CLNDA 2010, which stalled Jaitapur — and deletes Section 46.
• Caps operator liability at ₹100-3,000 crore by plant size and gives the AERB statutory backing.
Two technology pathways
• PFBR at Kalpakkam: Stage 2 of the three-stage programme — it breeds more fuel than it consumes, bridging to Stage 3 thorium, India’s long-term resource logic.
• SMRs, including Bharat Small Reactors: factory-built, 30-300 MW, deployable on retiring coal sites using existing grid and land, with passive safety and lower capital at risk.
• PFBR answers fuel security; SMRs answer deployment speed.
What remains unresolved
• The cap is small against real accident cost; disaster indemnity blunts the safety incentive; victims lose the Section 46 route.
• The AERB’s board is selected by a committee of the Atomic Energy Commission, so independence remains formal, not structural; and SMR economics need serial production that does not yet exist.

CONCLUSION Give the AERB separate appointment and its own budget; settle spent-fuel management; standardise SMR designs to capture factory economics. The law has removed the commercial obstacle; safe scale-up now depends on a regulator able to say no to the government that appoints it.
topics.draw: One fork, two labels: SHANTI Act 2025 (private entry, recourse removed, AERB statutory) → PFBR (Stage 2, breeds fuel, leads to thorium) and SMR/BSR (factory-built, coal sites). Caption: fuel security versus deployment speed.
bank: Energy transition
Baseload firmness is the argument — 500 GW non-fossil by 2030 needs a non-weather-dependent core.
Three-stage programme
Thorium is the strategic endpoint; without Stage 2 breeding, Stage 3 remains a laboratory proposition.
Foreign investment
Recourse removal is aimed squarely at Westinghouse, EDF and Rosatom — the test is a signed contract, not a signed Act.
Just transition
SMRs on retiring coal sites retain the workforce, grid and land — the cheapest politically acceptable siting available.
Safety governance
A regulator appointed by the promoter is the structural flaw the Act left untouched — compare NRC-type independence.
Non-proliferation
Private operation raises material-accounting and IAEA safeguards questions that domestic law must answer explicitly.

topics.t: Public--Private Partnerships and the Allocation of Risk
topics.q: A PPP creates value only when each risk is borne by the party best able to control or absorb it. Critically examine India’s PPP experience and suggest reforms.
body: A PPP creates value only when each risk is borne by the party best able to control or absorb it. Transfer alone is not eﬀiciency: a risk pushed onto a party that cannot manage it returns to the state as renegotiation, default or a stranded asset.
Mapping the four risks
• Construction risk: cost and time overruns belong with the private partner, who controls execution.
• Demand risk: largely exogenous to the concessionaire; assigning it wholly to the private side produced the BOT-era toll-road distress, which is why the Hybrid Annuity Model splits it.
• Financial risk: aggravated by tenor mismatch, since banks lend short against thirty-year assets.
• Regulatory and land risk: clearances, right of way, tariff orders — controlled by the state, and it should stay there.
Why Indian PPPs failed
• Aggressive bidding on optimistic traﬀic forecasts; land not acquired before award; no orderly renegotiation route, so disputes ended in court.

• The Kelkar Committee’s diagnosis — renegotiation is inevitable, so it must be institutionalised rather than criminalised — drove the shift to HAM, the InvIT and REIT monetisation route, and dispute-resolution boards.
Reforms
• Complete land and clearances before award; use HAM or availability payments where demand is genuinely uncertain; deepen bond and InvIT finance to match asset tenor.
• Create independent sectoral regulators and a standing renegotiation framework; publish a fiscal-risk statement so contingent liabilities are visible.
CONCLUSION The test of a PPP is not how much risk was transferred but whether it was transferred to someone who could bear it.
topics.draw: Two-by-two matrix — rows ‘private controls it’ / ‘neither controls it’. Cells: Construction (private), Demand (share — HAM), Financial (private + market), Regulatory and land (stays public).
bank: Asset monetisation
The National Monetisation Pipeline transfers operating, not construction, risk — a different and easier proposition.
Municipal PPPs
Urban local bodies lack the contracting capacity to be a competent counterparty — capacity is the binding constraint.
Social-sector PPPs
In health and education, quality is unobservable and outcomes are contested, so output-based contracting fails.
Fiscal risk
Guarantees and annuities are off-budget borrowing in substance — the FRBM disclosure must capture them.
Dispute resolution
Arbitration awards stuck in appeal freeze capital; the Vivad se Vishwas route showed settlement releases more than litigation recovers.
Viability gap funding
VGF is justified by externality, not by low returns — otherwise it becomes a subsidy for weak projects.

topics.t: Intelligence Coordination in a Federal Democracy
topics.q: Intelligence coordination converts fragmented information into a common operational picture. Examine the structural obstacles to it in India and suggest reforms.
body: Intelligence coordination converts fragmented information into a common operational picture. In India this is structurally hard: police and public order are State subjects while the threats are transnational, so the collector, the analyst and the actor sit in different governments.
The structural obstacles
• Overlapping mandates: IB, R&AW, NIA, NTRO, State special branches and service directorates, with no single statutory authority to task them.
• Incentives against sharing: information is hoarded because sharing risks exposing sources and dilutes institutional credit.
• Technical fragmentation: legacy systems are not interoperable, and much sharing is personality-driven rather than protocol-driven.
• Coordination without command: the Multi-Agency Centre coordinates but cannot direct; and a fusion centre is only as good as the weakest branch feeding it.
The accountability deficit
• Indian agencies operate without a statutory charter — no legislative oversight, no defined mandate limiting collection, no independent complaints mechanism.
• This is not only a civil-liberties concern: it also weakens the agencies, leaving budgets, tenure and inter-agency authority to convention rather than law.
Reforms
• Enact a statutory charter defining mandate, powers and limits, with a parliamentary oversight committee holding security clearance.
• Strengthen NATGRID and MAC–SMAC with mandatory contribution and audited access; adopt a federated architecture so States retain custody while enabling search.
• Institutionalise joint training and cross-posting, and build State fusion capacity so federalism becomes a source of granularity, not a gap.
CONCLUSION Coordination is a question of authority and trust before it is a question of technology — a network cannot fuse what its members have no duty to share.
topics.draw: Hub with spokes — MAC at the centre, IB / R&AW / NTRO / NIA / State special branches around it. Draw the spokes as dashed lines and label ‘coordination without command’; add NATGRID as a separate data layer beneath.
bank: 26/11 lessons
MAC, NATGRID, NIA and NSG hubs were all post-26/11 — the reform was structural but stopped short of statutory.
Second ARC
Recommended a National Counter Terrorism Centre; federal objections over State policing powers stalled it.
Privacy / Puttaswamy
Proportionality and judicial authorisation are constitutional requirements surveillance law has not yet met.
Technical intelligence
OSINT, financial and cyber intelligence now outweigh HUMINT in volume — analytic capacity is the scarce resource.
Border management
Multiple forces on one border need a single intelligence picture; the Madhukar Gupta report’s ‘one border, one force’ logic applies.
Comparative
The US DNI and UK JIC show a statutory coordinator with budgetary authority is what converts coordination into command.

topics.q: India processes only a small share of its produce despite being a leading producer. Examine the upstream and downstream constraints on food processing and suggest reforms.
body: Food processing links agriculture to industry. India leads the world in milk and is second in fruits and vegetables, yet processes only about 10% of produce against 40-80% in comparable economies — the gap where farm income and non-farm employment are lost.
Upstream requirements
• Raw material of processing grade: varieties with the right solids content and uniform maturity, which needs research aimed at processors, not only at yield.
• Aggregation: FPOs and contract farming to secure assured volume from fragmented holdings.

• Post-harvest infrastructure: pack houses, pre-cooling, ripening chambers, reefer transport and cold storage — plus cluster-level primary processing (grading, sorting, drying) that retains value locally.
Downstream requirements
• FSSAI safety and traceability compliance and export certification, where non-tariff barriers bind.
• Cold retail, packaging, branding and shelf-life technology; and market access through modern retail, e-commerce and ONDC.
Why value addition stays low
• Fragmented, seasonal supply raises procurement cost and leaves capacity idle, destroying unit economics.
• The cold chain is concentrated in potato and dairy — cold storage without pack houses and reefers does not prevent loss.

• Regulatory friction persists — direct-purchase restrictions, multiple licences, GST disputes; finance is workingcapital-intensive against seasonal cash flow; and preference for fresh produce limits demand.

CONCLUSION PMKSY cold-chain components, PLI for food processing, PM Formalisation of Micro Food Processing Enterprises and One District One Product should all be anchored on FPO aggregation rather than standalone units. Value addition is a supply-chain problem before it is a factory problem.
topics.draw: Draw a U: farm → FPO aggregation → pack house, pre-cooling → processing unit → FSSAI, traceability → retail, ONDC, export. Mark the missing link in India at the pack-house and reefer step, not the factory.
bank: Employment
Food processing is the most employment-elastic manufacturing sector and locates near the farm, not in metros.
Millets / Shree Anna
Processing and taste-recovery investment is what converts a production push into consumer demand.
Export competitiveness
Sanitary and phytosanitary rejections, not tariffs, are the binding constraint on agri exports.
Food loss
Post-harvest loss is a supply-side inflation source — reducing it raises availability without raising acreage.
Women's employment
Processing units employ women at high rates — cluster siting near villages is an FLFP instrument.
Mega Food Parks critique
Anchor-unit-led parks failed where farm linkage was absent — aggregation must precede infrastructure.

topics.q: Examine the causes of the rupee’s depreciation and its consequences for the Indian economy. What should the policy response be? The rupee floats, with the RBI smoothing volatility rather than defending a level. Depreciation is the price at which the external account clears — what matters is whether it is orderly and what it does to the real economy.
body: Causes
• External: a strong dollar and tight global financial conditions; higher crude and gold prices widening the import bill; reciprocal tariffs compressing export earnings.
• Capital flows: portfolio outflows respond to interest-differential compression and risk-off episodes, and are far more volatile than trade.
• Structural: a merchandise deficit concentrated in energy, electronics and gold, partly offset by services and remittances; and inflation differentials eroding the real exchange rate.
Consequences
• Adverse: imported inflation through crude, fertiliser, edible oil and electronics; costlier external debt service; dearer capital goods that slow investment.
• Favourable: improved competitiveness for services, textiles and pharmaceuticals, and higher rupee value of remittances.
• The qualification: depreciation helps only where import intensity is low — for assembly-led electronics the gain is neutral.
Policy response
• Short run:   use reserves to smooth volatility, not defend a level; deploy forward and swap operations; keep the inflation anchor credible.

• Medium run: deepen bond and currency-hedging markets; broaden the export basket and destinations; expand rupee settlement; and cut import dependence at genuine chokepoints — energy through renewables, electronics through domestic value addition.
CONCLUSION A currency’s strength is a symptom, not a target — the policy objective is an economy that can absorb depreciation without importing inflation.
topics.draw: Balance-of-payments T-account: outflows (crude, gold, electronics, portfolio outflow) against inflows (services exports, remittances, FDI). Below, two arrows from ‘depreciation’ — ‘imported inflation’ and ‘export competitiveness’ — with a note that import intensity decides which dominates.
bank: Forex reserves
Adequacy is measured in months of imports and short-term debt cover, not in headline dollars.
Impossible trinity
India accepts partial capital mobility and a managed float precisely to retain monetary autonomy.
Internationalisation of rupee
Vostro accounts and local-currency settlement reduce dollar demand at the margin but need convertibility depth.
Inflation targeting
The MPC targets headline CPI, not the exchange rate — pass-through is an input to that decision, not a separate mandate.
External debt
India’s external debt-to-GDP is moderate and largely long-tenor — the vulnerability is roll-over, not stock.
Gold imports
Gold is a savings instrument in India, so import demand rises exactly when confidence falls — financialisation is the structural fix.

topics.q: Crop insurance is intended to stabilise farm income against weather risk. Evaluate the performance of PMFBY and suggest reforms.
body: Crop insurance converts a covariate weather shock into a manageable financial loss. PMFBY does this through uniform farmer premiums — 2% kharif, 1.5% rabi, 5% commercial — with the balance shared by Centre and States, and cover voluntary since 2020.
Achievements
• Among the world’s largest crop-insurance programmes by enrolment, extending cover to non-loanee farmers.
• Technology has cut the worst frictions — YES-TECH remote-sensing yield estimation, WINDS weather stations and the DigiClaim module for direct transfer.
• It protects the credit system as much as the farmer — an insured loss keeps a KCC account from turning nonperforming.
Persistent problems
• Unit of assessment: the unit is a village or block, so a farmer whose field failed while the block did not receives nothing — basis risk is the central grievance.
• Delayed settlement: States’ premium subsidy arrears stall payouts, and a claim received after the next sowing has already failed to serve its purpose.
• Exclusion: tenants and oral lessees cannot prove cultivation; enrolment fell after cover became voluntary and after loan-linked automatic enrolment ended.
• Design: high-risk States face high premiums and several exited; localised perils — hail, inundation, wild animals — fit an area-yield product poorly.

CONCLUSION Move to plot-level assessment using satellite and drone data; enforce a statutory settlement deadline with interest for delay; use AgriStack records so tenants can enrol; expand parametric products for localised perils. Crop insurance succeeds only when the payout arrives before the next sowing decision.
topics.draw: Timeline: sowing → loss event → assessment (area yield vs plot-level) → claim → payout → next sowing. Mark two failure points — ‘basis risk’ at assessment and ‘delay’ between claim and payout.
bank: Climate adaptation
Insurance prices risk; if the premium signals rising climate risk, it becomes an adaptation instrument, not just compensation.
State exits
Bihar, Andhra Pradesh and others built own schemes — a federal design question about premium-sharing burden.
Insurer profitability
Claims ratios vary hugely by year; without reinsurance depth, insurers price in uncertainty and farmers pay for it.
Restructured PMFBY
Cluster-based bidding and a three-year tenure were meant to stabilise insurer participation.
Livestock / horticulture
Allied-sector cover is thin, though these carry the household’s most liquid assets.
Behavioural
Voluntary enrolment falls after good years — exactly the moment reserves are built; nudges and default enrolment matter.
6A. Agricultural Credit Delivery

15 marks ◆ 247 words Q. Institutional agricultural credit has expanded, yet it has not converted into productive investment. Examine why, and suggest what a productive-credit archi- tecture requires. Credit targets and the Kisan Credit Card have expanded formal lending, but aggregate disbursement conceals unequal access and repeated rollover. The mismatch is between credit delivered and investment completed. The nature of the mismatch • Who borrows: tenants, sharecroppers and women lack proof of cultivation, so the actual cultivator is often not the borrower.
• Where it flows:

much ‘agricultural’ credit reaches larger borrowers or funds routine working capital, not productivity-enhancing assets. • Regional unevenness: banking density and cooperative health vary sharply, so credit-deficit regions are productivity- deficit regions. • Product mismatch: collateral-based lending and standard repayment schedules do not match biological cycles; de- layed claims and price shocks turn viable loans into distress. Why the moneylender survives • Informal credit is faster and available at the moment of need — illness, a wedding, a failed sowing. • It reschedules implicitly after a bad harvest where a bank must classify the account as non-performing; it lends against relationships, so tenants can access it; and it finances consumption, which formal agri credit does not cover. • The two are therefore complementary, which is why formal disbursement rises while informal dependence stays flat. Waivers worsen this by damaging repayment culture and making banks cautious about marginal borrowers. CONCLUSION Recognise cultivation through consent-based, appealable records rather than title alone; scale joint liability groups and SHG–bank linkage; use cash-flow assessment and warehouse receipts for working capital and longer tenors for assets; provide consumption lines within formal products; and replace waivers with restructuring. Priority-sector policy should shift its metric from credit pushed to investment completed and income generated. DRAW Two columns — ‘Formal credit’ (rate low, speed slow, collateral required, purpose restricted) against ‘Moneylender’ (rate high, speed immediate, relationship-based, purpose open). Caption: he is displaced by matching his speed, not by undercutting his rate. VARIANT EXPANSION BANK -- six surgical lines to bolt on when the question turns

topics.q: Unregulated transboundary migration has security, demographic and humanitarian dimensions. Examine India’s challenges and evaluate the adequacy of its legal and institutional response.
body: India’s land borders run through settled societies with shared ethnicity and kinship, so movement across them is socially normal even where legally irregular. The policy problem is to separate security risk from livelihood movement.
Drivers and dimensions
• Push and pull: instability and persecution — Myanmar after 2021, Bangladesh’s turmoil — alongside wage differentials pulling labour into Indian towns.
• Demographic and political: altered land-holding and voter composition in border districts of Assam, Tripura and Bengal, converting a migration question into identity conflict.
• Security: infiltration cover for cadres, arms and narcotics; forged documents through local complicity; traﬀicking of women and children.
• Humanitarian: India is not party to the 1951 Refugee Convention and has no refugee law, so status is decided administratively and inconsistently.
The response and its gaps
• The Immigration and Foreigners Act, 2025 consolidates four colonial-era laws, mandating carrier reporting and clarifying entry, stay and removal.
• The Free Movement Regime with Myanmar has been curtailed and border fencing extended — a security gain that cuts across kinship economies the border communities depend on.

• Gaps: riverine and forested stretches are unfencible; multiple forces split responsibility; deportation depends on the other state accepting nationality; and NRC-type exercises show documentary determination of citizenship is fragile.

CONCLUSION  Enact a refugee law distinguishing asylum from illegal entry, with non-refoulement and time-bound determination; use smart fencing where physical fencing is infeasible; issue work permits for regulated circular movement; pursue readmission agreements. Borders are managed by making lawful movement easier than unlawful movement, not by attempting to stop movement altogether.
topics.draw: Three concentric bands — outer ‘border management’ (fence, sensors, forces), middle ‘status determination’ (refugee law, work permits, documents), inner ‘internal enforcement’ (registration, employer verification). Note that each band leaks into the next when the previous one fails.
bank: Section 6A verdict
The Supreme Court upheld the Assam Accord cut-off, settling law but not the administrative burden of proof.
Climate migration
Sea-level rise in the Bengal delta will generate movement no immigration law currently anticipates.
Internal migration link
Inter-State migrants face similar documentation exclusion — One Nation One Ration Card is the portability model.
Myanmar policy
Border stability now depends on which armed actor controls the Myanmar side — a foreign-policy variable, not a policing one.
Human traﬀicking
Migration corridors and traﬀicking routes coincide; victim-centric law enforcement must not treat the traﬀicked as offenders.
Labour economics
Border-district economies absorb migrant labour because Indian workers have exited those wage bands — criminalisation alone will not clear the market.

topics.t: Human Capital and the Demographic Dividend
topics.q: India’s demographic dividend depends on human capital rather than numbers. Examine the deficits in India’s human capital formation and suggest the reforms required.
body: A demographic dividend is not a stock of young people but a stock of productive young people. India’s working-age share peaks through the 2040s, so the dividend has a closing window — and human capital, not labour supply, determines whether it is realised.
The deficits
• Learning, not schooling: enrolment is near universal but foundational literacy and numeracy remain weak, so years of schooling overstate the human capital acquired.
• Health and nutrition:    stunting and anaemia in early childhood permanently lower cognitive attainment; public health spending stays near 2% of GDP against the 2.5% policy goal.
• Skilling mismatch: training is supply-driven and certification-led rather than employer-demand-led, so placement and wage premiums remain low.
• Higher education: research intensity is about 0.65% of GDP with a small private share; faculty vacancies and weak industry linkage limit the innovation return.
• Gender: women’s educational attainment has risen far faster than their labour force participation — the largest single wasted investment in Indian human capital.
What reform requires
• Anchor NEP 2020 implementation on measured foundational outcomes (NIPUN Bharat) rather than inputs, with teacher capacity as the binding constraint.
• Converge Poshan 2.0, PM POSHAN and WASH so the first thousand days are protected — the highest-return humancapital investment available.
• Shift skilling to apprenticeship-led, employer-co-funded models with credit transfer between vocational and academic streams.
• Fund translational research through ANRF with industry co-investment, and expand care infrastructure so women’s attainment converts into employment.
